title: Bangladesh: National GBV Cluster Update #1 - Chattogram Division: Flash Flood & Landslides
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

Due to the well-marked low persisting over Madhya Pradesh & adjoining Uttar Pradesh in India, and the strong monsoon active over the North Bay, rainfall is forecasted across the Sylhet, Mymensingh, and Chattogram divisions of Bangladesh from 5–12 July 2026. The situation may be further aggravated by heavy rainfall in the adjoining upstream areas of Meghalaya, Assam, the Barak Basin, and Tripura in India. The above-normal rainfall may trigger rapid inundation and flooding in different places of the Sylhet and Chattogram Divisions The Needs Assessment Working Group (NAWG) issued the Anticipatory Impact Analysis on 08th July, followed by the first flash update#1 on 9th July 2026 and Flash Update#2. The latest update shows the rainfall has caused rising water levels and flooding in several locations across the Chattogram Hill Tracts. Landslides have been reported in Bandarban and Cox’s Bazar districts. The severely affected areas are Chattogram, CoxS Bazar, Sunamganj, Khagrachhari, Moulvibazar, Sylhet, Feni, Rangamati, Bandarban, and Cumilla.

The latest update is that 1.07 million people are affected in 10 districts. 36,500 people are displaced and have taken shelter in 1,7000 shelters. There are 217,259 girls, 317,817 women, and 12,266 persons with disabilities reported to have been impacted by the flash flood and landslides.

title: UNHCR Ecuador: Operational Update N.6 | June 2026
content:
Operational context

Ecuador’s operational environment continues to be shaped by a combination of security, socioeconomic, and community-level challenges that affect well-being, access to services, and opportunities for inclusion. In response to evolving challenges, national authorities have continued implementing measures aimed at strengthening public safety, maintaining stability, and reinforcing institutional responses. In this context, UNHCR works closely with national and local authorities, partners, and communities to support refugees, asylum-seekers, displaced populations, and host communities, facilitating access to protection, essential services, and opportunities for inclusion.

During the first months of 2026, several provinces, particularly in coastal and border areas, continued to face security challenges that affected communities and humanitarian service delivery. In some locations, disruptions to public life due to violent incidents highlighted the importance of maintaining access to information, protection services, and community support mechanisms, particularly for people in vulnerable situations.

In northern and border provinces, including Esmeraldas and Sucumbíos, evolving local protection dynamics continue to influence the operational environment. These conditions may affect mobility, access to services, and community well-being, including exacerbated impacts to Indigenous populations and other groups with specific needs.

Continued engagement with communities and local institutions remains essential to ensuring access to assistance, information, and support.

Alongside these developments, Ecuador continues to experience economic pressures linked to rising living costs. These challenges particularly affect low-income households, including refugees, asylum-seekers, and host communities, and may limit access to basic services, livelihoods, and opportunities for socioeconomic inclusion. Humanitarian operations continue in this context, with UNHCR in Ecuador adapting their approaches to ensure the safe and effective delivery of assistance. The operation continues to monitor developments, strengthen coordination with national and local authorities and partners, and adapt its activities to maintain access to communities and support field operations across affected areas.

UNHCR remains present across the country, supporting refugees, asylum-seekers, displaced populations, and host communities through protection services, legal assistance, community-based interventions, and initiatives that promote inclusion and self-reliance. These efforts help people access rights, essential services, and opportunities to rebuild their lives in the country.

title: UNICEF Venezuela Humanitarian Situation Report No.6 (Earthquake Response), 21–24 July 2026
content:
Highlights

  • One month after two powerful earthquakes struck Venezuela’s north-central coast, children and families continue to face the lasting impacts of displacement, damaged infrastructure and disruption to essential services.
  • UNICEF has provided hygiene supplies to 8,906 people and integrated WASH services to 3,237 people; enabled 21,000 people to access primary health care, including 16,006 people vaccinated; and reached 5,282 children and women with nutrition services. UNICEF also supported more than 4,000 children, adolescents and caregivers with child protection services, including 205 referrals for specialized care, while strengthening education support.
  • Through an integrated humanitarian response, UNICEF aims to reach 470,000 people, including 169,000 children, with life-saving assistance and early recovery support. In addition to its US$137.6 million HAC appeal, UNICEF requires an additional US$65.7 million to sustain critical interventions and support the implementation of the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan Addendum.

title: WHO Situation Report No. 2: Flash Floods in Eastern Afghanistan (July 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

Heavy rainfall and flash floods impacted the eastern, southeastern, and central regions of Afghanistan between 20 and 25 July 2026, causing widespread humanitarian consequences across multiple provinces. The floods affected communities across eastern Afghanistan, including Nuristan, Nangarhar, and Laghman provinces; southeastern Afghanistan, including Paktika, Paktia, Khost, and Ghazni provinces; and the central region, including Kabul, Kapisa, Panjshir, Parwan, Logar, and Maidan Wardak provinces. The disaster resulted in loss of life, injuries, displacement of families, and extensive damage to homes, public facilities, and community infrastructure.

In the eastern region, the most severe impacts were reported in Parun City of Nuristan Province, along with several affected areas of Nangarhar and Laghman provinces. The floods caused significant damage to homes, livelihoods, and public infrastructure, leaving affected communities in urgent need of humanitarian support and recovery assistance.

Across the southeastern region, flash floods caused widespread damage to homes, agricultural land, roads, water supply systems, and other critical infrastructure in Paktika, Paktia, Khost, and Ghazni provinces, disrupting livelihoods and access to essential services for affected communities.

In the central region, flash floods affected families across Kabul, Kapisa, Panjshir, Parwan, Logar, and Maidan Wardak provinces. Extensive damage to residential housing and community assets was reported in several districts, leaving many families displaced and in need of humanitarian assistance, including shelter, health care, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), and livelihood support.

WHO, together with Health Cluster partners, is closely coordinating with local health authorities to support rapid assessments, deploy emergency health supplies and ensure the continuity of essential health services, including trauma care and treatment for injured and flood-affected populations.

title: Cholera Outbreak in Chad - 2026: DREF Operation (MDRTD026)
content:
Description of the Event

Date when the trigger was met

15-07-2026

What happened, where and when?

On 15 July 2026, the Secretary General of the Ministry of Public Health and Prevention (MoPHP), through the Public Health Emergency Operations Centre (COUSP), issued official correspondence No. 2533/MSPP/SE/SG/COUSP/2026 requesting urgent support from technical and financial partners to strengthen cholera preparedness and response efforts in Chad. The letter called for the mobilization of additional resources to support the national response plan and prevent further spread of the outbreak to other provinces of the country and beyond its borders.

The request was made in the context of an ongoing cholera outbreak in Karal Health District, Hadjer-Lamis Province. Following the notification of the first suspected cases on 13 June 2026, laboratory confirmation of Vibrio cholerae O1 Ogawa, and the official declaration of the outbreak on 18 June 2026, transmission has continued to evolve. As of 9 July 2026, a cumulative total of 167 cases and 5 deaths, including 3 community deaths, had been reported, corresponding to a 3 per cent case fatality rate (CFR). The outbreak is currently concentrated in four active health areas: Karal 1, Karal 2, Baltram and Alkouk where 23 villages and neighbourhoods have reported at least one cholera case. The Epidemic Response Committee meeting referenced in the document shared on 7 July reported suspected cases in N'Djamena, which further supports the risk of the outbreak spreading to health areas close to Karal.

The absence of a new situation report (SitRep) does not allow for an assessment of how the situation has evolved to date. However, the letter from the Ministry of Health requesting support as well as all coordination in place reinforces the fact that the situation is not yet fully under control. Vigilance must therefore be maintained.

Despite ongoing efforts by health authorities and partners, important operational gaps remain. The risk of further expansion remains high due to significant population movements, commercial exchanges, the mobility of nomadic populations, and the presence of vulnerable communities and displacement sites in the area. Health authorities have also highlighted inadequate sanitation conditions and limited access to safe water as factors increasing the likelihood of transmission to neighbouring health areas, districts and provinces. The Ministry's request for support therefore seeks to reinforce response activities in affected communities while strengthening surveillance, early warning and prevention measures in surrounding high-risk areas to contain the outbreak and prevent further geographical spread

title: Palestine Complex Emergency 2023 - DREF Final Report (MDRPS015)
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event

07-10-2023

What happened, where and when?

In response to the escalation of violence on 7 October 2023, the Palestine Red Crescent Society (PRCS) declared a Level 3 state of emergency across the Gaza Strip and the West Bank (WB). Large-scale air and ground operations, combined with famine conditions in parts of Gaza (IPC classification in August 2025), resulted in a devastating humanitarian crisis. During the first two years in Gaza (October 2023 to the October 2025 ceasefire), more than 70,000 people were killed and at least 170,000 people were injured. This DREF operation was launched at the onset of the crisis, when the scale and severity of humanitarian needs were only beginning to emerge.

Throughout the Gaza Strip, humanitarian access was severely constrained, with multiple border crossings closed and the flow of humanitarian goods, including critical health care supplies, remaining highly unpredictable even when entry points were opened. The destruction of the water infrastructure, the near collapse of the health system, and the scarcity of basic services further exacerbated humanitarian needs. Commercial trade was also heavily disrupted, resulting in acute fuel shortages and limited access to essential construction materials.

From the start of the escalation of the violence until time of writing (April 2026), 58 PRCS staff and volunteers, including two in the West Bank, have been killed. Thirty-two lost their lives while on duty, wearing clearly identifiable Red Crescent uniforms, several of these while operating in clearly marked PRCS ambulances.

Despite extreme challenges, PRCS maintained its emergency medical services (EMS), medical points and hospitals throughout the crisis, with five operational in Gaza at the time of writing. Across the occupied Palestinian territory (oPt), dedicated staff and volunteers continued to provide lifesaving assistance under exceptionally difficult conditions. This DREF operation formed part of the initial support provided to PRCS before and during the launch of its Emergency Appeal and, as of 2025, the implementation of its three-year Emergency Master Plan.

title: Cape Verde | Floods: 6-Month Operation Update (MDRCV005)
content:
A. SITUATION ANALYSIS

Through this Operations Update, the National Society seeks an extension of the Emergency Appeal to sustain and complete all planned activities, address remaining humanitarian needs, and ensure the effective utilization of available resources. The proposed extension of the Emergency Appeal from 31 August to 31 December 2026 is strategically critical for consolidating the gains achieved under the response, while enabling a coherent transition from emergency interventions to recovery, preparedness, and longer-term resilience-building efforts. As of the time of reporting, the NS reports an unspent balance of about CHF 500,000 which has been earmarked for the different sectoral activities that will be prioritized during the extension period. This additional timeframe will allow the National Society to strengthen community capacities, complete outstanding sectoral activities, and reinforce institutional development priorities, fully aligned with its strategic ambitions and commitment to supporting affected populations in a sustainable manner.

Description of the crisis

On 10–11 August 2025, Tropical Cyclone Erin brought torrential rains that caused severe flash floods and landslides across Cabo Verde, with São Vicente and Santo Antão experiencing the most significant devastation and partial impacts in São Nicolau. In just a few hours, rainfall exceeded annual averages, overwhelming drainage systems, and leading to widespread destruction of homes, public infrastructure, and essential services. At least 12 people lost their lives; five went missing, and more than 27,500 people were directly affected, including 1,500 displaced in São Vicente. According to the Public Health Situational Analysis (PHSA) by WHO, about 20,000 people have been injured1 . Over 2,500 buildings were damaged, five bridges collapsed, and more than 60 km of roads were cut off, isolating entire communities. Mindelo’s central hospital and several health centers were inundated, resulting in the destruction of vaccine stocks and interruption of critical health services. Water and sanitation systems collapsed, forcing reliance on emergency water trucking, while markets and food stocks were destroyed, disrupting livelihoods and increasing food insecurity.

The situation has heightened protection risks for vulnerable groups, including women, children, the elderly, and people with disabilities, who face displacement, loss of income, and reduced access to assistance. The compounding effects of the floods, combined with Cabo Verde’s existing vulnerabilities such as high food import dependency, recurrent droughts, and fragile health systems, have created a complex humanitarian emergency requiring sustained relief and early recovery efforts.

Exactly one month later, on 11 September 2025, new heavy rains struck São Vicente, causing additional localized flooding in Mindelo. However, since the previous report, the overall situation has stabilized and has not further deteriorated. Most roads and damaged public infrastructure have been cleared, and the majority of displaced families have returned home, yet 74 families are still residing in government-funded temporary accommodation. Affected communities have begun rebuilding and restoring their livelihoods, with the current focus shifting toward recovery and rehabilitation of the most impacted areas.

On 13 November 2025, the island of Santiago in Cabo Verde was hit by an unprecedented storm, triggering severe flooding and landslides that overwhelmed infrastructure and disrupted communities. The hardest-hit municipalities of Tarrafal de Santiago, Santa Cruz, and São Miguel suffered major damage to roads, bridges, drainage systems, and crops, with one fatality and around 7,080 people (1,480 families) affected. A state of disaster was declared, and the national civil protection system, including the Cruz Vermelha de Cabo Verde, was activated to lead the emergency response. Following a rapid assessment, the CVCV presented targeted response for 500 families in northern Santiago, with a budget of CHF 251,386.92. The operation focuses on essential relief (NFIs), WASH, community health, and livelihoods through cash assistance, alongside cross-cutting actions on CEA and PGI.

The IFRC has integrated this intervention into the ongoing Emergency Appeal, committing to CHF 115,000 while continuing to mobilize additional and longer-term support. This expansion brings the operation to four geographic areas, reinforcing a coordinated, scalable response. While resources remain below needs, engagement with partners continues to secure further support and sustain impact.

title: Kyrgyz Republic Market and Price Monitoring Bulletin, Issue #101 | 12 June 2026 [EN/RU]
content:
Market context and drivers

• Higher energy, fertilizer, transport and food costs are increasing pressure on poorer households. Monitoring fertilizer availability and transportation costs remains critical. (World Bank, 2026)

• The government introduced temporary subsidies on fuel imports to ensure availability and stabilize retail prices. (Cabinet of Ministers, 2026)

• The Government also temporarily restricted coal exports by road to help protect domestic supplies ahead of the heating season. (Cabinet of Ministers, 2026)

• From July 2026, the new “Bala Yrysy” programme will be provided as a monthly support to families with children under three years old. (Cabinet of Ministers, 2026)

Risks

• Despite strong economic growth, high inflation, elevated food prices, declining remittances, and climate-related risks continue to pressure household purchasing power and food security, especially among vulnerable households.

• El Niño may bring more rain to Central Asia in second half of 2026. In the Kyrgyz Republic, this could increase the risk of floods, mudflows, soil erosion and damage to roads and farms.

• Fuel prices and supplies remain a concern. If regional supplies fall or wholesale prices rise, fuel and transport costs may increase despite government support.

title: Nigeria Flood Operation: Imminent DREF Operation (MDRNG045)
content:
Nigeria is entering the peak ood season (July–September 2026), with forecasts from the Nigeria Hydrological Services Agency (NIHSA) indicating a high likelihood of widespread riverine and ash ooding across several parts of the country. The 2026 Annual Flood Outlook projects that approximately 250,788 km² of the country could be inundated during the season, of which 138,227 km² (55.1%) are classied as high-risk areas expected to experience severe to extreme ooding.

The Annual Flood Outlook further identies more than 14,000 communities across 266 Local Government Areas (LGAs) in 33 states and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) as being at high ood risk, while an additional 15,500 communities across 35 states fall within the moderate ood risk category. July to September is projected to be the period of highest ood likelihood, with rising water levels expected across major river basins, including the Benue, Kaduna, Gongola, Hadejia–Jama'are, Cross River, and Niger river systems.

On 14 July 2026, NIHSA issued National Flood Advisory No. NFA-2026-195, placing 13 states - Adamawa, Akwa Ibom, Anambra, Bauchi,
Benue, Borno, Cross River, Edo, Enugu, Imo, Kaduna, Niger and Plateau, under a Medium Flood Risk alert. The advisory identied 16 hydrological stations with river levels approaching critical thresholds and forecast localized ooding along the Karam, Waya and Amber Rivers in Adamawa and Bauchi States. Communities, schools, health facilities, markets and places of worship located within the projected ood footprint are expected to be aected should the forecast rainfall materialize.

Preliminary exposure mapping undertaken by NIHSA indicates that the projected ood footprint includes at least 151 communities, 49 schools, 46 health facilities, 11 markets and 38 places of worship, highlighting the potential for signicant humanitarian impacts should river levels continue to rise.

The current forecasts are consistent with the 2026 Seasonal Climate Prediction issued by the Nigerian Meteorological Agency (NiMet) and the IFRC West and Central Africa Risk Analysis, which classies Nigeria as "High Risk – Prepare", with an estimated 6.51 million people exposed to imminent ood risk, particularly in vulnerable riverine and coastal communities. The anticipated humanitarian impacts include loss of life and injuries, displacement of households, damage to homes and essential household assets, disruption of livelihoods, contamination of water sources, interruption of basic services, and an increased risk of waterborne diseases, particularly in communities with limited preparedness and coping capacity.

Based on the latest hydrological and meteorological forecasts, signicant ood impacts are expected between late July and September 2026, with the highest likelihood occurring during periods of sustained heavy rainfall and peak river discharge. Although the exact timing and location of ood impacts may vary across river basins, current forecasts provide sucient lead time to implement anticipatory actions before oodwaters reach critical levels in the targeted communities. In addition to scientic forecasts, reports from state authorities indicate that localized ooding has already occurred in parts of Lagos, Akwa Ibom, Bauchi and Plateau States, reecting saturated ground conditions and reduced drainage capacity in several locations.

The available forecast information provides an operational lead time of approximately four to eight weeks before the anticipated peak ood impacts during August and September, although localized ash ooding may occur earlier following intense rainfall events. This window is sucient to implement time-critical anticipatory actions, including early warning dissemination, volunteer deployment, household preparedness, evacuation planning, community clean-up campaigns and protection of livelihoods before river levels reach their seasonal peaks.

In response to these anticipated impacts, this Imminent DREF has been designed to complement existing Movement interventions and avoid duplication of assistance. Following consultations with Movement partners, the operation will target 16 priority LGAs across eight states - Adamawa, Akwa Ibom, Bauchi, Benue, Cross River, Edo, Lagos and Plateau, where there are identied gaps in existing anticipatory action support. Given the available funding, the operation will focus on two of the most at-risk LGAs in each state, prioritized based on the latest ood forecasts, exposure, vulnerability and anticipated humanitarian impact. The proposed interventions will focus on reducing preventable loss of life through early warning and evacuation preparedness, protecting essential household assets and livelihoods, reducing public health risks through water, sanitation and hygiene measures, and strengthening community preparedness and local response capacity before the anticipated oods occur.

title: WFP Bangladesh Market Monitor (June 2026)
content:
Key Messages

Inflation: General inflation eased slightly in June reaching 9.16 percent, down from 9.42 percent in May 2026, driven by lower price pressure across both food and non-food sectors. Food inflation declined to 8.6 percent, down from 9.06 percent in the previous month attributed to improved seasonal supply. Non-food inflation also eased slightly hitting 9.61 percent in June 2026 from 9.71 percent in May.1 This marginal decline unlikely to have provided meaningful relief to households amid recent hikes in fuel oil, electricity, and transport tariffs. On a year-on-year basis, both food and non-food inflation increased by 1.21 and 0.24 percentage points respectively. The overall inflation has remained at a persistently high level that continues to outpace wage growth for 53rd consecutive months 2 , disproportionately affecting people in lower-income groups. Both rural and urban food inflation showed slight downward trends in the reporting month, hitting 8.52 and 8.76 percent, respectively.

Bangladesh Economy: The country's gross foreign exchange reserves revived sharply in June hitting USD 37.58 billion, about 9 percent higher as compared to May 2026. The reserves stood at USD 32.93 billion as per IMF (BPM6) calculations.3 Officials referred the reserves as satisfactory, having a year-on-year growth of about 26 percent, backed by higher remittance inflows, lower import-payment obligations and the Central Bank's dollar purchases from commercial banks in this period. This stable growth in reserves would cover around five to six months of import bills,4 which may help keep the country's foreign exchange market stable. The remittance inflow stood at USD 2.8 billion in June 2026, a decline by about 18 percent from the previous month, largely due to temporary post-Eid seasonal slowdown. However, Bangladesh records a historic high remittance inflow of USD 35.56 billion during the departing FY25-26, about 17 percent growth year-on-year,

title: Bangladesh Monsoon Floods 2026: DREF Operational Update (MDRBD040)
content:
Bangladesh is experiencing a severe monsoon-induced ood and landslide emergency following a period of exceptionally heavy rainfall associated with an active monsoon system and a low-pressure area over the Bay of Bengal. The emergency began in early July 2026 and intensied between 9 and 18 July, triggering widespread ash oods, riverine ooding, waterlogging, and landslides across several parts of the country. Rainfall was particularly intense in the south-eastern and north-eastern regions, with Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar,
Bandarban, Khagrachhari, Rangamati, Sylhet and Sunamganj experiencing prolonged heavy precipitation. Rising water levels in major rivers, including the Sangu, Kushiyara, Monu and Khowai, resulted in widespread inundation of low-lying areas, landslides in hilly terrain, destruction of critical infrastructure, and disruption of essential services.

The emergency has aected multiple districts across Bangladesh, with the most signicant impacts recorded in Cox’s Bazar, Chattogram, Bandarban, Rangamati, Khagrachhari, Sylhet, Sunamganj, Moulvibazar, Habiganj and adjacent ood-prone areas. The impacts have been particularly severe in the Chattogram Hill Tracts and Cox’s Bazar, where steep slopes, saturated soils and prolonged rainfall have increased the occurrence of landslides and infrastructure damage. In Cox’s Bazar, the eects have extended across all 33 Rohingya refugee camps and surrounding host communities, causing damage to shelters, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) facilities, roads, retaining walls and community infrastructure, while disrupting access to basic services and livelihoods.

Although rainfall has gradually decreased and water levels in many rivers have started to recede, the emergency remains ongoing.
Localized ooding, waterlogging, contaminated water sources, damaged infrastructure and landslide risks continue to aect vulnerable communities. According to tInter-Cluster Coordination Group sitrep dated 13 July 2026, more than 1.1 million people have been aected across 10 districts. As of 18 July 2026, 374 unions and four municipalities across 56 upazilas had been aected, with approximately 38,500 people temporarily displaced and more than 267,000 households stranded or isolated by oodwaters. The oods and landslides have also resulted in reported fatalities and substantial damage to housing, livelihoods, agriculture, sheries, livestock and public infrastructure, generating signicant humanitarian needs that require sustained response and recovery support.

title: WFP Myanmar Market Monitor (June 2026)
content:
KEY Highlight June 2026

Rising Food Basket Cost

By the first week of July (3 July), the national average food basket cost was 20 percent higher than in the last week of February. In June, it increased by 2 percent month-on-month to MMK 51,187, reflecting rising prices of key food commodities. Elevated transportation costs, driven by continued fuel shortages, remained a key factor contributing to higher household food costs.

Impact of Fuel Price Surge

Despite a gradual decline in diesel prices during the reporting period, prices remained substantially above pre-crisis levels. Nationwide, diesel prices were still 45 percent higher on average, with Yangon recording the largest increase at around 1.5 percent above the pre-crisis benchmark. In conflict-affected areas, fuel costs remained particularly elevated, with diesel selling at approximately MMK 11,000 per liter in Sittwe and MMK 12,500 per liter in Myitkyina—nearly five times the benchmark price previously observed in Yangon.

Significant Price Increases

Tomato prices increased sharply in Central Rakhine and recorded modest increases in several other areas, reflecting seasonal declines in market supply. At the same time, key basket commodities, including rice, chickpeas, and salt, also rose in some areas. Prices of other commonly consumed items, such as Tomato and onions, increased as well. According to traders, these price increases were driven by supply chain disruptions, high transportation costs, seasonal fluctuations in production areas, and continued market instability resulting from ongoing conflict in several parts of the country.

Notable Price Decreases

Egg prices decreased across most markets in Myanmar in June 2026 compared with the previous month, driven primarily by improved supply. Reduced consumer purchasing power also weakened demand, contributing to the price decline. In contrast, prices remained elevated in conflict-affected areas of Northern Shan, where transport disruptions continued to limit the flow of supplies into local markets.

title: Minimum Expenditure Basket, Quarterly Bulletin (June 2026)
content:
BACKGROUND

Classification of MEB/ SMEB change: In November 2024, WFP Cameroon, in collaboration with the national Cash Working Group (CWG), initiated the revision of the Minimum Expenditure Basket (MEB), the Survival Minimum Expenditure Basket (SMEB), and Cash Transfer Values (TV) for the three major crisis areas in Cameroon: the Lake Chad Basin (LCB) crisis in the Far North region; the Central African Republic (CAR) crisis affecting the North, Adamaoua, and East regions; and the North-West and SouthWest crisis.

A hybrid approach was used to estimate the MEB, combining household expenditure data (ENSAN 2024) with a rights-based approach to identify existing gaps. This revision builds on the previous update conducted in December 2022.

The process updated the TV for each crisis to cover an average of 49.3% of households' unmet basic needs, compared to 45.6% for the survival basket. The national CWG and the Inter-Sector endorsed these findings in February 2026.

title: Monthly market update #2 – June 2026, Middle East, Northern Africa and Eastern Europe
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

The temporary reopening of the Strait of Hormuz following a June US–Iran agreement eased global commodity and inflationary pressures, with Brent crude falling 20% in June (compared to May) reaching USD 73/bbl, and urea prices dropping 21% below pre-conflict levels. Cereals and natural gas prices also declined slightly (45%), although natural gas remained 37% above pre-conflict levels.

Annual Inflation remained highly uneven across the region in June, with Iran and Türkiye continuing to face the region’s highest price pressures, while most countries recorded stable or easing inflation and Gaza’s deflation reflected ongoing normalization from conflict-driven price spikes.

Food basket costs were broadly stable in June across most of the region, reflecting easing inflationary pressures; with Iran as a notable exception (+8% MoM, +120% YoY).

Inflationary pressures continue to erode purchasing power of cash transfer values in Iran and Türkiye, constraining vulnerable households’ access to adequate and nutritious food

Most regional currencies remain weaker than pre-escalation levels (February 2026), despite modest June recoveries in some markets, most prominently in Iran (+6%) and Egypt (+4%), while currencies in Armenia, Palestine, and Yemen (IRG) maintained relative stability or strengthening over the past year.

Regional fuel prices eased in June following declining global energy prices and improving geopolitical conditions, with cooking gas and diesel recording the largest month-on-month declines, while generally remaining above pre-conflict levels.

title: NRC Somalia: Monthly Programme Update (June 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • Food Security: A third of Somalia population remains at crisis or worse levels of hunger according to the IPC. This includes 1.9 million in Emergency (IPC Phase 4) with a credible Famine (IPC 5) risk in Bay, Bakool, Gedo, Hiiraan and high-risk IDP sites if severe El Niño flooding occurs in the fall.
  • Displacement continues to be driven by drought, conflict, and livelihood deterioration, with the highest concentrations in Mudug, Galgaduud, Banadir, and Middle Shabelle.
  • Access & Protection: Political tensions, wider conflict and insecurity compounding by inter-clan conflict will continue to restrict humanitarian access, disrupt operations an heighten protection risks, particularly in central and south-central Somalia.
  • Climate Risk: 97–100% probability of El Niño is expected to shift Somalia from a drought crisis to high flood risk during the next rainy season September – November this year, potentially driving further displacement, crop losses and humanitarian needs.
  • Humanitarian Response: The 2026 HNRP is lacking 80 % of requested funding (US$675M gap). Only 507,000 people reached with multi-sector assistance, while 16 of 21 priority districts remain below 25% response coverage.

title: Afghanistan: Flash Update #1 (23 July 2026)
content:
SITUATION UPDATE

On 20 July 2026, heavy and continuous rainfall triggered severe flash flooding across several parts of eastern Afghanistan. The most serious impact was recorded in Parun City, Nuristan Province, while flooding was also reported in Torkham, Nangarhar Province, and Alingar District, Laghman Province. The floods are the latest in a series of increasingly frequent climate-related disasters affecting Afghanistan, where extreme weather events continue to compound humanitarian needs and undermine community resilience.

title: WFP Rwanda Macroeconomic and Food Security Update, June 2026
content:
Background

Rwanda entered 2026 with strong economic momentum and a generally stable macroeconomic outlook. Real GDP growth reached 9.4 percent in 2025, supported by strong performance across services, construction, tourism, and agriculture. The country has also continued to benefit from sound economic management, IMF engagement, and access to concessional financing.

At the same time, the cost of living has increased sharply since early 2026. Inflation rose above the National Bank of largely external in origin, reflecting higher global fuel and fertilizer prices, increased shipping and logistics costs, and exchange rate pressures.

The current situation presents a mixed picture. At the macroeconomic level, Rwanda remains more resilient than many regional peers. At the household level, however, rising prices are reducing purchasing power, particularly for households that rely on markets to access food and have limited capacity to absorb higher living costs.

This update examines recent macroeconomic developments in Rwanda and their implications for food security. The main concern is not a national shortage of food, but the potential erosion of household financial access to essential needs as food and non-food costs increase.

The Concern Worldwide (CWW) Accountability to Affected Populations project, supported by WFP, aims to create a bottom-up feedback and communication mechanism between responders and people we serve, that is community-based, easily accessible, and built on mutual understanding and genuine information-sharing.

Through local responders and community correspondents, Concern, Community Engagement Network (CEN), and the Radio Community (TRC) work together to deliver a complete community feedback mechanism that is accessible to all participants regardless of their literacy levels and access to assets and internet. title: Jordan strengthens local resilience through climate action and wildfire prevention
content:
In Jordan's northern governorate of Irbid, a local resilience planning process supported by the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) has evolved into a growing movement of community-led action, government ownership and climate resilience. More than a year after the completion of the project, its recommendations are continuing to shape local priorities, demonstrating how risk-informed planning can translate into tangible action on the ground.

Through the project "Harnessing Synergies between Climate Change Adaptation and Disaster Risk Reduction in Responses of Inclusive Health Systems for Migrants in Jordan," implemented by the Jordan Climate Action Network (CAN) with support from UNDRR, Irbid Governorate developed its first Local Resilience Action Plan (LRAP). The initiative strengthened institutional coordination, assessed climate and disaster risks, integrated public health considerations into resilience planning, and identified practical actions to reduce vulnerabilities across communities.

Today, those recommendations are no longer confined to a planning document.

One of the priorities identified through the Local Resilience Action Plan was the growing risk posed by wildfires and the degradation of vegetation resulting from climate change, prolonged dry seasons and increasing temperatures.

Recognizing the importance of acting before disasters occur, the Governor of Irbid has launched a national campaign to remove invasive and highly flammable vegetation in Kufrabil, Al Koura District. The campaign brings together government institutions, local communities and volunteers to reduce wildfire risks while protecting one of Jordan's important natural landscapes.

Building on the resilience priorities identified through the UNDRR-supported project, the Jordan Climate Action Network (CAN) is contributing to the campaign by providing technical expertise, community outreach and logistical support.

The initiative represents a practical example of how disaster risk reduction begins long before an emergency occurs through prevention, preparedness and community engagement.

As part of its contribution, CAN is mobilizing volunteers and local communities through its "Climate Watcher" (Al-Munther Al-Monakhi) initiative, promoting greater understanding of the links between climate change, wildfire risk, environmental degradation and public safety.

The campaign combines awareness sessions with practical field activities, equipping volunteers with the knowledge and tools needed to safely participate in vegetation management while strengthening community preparedness and environmental stewardship.

By connecting climate awareness with local action, the initiative is helping communities become active partners in reducing disaster risks rather than passive recipients of emergency response.

"The true measure of resilience is not the completion of a plan, but the actions it inspires. The experience in Irbid demonstrates how local resilience planning can become a catalyst for sustained action, empowering local institutions and communities to translate risk knowledge into practical solutions that protect lives, livelihoods and ecosystems. This is exactly the type of locally led resilience that the Sendai Framework seeks to promote." Said Sandra Amlang, UNDRR ROAS Chief.

The continued implementation of resilience activities demonstrates the lasting value of investing in local resilience planning.

Since completing the UNDRR-supported project, CAN has continued to expand its resilience work across Jordan through partnerships with national and international organizations. Current initiatives include strengthening early warning systems, promoting nature-based solutions, enhancing water resilience, supporting community preparendess and advancing climate adaptation in municipalities.

These efforts build directly upon the institutional capacities, partnerships and local ownership established through the resilience planning process in Irbid.

“The Local Resilience Action Plan was never intended to be an end in itself, but rather a starting point for sustained action. We are proud to see how the partnerships, knowledge, and priorities established through this process continue to generate tangible benefits for communities in Irbid and contribute to strengthening climate resilience and disaster preparedness in Jordan.” Eng. Doa'a Al-Derabani, Chief Executive Officer (CEO), Climate Action Association in Jordan (CAN Jordan)

The experience in Irbid highlights an important lesson: resilience planning is only the beginning.

When local governments, civil society, communities and development partners work together around a shared vision, resilience plans become living frameworks that guide investments, mobilize partnerships and inspire collective action.

Rather than ending with the completion of a project, the Local Resilience Action Plan has become a catalyst for continued implementation, demonstrating how disaster risk reduction can be embedded into local development priorities and community initiatives.

For UNDRR, this represents the ultimate objective of resilience-building, not producing plans, but enabling local actors to lead their own resilience journey.

As climate-related hazards continue to intensify across the region, the experience of Irbid offers a compelling example of how locally owned, risk-informed planning can create lasting impact, strengthen partnerships and translate resilience from policy into practice.

title: European Union Strengthens Support To WFP Assistance For Vulnerable Refugees And Conflict-Affected People In Iran
content:
TEHRAN, Iran – The United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) today welcomed a EUR 3.08 million contribution from the European Union (EU) to support vulnerable refugees and conflict-affected people in Iran, helping sustain life-saving assistance over 12 months.

This contribution will enable WFP to maintain food security support for populations facing increased economic pressures and humanitarian needs, helping families meet their essential needs and protect their well-being.

Iran hosts one of the largest refugee populations in the world, the majority from Afghanistan. With support from the European Union and other partners, WFP provides food assistance to over 35,000 of the most vulnerable refugees across 20 settlements, including cash-based transfers, school feeding programmes and livelihood support.

“Many vulnerable families in Iran are facing growing economic pressures that threaten their ability to put food on the table,” said Mayssa Alghribawy, WFP Representative in Iran. “Thanks to the support of the European Union, WFP can continue providing critical assistance that not only meets immediate needs but also helps strengthen resilience over time.”

The contribution will also support WFP’s assistance to conflict-affected Iranians, ensuring that humanitarian assistance reaches those most in need in a timely, principled and needs-based manner.

Through its partnership with the European Union, WFP provides monthly cash assistance to vulnerable households, enabling families to purchase food from local markets based on their needs and preferences, while supporting local economic activity.

The European Union is a longstanding partner of WFP, and its support in Iran plays a vital role in enabling the organization to maintain operations and respond to evolving humanitarian needs. With this contribution, WFP plans to reach 52,000 (17,000 Iranians and 35,000 refugees) ensuring continued access to food assistance for vulnerable communities across the country.

# # #

About WFP

The United Nations World Food Programme is the world’s largest humanitarian organization saving lives in emergencies and using food assistance to build a pathway to peace, stability and prosperity for people recovering from conflict, disasters and the impact of climate change.

Follow us on X, formerly Twitter, via @wfp_media and @wfpiran.

title: UNHCR Syria Operational Update - June 2026
content:
Syria has entered a new phase marked by large-scale returns and persistent humanitarian vulnerability.

While around 1.7 million refugees and 1.9 million internally displaced persons (IDPs) have returned since December 2024, 15.6 million people still require humanitarian assistance.

As return movements continue, ensuring sustainable reintegration through access to housing, services, documentation, livelihoods and community support is becoming a defining priority for Syria’s recovery.

In line with Syria’s National Recovery Priorities and the Government’s “No Tents, No Camps” vision, UNHCR supports this maintaining transition protection while and humanitarian assistance for vulnerable populations.

Operational Context

Syria is experiencing sustained refugee and IDP returns while humanitarian needs remain widespread. Conditions remain volatile in parts of the country, while damaged housing, limited access to services, documentation barriers and economic hardship continue to affect communities receiving returnees and constrain sustainable reintegration.

Recognizing that sustainable return increasingly depends on economic recovery, UNHCR participated in the Private Sector National Conference, organized by the Ministry of Economy and Industry and UNDP, to discuss economic recovery priorities. Through its side event, From Return to Recovery: Private Sector Engagement with Returnees, UNHCR highlighted the role of private-sector investment, employment opportunities and entrepreneurship in supporting reintegration and reducing long-term dependency on humanitarian assistance.

The second round of the Enhanced Regional Perceptions and Intentions Survey, covering Syrian refugees in Lebanon, Jordan, Iraq, and Egypt and published by UNHCR and the World Bank in April, found that only 14% of refugee households intend to return within the next 12 months, while 77% express a long-term aspiration to return, indicating that willingness to return remains higher than confidence in current conditions inside Syria. Those who did not intend to return cited lack of adequate housing, limited access to basic services, safety and security concerns, and lack of employment and economic opportunities as the main barriers to return.

Through community- and area-based approaches, UNHCR supports refugees, IDPs, returnees, host communities across Syria, focusing on protection, selfreliance, and local recovery in areas of greatest need.

In 2026, UNHCR collaborates with 26 partners, including ministries, other UN agencies and international and national non-governmental organizations in all 14 governorates.

title: WFP Pakistan Monthly Market Monitor-July 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS JULY

  • Month-on-month, the Consumer Price Index (CPI) decreased by 0.3 percent in June compared to the previous month. The annual inflation increased by 11.07 percent (YoY) compared to June 2025, driven mainly by higher transport, housing, water, and energy costs. It is marginally lower compared to May 2026 CPI which stood at 11.7 percent.
  • Month-on-month food inflation increased by 0.96 percent mainly driven by increased costs of perishable food Items, while annual food inflation reached 9.4 percent compared to June 2025, driven by higher cost of wheat and wheat flour, cooking oil and perishable food items, meaning households paid 9 percent more for food - with low-income groups hit the hardest.
  • Prices of wheat and wheat flour increased in June compared to May, with wheat rising by 4.0 percent and wheat flour by 3.0 percent,signalling growing pressure on key staples. In contrast, rice prices remained largely stable with only a slight increase for rice Irri-6.
  • Petrol prices decreased month-on-month in June 2026, mainly due to lower global oil prices and domestic adjustments; however, year-on-year, petrol and diesel prices remained significantly higher by 15.9 percent and 18.6 percent, respectively.
  • Pakistan received USD 3.5 billion in remittances in June 2026, up 2 percent year-on-year but down 18.3 percent from the pre-Eid peak in May 2026.

title: The Gambia Monthly Joint Market Monitoring Bulletin, May 2026
content:
Key messages and operational implications

FOOD ACCESS PRESSURE

Many households spend more than half of their income on food. Protecting purchasing power remains central to food access during the lean period.

SUPPLY AND AVAILABILITY

Markets are functioning and commodities are available, but import dependence, limited local production capacity, storage gaps and high transport costs constrain stable supply.

PURCHASING POWER

High food prices and stagnant incomes mean households buy smaller quantities, switch to cheaper foods, or rely more on borrowing and remittances.

title: WFP South Sudan Weekly Market Monitor (6 –12 July 2026)
content:

title: Liberia: Market Monitoring Bulletin, June 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHT

• Imported rice (5% broken) prices averaged LRD 2,842/25kg, declining by 2% MoM from LRD 2,886 in May 2026 and by 23% YoY from LRD 3,679 in June 2025, reflecting improved market availability and stable supply conditions.

• Cassava prices averaged LRD 1,125/25kg, remaining broadly stable compared to May 2026 (−1% MoM) while declining by 12% YoY from LRD 1,284, indicating adequate supplies across most monitored markets.

• Palm oil prices averaged LRD 1,140/gallon, increasing slightly by 1% MoM from LRD 1,125 and by 12% YoY from LRD 1,014, reflecting transportation costs and localized supply constraints in some markets.

• Gasoline prices averaged LRD 1,020/gallon, remaining largely stable compared to May 2026 (−1% MoM) but 20% higher than June 2025, despite reports of declining prices in some markets during the month.

• Diesel prices averaged LRD 1,213/gallon, showing minimal month-on-month change (−1% MoM) while remaining 31% above June 2025 levels, reflecting sustained transport and distribution costs.

• The exchange rate remained stable at around LRD 181 per US dollar, unchanged from May 2026, while the Liberian dollar appreciated by about 8% YoY compared to June 2025.

• Daily wage labor rates remained stable. Agricultural wages increased to LRD 601/day for men and LRD 514/day for women, while construction wages rose to LRD 858/day. Improved wages combined with lower rice prices strengthened the purchasing power of casual labor households compared to June 2025.

title: Vanuatu Dengue Outbreak Situation Report #8 (South-West Efate, Shefa Province)
content:
Key highlights (as of EW29):

  • 48 cumulative laboratory-confirmed dengue cases reported since the outbreak began.
  • 2 new confirmed cases were reported in EW29.
  • Weekly case numbers remain below the outbreak alert threshold (fewer than 4 cases per week), indicating reduced outbreak activity.
  • Ongoing transmission continues, therefore the outbreak status remains unchanged.
  • 9 cumulative hospitalisations (18.8%) have been recorded; 1 patient remains hospitalised and all others have recovered and been discharged.
  • No dengue-related deaths have been reported.
  • Dengue Virus Type 1 (DENV-1) has been confirmed as the circulating serotype.
  • Highest proportion of cases reported from Pango Area Council (31%), followed by Erakor Area Council (25%).
  • 67% of cases are among individuals under 26 years of age, and 54% are male.
  • Response efforts continue, including enhanced surveillance, vector control, community awareness campaigns, and outreach activities, reaching over 450 community members.

title: WFP Chad Country Brief, July 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• Against a backdrop of severe funding constraints, WFP has had to progressively prioritize limited resources, including focusing emergency food assistance on refugee populations and reducing support to other beneficiaries. In parallel, WFP, UNHCR and government counterparts are implementing vulnerability-based targeting (VBT) to ensure that available resources are allocated according to household vulnerability levels, improving the efficiency and equity of assistance while safeguarding support for those most in need.
• After the Anticipatory Action (AA) trigger was activated in May, WFP commenced assistance in June for households at risk from the anticipated drought. The response will reach a total of 170,500 people by August 2026.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Chad continues to host Africa’s second-largest refugee population after Uganda, with nearly 1.54 million refugees recorded as of 6 July 2026 (UNHCR). Most (88 percent) are Sudanese refugees sheltering in Chad’s eastern provinces.
• According to UNHCR, Chad has received 936,900 Sudanese refugees (271,060 households since April 2023, including 53,560 people who arrived following the October 2025 attack on El Fasher and 33,200 since January 2026.
• The sustained arrival of refugees and returnees from Sudan continues to place considerable strain on already vulnerable host communities. Increased pressure on food supplies, essential services, and natural resources highlights the need for continued humanitarian assistance alongside efforts to strengthen resilience and promote long-term stability. In Chad’s Lac Province, recurrent attacks by non-state armed groups and ongoing military operations continue to drive new population displacement, leaving affected families in urgent need of humanitarian assistance.

title: Situation Report 4 - Extreme Weather Events in India - Assam, Jammu & Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Gujarat and Maharashtra (Date: 25th July 2026)
content:
SITUATION UPDATE

A. Situation Overview:

India is experiencing multi-state monsoon emergencies across Assam, Jammu & Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Gujarat and Maharashtra (Palghar District). Among all affected regions, Assam remains the worst-hit, with widespread flooding, massive displacement, and extensive crop and livestock losses.

1. Assam Flood - Severe Flooding Across 12 Districts

Assam is facing one of its most severe flood waves in recent years, with 12 districts, 856 villages, and over 7 lakh people affected. Sivasagar, Jorhat, Charaideo and Golaghat are the worst-hit. Human casualties have reached 14, and livestock losses exceed 3.34 lakh, with massive crop damage across 56,600 hectares. Relief camps are sheltering 115,205 people, while another 2 lakh depend on external relief. The humanitarian, agricultural, and infrastructure impacts are extensive and escalating.

title: WFP Bangladesh Country Brief, July 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• WFP strengthened Bangladesh’s climate resilience and disaster preparedness ahead of the 2026 monsoon season by updating an anticipatory action database for over 500,000 households and allocating USD 12 million to enable rapid activation.
• With WFP’s support, Bangladesh launched its first sovereign flood insurance scheme, covering over 100,000 vulnerable households.
• WFP continued providing critical assistance to 1.1 million Rohingya refugees while supporting nutrition, education and resilience activities for refugees and host communities in Cox’s Bazar and Bhasan Char.

SITUATION OVERVIEW
• Bangladesh continues to face significant food security, nutrition and climate-related challenges despite notable socioeconomic progress. Economic pressures, elevated food prices and global commodity market volatility continue to affect vulnerable households, while climate-related shocks, including floods and cyclones, threaten livelihoods, agricultural production and food security.
• In 2025, an estimated 16 million people were projected to experience crisis-level or worse food insecurity, while the country’s first IPC Acute Malnutrition analysis estimated that 1.6 million children under five were acutely malnourished, including 144,000 children severely malnourished, alongside nearly 117,000 pregnant and breastfeeding women (PBW). A new PC is expected to be released in July 2026.
• Bangladesh remains climate-related hazards, with monsoon-related risks and the potential El Niño conditions in late 2026 posing additional risks to vulnerable communities. At the same time, the country hosts approximately 1.2 million Rohingya refugees, with limited prospects for large-scale returns.

title: Kyrgyzstan Pluvial/Flash Flood 2026 - DREF Operation (MDRKG022)
content:
Description of the Event
Date of event
13-07-2026
What happened, where and when?

On 13 July 2026, at approximately 19:30 local time, intense short-duration rainfall over the mountainous catchment areas of Nooken district triggered mudflows along two separate channels. The Besh-Korgon channel overflowed and inundated the lower streets of Kochkor-Ata city, destroying 3 electricity poles in the Besh-Korgon settlement. Simultaneously, the Kara-Bulak channel overflowed into Ergesh Aliev village, while separate mudflows descending from higher elevations submerged the villages of Kurulush, Boston, and Kop- Tam in the Mombekov village area. The event occurred in Nooken district, Jalal-Abad oblast, Kyrgyzstan, affecting Kochkor-Ata city and the villages of Ergesh Aliev, Kurulush, Boston, and Kop-Tam.

The mudflows struck the evening of 13 July 2026 (19:30 local time). District civil protection authorities were mobilized the same evening, and clearance and mud-pumping operations were still ongoing as of 02:00 on 14 July 2026. A state of emergency has been declared in the district, and the situation is being monitored by RCSK in coordination with local civil protection authorities.

title: Tajikistan Flood 2026: DREF Operation (MDRTJ038)
content:
Description of the Event
Date of event
11-07-2026

What happened, where and when?

On 11 July 2026, at approximately 15:40 local time, following intense rainfall, flash floods and mudflows affected the villages of Darg and Kazdon in Shamtuch Jamoat, Ayni District, Sughd Region. The disaster caused significant damage to residential houses, auxiliary structures, agricultural land, drinking water supply and irrigation systems, electricity infrastructure, internal village roads, and private property. The affected population experienced disruptions to essential services and livelihoods.

On 15 July 2026, the Red Crescent Society of Tajikistan (RCST) received an official request from the Executive Authority of Ayni District seeking humanitarian assistance for the population affected by the disaster. The local authorities requested RCST to provide support to the most affected households. According to the official assessment, 672 households in the villages of Darg and Kazdon were affected by the flash floods and mudflows. Further assessments are ongoing to determine the full extent of the damage, humanitarian needs, and priority areas for response.

title: Yemen | Floods - Simplified Early Action Protocol - Final Report, May 2026 (sEAP №: sEAP2023YE01, Operation №: MDRYE015)
content:
SUMMARY - SIMPLIFIED EARLY ACTION PROTOCOL

The IFRC Disaster Response Emergency Fund (DREF) has allocated CHF 220,000 for the (Yemen Red Crescent
Society) to implement early actions to reduce and mitigate the impact of Floods in Yemen. The early actions conducted have been pre-agreed with the National Society and are described in the Early Action Protocol.
https://www.ifrc.org/appeals?date_from=&date_to=&location%5B%5D=6325&search_terms=&search_terms=&
appeal_code=&search_terms=&text=

Below is a summary of key achievements focusing only on the key results against the planned activities under this sEAP including early actions, readiness and pre-positioning activities. Further details are provided under each sector/strategic priority and enablers.

Early Actions:

• Activated sEAP on 21st Aug 2025
• Distributed 100 emergency shelter and repair kits to highly vulnerable households living in degraded shelters, enabling timely reinforcement and repairs prior to anticipated flooding.
• Successfully cleaned drainage systems within and around targeted IDP sites following trigger activation, improving water flow, reducing water stagnation, and minimizing flood risks in coordination with CCCM, Shelter/NFI partners, and community committees.
• Implemented flood mitigation measures in Bani Al-Mashṭā’ and Al-Mithaq IDP sites through strategic placement of sandbags, construction of stone gabions, and earthen embankments to redirect floodwater and protect shelters and infrastructure.
• Delivered anticipatory Multi-Purpose Cash Assistance (MPCA) to 700 HHs 2–3 days before forecasted flooding, enabling vulnerable households to reinforce shelters, relocate temporarily, protect household assets, and meet urgent needs such as food, hygiene items, and rental support.
• Distributed 30 first aid kits and stretchers to community committees, local authorities, and civil defense actors, strengthening frontline emergency response and evacuation capacity prior to flooding.
• Installed 6 flood risk signposts in high-risk locations within and around targeted IDP sites to improve community awareness of flood hazards, mitigation measures, and safe movement routes.
• Distributed IEC materials containing early warning messages and practical guidance on shelter safety, flood preparedness, lightning safety, and hygiene promotion, enhancing community preparedness and risk awareness.
• Distributed 10 megaphones to community committees to strengthen community-based early warning dissemination and ensure timely communication of alerts and preparedness messages.

• Conducted community-based awareness campaigns and dissemination of early warning messages through YRCS volunteers, community committees, and local authorities using megaphones, community meetings, and door-to-door outreach.
• Activated PMER mechanisms to ensure real-time monitoring, quality assurance, accountability, and compliance with targeting and operational standards throughout implementation.
• Established accessible complaints and feedback mechanisms, including help desks and feedback boxes, to strengthen Community Engagement and Accountability (CEA/AAP), transparency, and beneficiary trust.
• Conducted a comprehensive Post-Distribution Monitoring (PDM) survey covering 249 households (1,876 individuals) to assess the effectiveness, accountability, and impact of anticipatory cash assistance interventions.

Readiness activities:

• Coordinated with community committees, local authorities, CCCM actors, and Shelter/NFIs partners to finalize cleaning kits and flood mitigation requirements for targeted IDP sites.
• Conducted assessments and prepared BOQs for flood mitigation works, while identifying and engaging local suppliers for sandbags and other mitigation materials under framework arrangements.
• Finalized pre-identified beneficiary lists for Cash-for-Work activities and emergency shelter repair kits in consultation with community committees prior to sEAP activation.
• Completed orientation sessions for pre-selected Financial Service Providers (FSPs) on cash distribution methodologies, Red Cross principles, code of conduct, beneficiary dignity, and data protection.
• Reviewed and validated targeting criteria for Cash and Voucher Assistance (CVA) through coordination between YRCS HQ, branch teams, staff, and volunteers.
• Conducted a one-week CVA training for 10 YRCS Hajjah branch staff and volunteers (5 male and 5 female) on beneficiary registration, cash distribution processes, CVA tools, key messaging, and code of conduct.
• Oriented community committees and camp management teams in the targeted sites on sEAP activities, vulnerability-based targeting, and beneficiary selection processes for MPCA and shelter assistance.
• Finalized the initial registration and selection of vulnerable households eligible for MPCA and emergency shelter assistance in the targeted sites.
• Coordinated with IFRC and YRCS health teams to finalize specifications and contents of first aid kits and stretchers for emergency preparedness activities.
• Trained 60 participants from community committees, camp management, and civil defense on disaster preparedness, emergency response, anticipatory actions, and basic first aid through two six-day training sessions.
• Developed and finalized early warning, mitigation, and prevention messages in coordination with Civil Defense, YRCS DM, and communication teams, including translation and adaptation for local contexts.
• Reviewed, updated, and finalized IEC materials, including posters and brochures on flood preparedness, shelter safety, mitigation measures, and hygiene promotion.
• Finalized Post-Distribution Monitoring (PDM) tools and guidelines for cash assistance activities to support accountability and monitoring processes.
• Conducted orientation and planning sessions for YRCS HQ and Hajjah branch staff and volunteers on anticipatory action approaches, planned sEAP activities, and operational readiness, with participation of more than 20 personnel.
• Successfully designed and conducted a simulation exercise in collaboration with IFRC, YRCS, and Civil Defense to test the feasibility and operational readiness of the sEAP prior to activation, generating valuable lessons learned for the actual response phase.

Pre-Positioning Activities:

• Finalized the Bill of Quantities (BOQ) for emergency shelter repair kits in coordination with the Shelter/NFIs Cluster and successfully procured and pre-positioned 250 emergency shelter kits prior to sEAP activation.
• Coordinated with community committees, CCCM actors, and Shelter/NFIs partners to finalize the contents of cleaning kits and successfully procured and pre-positioned 6 cleaning kits/tools (3 per targeted site).
• Finalized specifications and contents of first aid kits and stretchers and successfully procured and prepositioned 30 first aid kits and stretchers to support emergency preparedness and response activities.
• Coordinated with YRCS DM and IFRC logistics teams to finalize specifications and complete procurement of 10 megaphones for early warning and community alert dissemination prior to sEAP activation.
• Finalized and printed IEC materials, including posters and brochures containing early warning messages and practical guidance on flood risk reduction, shelter reinforcement, safety during thunderstorms and lightning, and hygiene practices during flooding.

title: AFG: Flood - 07-2026 - Afghanistan Flash Flood 2026 #2 (2026-07-25)
content:
Description

Following heavy and sustained rainfall, flash floods occurred in July 2026 across the country, affecting communities in Nuristan,Laghman, Parwan, Logar, Kabul, Kapisa, Panjsher,Nangarhar,Ghazni,Khost,Maidan Wardak,Paktika and Paktia provinces. Low-lying areas and settlements located along riverbeds were particularly impacted. The floods resulted in loss of life, injuries, and widespread damage to shelters, livelihoods and agricultural land, reflecting the broader pattern of seasonal flooding currently affecting several parts of the country.

According to preliminary information compiled by the Afghan Red Crescent Society (ARCS), more than 910 families were affected. The floods caused 31 deaths and 11 injuries, with 77 cases of missing persons reported. Shelter damage was significant, with 910 houses completely and partially damaged, particularly in several provinces of Nuristan,Laghman, Parwan, Logar, Kabul, Kapisa, Panjsher,Nangarhar,Ghazni,Khost,Maidan Wardak,Paktika and Paktia provinces. In addition, the floods had a severe impact on livelihoods, resulting in the loss of 330 livestock and damage to approximately 5240 jeribs of agricultural land, further increasing vulnerabilities among farming and pastoral households.

As part of ongoing support of ARCS, distributed 600 Parcel hot meal in Laghman Province ,NFI for one affected HHs in Maidan wardak province to the families who have been affected severely by floods.

ARCS, through its provincial branches and volunteers, is monitoring the evolving situation and conducting initial assessments in coordination with local authorities and Movement partners. Priority humanitarian needs identified include emergency shelter and essential household items for families whose homes were destroyed or damaged, food assistance and multipurpose cash support, as well as livelihood and agricultural recovery assistance, including livestock support. With possibility of further rainfall, affected communities remain at risk of additional flooding, underscoring the need for timely humanitarian support.
