title: Afghanistan: Weekly Market Report: Issue 304: Week 3 – July 2026
content:
Key Highlights

Fuel Price Shock and Exchange Rate Dynamics:

A sharp spike in fuel prices is emerging as a primary driver of inflationary pressure, with the cost of transportation cascading into other food and non-food items. This increase is directly impacting supply chains and delivery costs, driven by rising diesel prices. The main catalysts are deepening supply shortages from Russia, exacerbated by the export ban and damage to critical refining infrastructure. Over the past two weeks, limited alternative supplies from Central Asian countries, Iran, and Iraq have contributed to the price surge. Beyond diesel, consumers in parts of the country are reporting shortage of gas used for cooking appliances, with prices rising sharply. Similarly, petrol prices have surged from around AFN 66 to AFN 82 per litre. Concurrently, while the Afghani remained broadly stable at AFN 65.9/USD, it has exhibited an upward trend in recent weeks, depreciating by 2.5% compared to the third week of June. However, it remains 4% stronger than last year and 13% stronger than the three-year average, which continues to partially moderate imported inflation.

Food Items:

• National average food prices showed broad-based upward pressure during the third week of July, with rising transportation costs increasingly contributing to price movements across several commodities.

• Wheat and Flour: All wheat categories rose by around 1% week-on-week, remaining elevated compared to last year—wheat grain (+14%), high-price flour (+8%), and low-price flour (+12%)—reflecting sustained production and transportation costs.

• Rice: Both rice categories edged up modestly and remained substantially above last year's levels, with high-price rice 27% higher and low-price rice 34% higher, standing significantly above their three-year average levels.

• Other Staples: Cooking oil surged by 4.6%, the sharpest weekly increase among staples, while sugar rose modestly (+0.5%) and pulses and salt remained largely stable. Year-on-year, prices of cooking oil (+8%), sugar (+10%), and salt (+8%) remains elevated, whereas pulses show a 14% decline.

• Vegetables: Potato prices continued to climb (+2.2%), while tomato and onion saw marginal increases. Year-on-year, tomato and potato remained significantly elevated by 35% and 55%, respectively, while onion prices eased by 9%, reflecting improved seasonal availability.
Non-Food Items:

• Fuel: Diesel prices continued their sharp upward trajectory, increasing by 3.1% during the week, mainly due to higher international oil prices and continued supply constraints from Russia. Compared to last year and the three-year average, diesel prices remained 19% and 21% higher, respectively.

• Fertilizers: Fertilizer prices rose during the week, with DAP increasing by 1.7% and Urea by 1.1%. However, compared to last year, DAP and Urea remained considerably higher by 19% and 51%, respectively. Improved seed and animal feed prices stayed below last year and the three-year average, reflecting weak consumer demand.

• Livestock: The price of a one-year-old live female sheep increased marginally by 0.4% during the week but remained 6% below last year's level and 2% below the three-year average, contributing to weaker pastoralist ToT.

• Labour Market: Daily wage unskilled labour availability remains limited at 2.0 days/week which is 17% lower than last year and the three-year average, indicating continued pressure on household income opportunities

title: UNHCR-IOM Pakistan Flash update # 103 on Arrest and Detention/Flow Monitoring, 15 Sep 2023 to 18 Jul 2026
content:
INTRODUCTION

In response to the Ministry of Interior's (MoI) decision of 26 September 2023 to enact an “Illegal Foreigners' Repatriation Plan”, UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency and IOM, the UN Migration Agency, have collated their data on the arrest, detention, and deportation of Proof of Registration (PoR) holders, Afghan Citizen Card (ACC) holders, and undocumented Afghan nationals as well as on the outflows of Afghan nationals at the Torkham, Ghulam Khan, Chaman, Badini and Bahramcha border crossing points, to better understand the protection environment and movements of Afghan nationals returning to Afghanistan from Pakistan.

In 2025, the Government of Pakistan (GoP) issued several directives impacting Afghan nationals. In January, the GoP announced that Afghan nationals should relocate from Islamabad Capital Territory (ICT) and Rawalpindi, or else face deportation. In April, further announcements indicated the implementation of the second phase of the “IFRP”, targeting ACC holders, in addition to undocumented Afghans. In July, the GoP issued a Statutory Regulation Order (SRO) directing the repatriation/deportation of PoR card holders following the expiry of PoR card validity on 30 June. The GoP later indicated a deadline of 1 September for PoR holders to leave Pakistan, before the start of the repatriation/deportation process. UNHCR issued a press briefing expressing concern regarding the decision and urging the GoP to exempt Afghans with international protection needs, as well as those with particular circumstances or vulnerabilities, from involuntary return.

title: Earthquakes in Venezuela: Situation Report #30 (23 July 2026, Time: 09:00 pm)
content:
Situation Report No. 30
Earthquakes in Venezuela
23 July 2026
Time: 9:00 pm

Highlights

  • Authorities report 1,463 aftershocks since the 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude earthquakes that struck on 24 June.
  • Official toll: 5,398 people dead and 16,740 injured.
  • The United Nations system and its partner organizations continue scaling up the multisectoral response to the emergency. To address the needs of 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months, an additional appeal of US$299 million was launched

Situation overview

Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre located along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). Authorities report 1,463 aftershocks.

Twenty-four days since the earthquakes, authorities report a toll of 5,398 people dead and 16,740 injured since the onset of the emergency. Authorities also indicated that 17,907 people lost their homes.

The Government response remains focused on the management of transitional camps and assistance to affected populations. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination with the authorities, continue implementing multisectoral response activities and scaling up assistance. On 10 July, United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher announced a US$299 million addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan to address the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months. The addendum complements the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, increasing the target population from 5.5 million to 6.2 million people and raising total funding requirements from US$632 million to US$931 million.

Note

Starting with this edition, the report will be published on a weekly basis. The next edition will be released on 30 July. We thank partner organizations, United Nations entities and donors for their valuable contributions, and encourage them to continue reporting their earthquake response activities through the 345W platform. For more information on reporting and the use of the tool, please refer to the presentation: 345W Preparedness and Response.

title: UNICEF Cameroon Cholera Outbreak Flash Update No. 2, 01-22 July 2026
content:
Situation update

  • Cholera outbreak continues to spread in Cameroon’s Far North Region, with 585 reported cases and 19 deaths as of 22 July 2026 across height affected health districts. The outbreak remains active, with a case fatality rate of 3.25% and 172 cases under treatment.
  • Children and vulnerable populations remain disproportionately affected, with a median age of 24 years. Ongoing cross-border movements and limited access to safe water and sanitation continue to increase the risk of further transmission.
  • UNICEF has activated a multisectoral response in support of government-led efforts, covering Health, WASH, SBC/AAP, Child Protection, Youth Engagement, and coordination. Additional flexible funding is urgently required to rapidly scale up life-saving interventions, strengthen preparedness, and prevent further transmission.

title: UNICEF Cameroon Humanitarian Situation Report No. 2, 01 Jan-30 June 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Cameroon continued to face a complex humanitarian situation during the first half of 2026, driven by protracted conflict in the North-West and South-West, insecurity in the Far North, the cholera outbreak and climate-related shocks. These overlapping crises continued to expose millions of children and vulnerable families.
  • UNICEF and partners sustained an integrated humanitarian response, expanding access to health, nutrition, education, child protection and WASH services while strengthening community engagement, accountability to affected populations, social cohesion, and outbreak preparedness despite persistent insecurity and humanitarian access constraints.
  • Humanitarian funding increased to US$4.9 million, reducing the 2026 Humanitarian Action for Children funding gap from US$52.3 million (97 per cent) to US$48.9 million (91 per cent). Despite this progress, critical funding shortages continue to constrain the scale-up of life-saving assistance.

SITUATION OVERVIEW AND HUMANITARIAN NEEDS

During the first half of 2026, Cameroon continued to face multiple and overlapping humanitarian crises driven by protracted conflict, population displacement, public health emergencies, climate-related shocks and recurrent localized disasters. The crises in the North- West and South-West (NWSW) regions and insecurity in the Lake Chad Basin (LCB) continued to affect children, women and vulnerable communities, limiting access to essential services, disrupting livelihoods and increasing protection risks.

The humanitarian situation further deteriorated during the second quarter with the emergence of a cholera outbreak in the Far North Region, affecting the health districts of Fotokol, Mada, Makary,
Kolofata., Maroua III and Kousseri. The outbreak occurred within a broader regional context, with neighbouring Chad and Nigeria simultaneously responding to cholera outbreaks, increasing the risk of cross-border transmission in this highly mobile border area.

Limited access to safe water and sanitation, poor hygiene conditions, seasonal flooding, population movements and weak health systems continued to fuel transmission and complicate response efforts. At the same time, Cameroon continued responding to Mpox and yellow fever outbreaks, further stretching already fragile health systems.

Across crisis-affected regions, children remained exposed to heightened risks of acute malnutrition, communicable diseases, violence, family separation, psychosocial distress and prolonged disruption of education. In the Far North, insecurity, recurrent attacks, climate shocks, food insecurity and cross-border population movements continued to undermine livelihoods and access to health, nutrition, WASH, education and child protection services. On July 2026, new displacement alert reported that approximately 100 households (600 people) had settled in a spontaneous emergency site in Andilbine 2, Makary, following repeated incursions by nonstate armed groups in the localities of Nage and Kimbelo, Hile Alifa.

Fires affecting internally displaced communities in Kolofata further increased humanitarian needs during the reporting period. In the NWSW regions, persistent insecurity continued to restrict humanitarian access and the delivery of essential services, particularly in hard-to-reach communities.

Despite continued humanitarian response efforts, needs consistently outpaced available resources. Persistent insecurity, access constraints, weak infrastructure, recurrent displacement and critical funding shortfalls continued to limit the scale and continuity of assistance. Additional flexible funding is urgently required to sustain integrated life-saving interventions, contain disease outbreaks including cholera, strengthen preparedness and cross-border coordination, and ensure that vulnerable children and their families receive timely, equitable and resilient support across Cameroon.

title: UNICEF Afghanistan Flash Update #1 (Eastern Region Flash Floods), 23 July 2026
content:
Situation Overview

• On 20 July, heavy rainfall triggered flash floods across three provinces in eastern Afghanistan. The most severe impact was reported in Parun City, Nuristan Province, where extensive flooding caused deaths, injuries, significant damages with disruption of services to the affected communities.

• Preliminary reports1 indicate 23 fatalities and 125 injuries, with additional individuals still missing. The floods destroyed and damaged 92 houses, while also impacting a health clinic, markets, and disrupting local livelihoods.

• Critical infrastructure and services sustained damages, including bridges, road sections, flood protection walls, agricultural land and damaged water supply networks, disrupting access to safe drinking water.

• Within 24 hours, UNICEF with partners were on the ground, providing immediate lifesaving emergency health services to cover over 600 people including children.

title: UNICEF Guinea-Bissau Flash Update No. 1 (Mpox Outbreak Response), 4–20 July 2026
content:
Situation Update

The Ministry of Public Health officially declared Guinea-Bissau’s first mpox outbreak on 4 July 2026. To date, three laboratory-confirmed cases have been reported: a 27-year-old female in Bissau (Cuntum) confirmed on 23 June; a 40-year-old male in Bissau (Bairro Militar); and a 19-year-old female in Safim (Biombo Region) confirmed on 13 July. A total of 26 contacts—9 in Bissau and 17 in Safim—are under active follow-up. No deaths have been reported.

The delay between symptom onset and isolation, alongside the lack of clear epidemiological links between cases, suggests undetected transmission is likely ongoing. While health authorities have not officially commented on the specific strain, the West African Clade II virus is the anticipated driver given its regional endemicity across West Africa. Finalizing the 42-day action plan remains a critical window of opportunity for early containment.

title: WFP Response to the Ebola Outbreak - External Situation Report (23 July 2026)
content:
SITUATION UPDATE

• The Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak continues to spread in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) affecting 47 health zones across five provinces: Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Tshopo, and Haut-Uele. While Ituri accounts for 90 percent of confirmed cases, recent spread to Tshopo (Kisangani) and Haut-Uélé increases the risk of wider transmission as Kisangani is a major transport hub. The outbreak is now spreading faster than previous Ebola outbreaks and has become the third-largest Ebola outbreak on record.

• In DRC, the outbreak is unfolding in a complex humanitarian environment, marked by conflict, large-scale displacement, limited access to basic services, including food, nutrition, clean water, shelter, health care, and protection, and an ongoing health workers strike.

• Community unrest continues to constrain surveillance and response activities. In July, WFP experienced two security incidents, including an attack that affected UNHAS operations in Niania, and community unrest in the Bule IDP site. WFP continues to engage local leaders and communities.

• In Uganda, no new cases have been reported since 21 June 2026. A 42-day enhanced surveillance period has started before the outbreak can be declared over in the country. National authorities in Uganda and the DRC, in collaboration with WHO and partners, continue to implement extensive preparedness and response measures.

title: UNHCR Somalia Protection and Solutions Monitoring Network (PSMN) Quarterly Report | April – June (Q2) 2026
content:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Somalia experienced three markedly different displacement patterns across Q2 2024, Q2 2025 and Q2 2026.
Total recorded displacement stood at 148,167 movements in Q2 2024, declined by 49 per cent to 75,843 in Q2
2025, and then rose sharply to 216,979 in Q2 2026. The 2026 total was therefore almost three times the Q2
2025 level and 46 per cent higher than Q2 2024.

The change was not only quantitative. The principal causes and geographical distribution of displacement also
shifted substantially:

  • Q2 2024 was dominated by widespread flooding, particularly in Belet Weyne and Afmadow.
  • Q2 2025 remained flood-dominated, but displacement was heavily concentrated in Jowhar and Balcad.
  • Q2 2026 became a compound conflict-drought crisis, with conflict accounting for 53 per cent and
    drought for 35 per cent of all movements.

Conflict and drought together generated 191,648 movements in Q2 2026, equivalent to 88 per cent of the national total. Flood displacement declined significantly, but remained locally severe in Belet Weyne, Jowhar and Banadir.

The geographical pattern also broadened. In Q2 2025, the three most affected districts accounted for 61 per cent of national displacement. In Q2 2026, this fell to 47 per cent, indicating that several major emergencies were occurring simultaneously across southern, central and northern Somalia.

Banadir became the leading displacement hub, recording 65,944 movements in Q2 2026, followed by Buuhoodle, Diinsoor, Laas Caanood, Bossaso, Galdogob, Jalalaqsi and Gaalkacyo.

Overall, the findings point to a transition from episodic, hazard-specific displacement to a more geographically dispersed and multi-causal crisis. Conflict, drought, livelihood erosion, market disruption, weakened coping capacity and urban concentration increasingly reinforce one another.

title: Sudan Protection Cluster Alert: Attacks on Critical Civilian Infrastructure in North Kordofan (23 July 2026)
content:
On 20 July 2026, local sources reported that three drones struck multiple locations in Al Rahad, North Kordofan.

The reported strikes impacted a health centre and an area adjacent to the main market during peak morning activity.

While casualty figures remain under verification, UNICEF subsequently reported tha at least 2 children were killed and 6 children, aged between 6 and 14, were injured. Local sources also reported that 4 adults were killed, and more than 20 others were injured.

The incident followed a reported attack on Al Musallamiya village on 19 July 2026, in which local sources reported that 13 civilians were killed.

On21 July 2026, local sources reported that in Al Hugeina village, approximately 30 km from Al Rahad a drone strike allegedly targeted a girls' primary school which is still under verification at the time of reporting. One teacher was reportedly injured.

title: Honduras - Operational update - June 2026
content:
Context

June was marked by continued violence, insecurity, forced displacement risks and legal developments affecting the protection environment in Honduras.

Reports during the month highlighted the persistence of organized criminal activity, extortion, violence against women, land-related conflicts, risks affecting children and adolescents, and climate-related pressures on communities with limited livelihood opportunities.

Forced displacement remained a key concern. The Norwegian Refugee Council ranked Honduras among the world's ten most neglected displacement crises, citing limited international attention, insufficient humanitarian funding and reduced political engagement. National human rights institutions also warned that violence continues to drive displacement, with many families facing insecurity and limited access to protection before leaving their communities or the country.

Violence continued to affect community safety and mobility. The Violence Observatory of the National Autonomous University of Honduras reported that some smaller municipalities are recording higher homicide rates than major urban centres, linking these trends to the expansion of organized crime and drug trafficking outside the country's largest cities. Authorities also reported increasingly fragmented extortion dynamics, with independent criminal actors accounting for a large share of complaints in recent years.

Women, children and adolescents remained exposed to heightened protection risks. Civil society organizations reported at least 135 femicides so far in 2026, while child protection actors documented a 12 per cent increase in violent deaths of children, adolescents and young people compared to the same period in 2025. During the reporting period, the National Congress approved legal reforms to increase penalties for femicide and strengthen sanctions under the Law against Domestic Violence.

The National Congress approved the Agro-industrial, Energy and Tourism Promotion Law and related reforms regulating evictions from occupied agricultural land. Indigenous, campesino and human rights organizations expressed concerns that the measures could increase risks of criminalization, displacement and tensions around longstanding land disputes.

Climate-related shocks added pressure to communities already affected by violence. National authorities warned that a prolonged dry spell could reduce basic grain production and affect food security for thousands of families. In southern Honduras, coastal communities in Cedeño, experienced impacts from storm surges associated with Tropical Storm Cristina, while human rights organizations called for a rights-based approach to the planned relocation of Cedeño.

title: WFP Eswatini Country Brief July 2026
content:
• WFP supported the Government in strengthening national food systems and resilience through continued implementation of the Home-Grown School Feeding Programme, smallholder farmer market access initiatives, and technical assistance aimed at improving local procurement, food quality, and nutrition-sensitive programming.
  • WFP continues to work closely with the Government of Eswatini and development partners to strengthen national social protection systems, enhance climate resilience, improve food systems, and support vulnerable populations through integrated food assistance, nutrition, school feeding and livelihood interventions.

title: Afghanistan: Flash Update #2: Flooding in Eastern Afghanistan (22 to 23 July 2026)
content:
Highlights

  • Heavy rainfall and flash floods have affected communities across several provinces in central, eastern and southeastern Afghanistan. The impacts range from loss of life and extensive damage to homes, public infrastructure and livelihoods to localized impacts affecting individual families.
  • Parun City in Nuristan Province remains the most severely affected location reported to date. According to figures shared by the local authorities with the inter-agency assessment teams, 23 people were killed, five remain missing and 125 were injured, including 38 with severe injuries and 87 with minor injuries. The completed inter-agency needs assessment identified 92 families eligible for humanitarian assistance.
  • In Paktika Province, flash floods affected Sara Qala village in Sharan City on 21 July. Initial reports indicate that three people were injured, 14 houses were destroyed, 37 livestock were killed, 10 vehicles were damaged and approximately 122 hectares of agricultural land were washed away.
  • In Paktia Province, flooding on 21 July affected 46 families in Ahmad Aba and Zurmat districts. The Provincial Disaster Management Committee (PDMC) is discussing the deployment of an assessment team.
  • In Ghazni Province, flooding on 20 July affected 66 households in Ghazni City. Joint needs assessment teams, comprising the International Organization for Migration (IOM), the World Food Programme (WFP), the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) and the Danish Refugee Council (DRC), have been deployed and the assessment is ongoing.
  • In Maidan Wardak Province, flooding in Sayedabad District affected two families, partially damaged their houses and resulted in one death. In Kapisa Province, the shelter of nine families in Tagab District was reportedly slightly affected.
  • Humanitarian partners are responding through emergency health, shelter, food, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), protection and other assistance, while assessments and early recovery planning continue across affected areas.

Regional Impact

As of 23 July, heavy rainfall and flooding have affected parts of the central, central highlands, eastern and southeastern regions, with significant variation in the scale of impact between locations.

Eastern Region

Nuristan Province

Parun City remains the most severely affected location reported to date. According to figures shared by the local authorities, the flooding resulted in 23 fatalities, while five people remain missing. A total of 125 people sustained injuries, including 38 with severe injuries and 87 with minor injuries.

The completed inter-agency needs assessment identified 92 families eligible for humanitarian assistance. Beyond the impact on affected households, the flooding caused extensive damage to community infrastructure, public facilities and livelihoods.

Six markets and approximately 70 shops were destroyed, significantly disrupting local economic activity. Approximately 400 metres of protection wall were damaged, increasing the risk of further flooding and erosion. One water-supply network, including approximately 500 metres of pipeline, was damaged, disrupting access to safe drinking water for an estimated 1,000 families. One of the two springs feeding the network was destroyed. The floods also damaged approximately 280 orchard trees and resulted in the loss of 30 livestock. Approximately 30 vehicles were damaged, four bridges were destroyed or severely damaged, and livelihood assets including carpentry workshops and two saw machines were affected. Public infrastructure damage included one mosque, one private clinic, approximately six kilometres of road and one micro-hydropower plant.

Nangarhar Province

Flooding affected Torkham and surrounding areas, including a returnee transit camp on the Pakistan side of the border. According to IOM and local sources, three Afghan refugees were reportedly killed and nine injured at the transit camp.

Flooding temporarily disrupted movement at the Torkham crossing, delaying the movement of returnees for approximately two hours. The floods also damaged the protection wall of the Directorate of Refugees and Repatriation compound at Zero Point, Torkham, where humanitarian partners are providing basic services to returnees. Private shops and livelihood-related installations at Torkham Zero Point were also reportedly damaged or washed away.

Laghman Province

Flash flooding was reported in Alingar District. According to the Afghanistan National Disaster Management Authority (ANDMA), no damage to residential houses had been reported at the time of the latest update. Agricultural land and irrigation systems were affected.

Ghazni Province

Flooding on 20 July affected 66 households in Ghazni City. Joint needs assessment teams have been deployed and the assessment is ongoing.

Southeastern Region

Paktika Province

Flash floods affected Sara Qala village in Sharan City on 21 July. Initial reports indicate that three people were injured, 14 houses were destroyed, 37 livestock were killed, 10 vehicles were damaged and approximately 122 hectares of agricultural land were washed away. Joint needs assessment teams were deployed on 22 July and the assessment is ongoing.

Paktia Province

Flooding on 21 July affected 46 families in Ahmad Aba and Zurmat districts. The Paktia Provincial Disaster Management Committee is discussing the deployment of an assessment team.

Central Region

Maidan Wardak Province

Flooding in Sayedabad District reportedly affected two families, partially damaged their houses and resulted in one person killed.

Kapisa Province

The shelter of nine families in Tagab District was reportedly slightly affected. No casualties or destroyed houses have been reported.

No reports related to the recent rainfall and flooding have been received from Kabul, Logar, Panjshir or Parwan provinces.

Central Highlands Region

No casualties, damage or destruction related to the recent rainfall and flooding have been reported from Bamyan or Daikundi provinces.

Humanitarian Needs and Response

The response has moved from immediate search and rescue and emergency life-saving assistance towards a broader, multi-sector response addressing shelter, health, food, WASH, protection, livelihoods and planning to address early recovery needs.

In Nuristan, the completed inter-agency needs assessment identified 92 families eligible for humanitarian assistance. Humanitarian partners are providing emergency assistance while coordinating the rehabilitation of damaged infrastructure and planning early recovery interventions.

In Ghazni and Paktika, joint needs assessment teams have been deployed and assessments are ongoing. In Paktia, coordination is underway to determine the deployment of an assessment team.

Across affected areas, humanitarian partners continue to monitor the situation and prioritize assistance based on verified needs and assessment findings.

Food Security & Agriculture (FSAC): The floods in Parun damaged approximately 280 orchard trees and resulted in the loss of 30 livestock. WFP has distributed High Energy Biscuits (HEBs) to 250 families, with additional supplies dispatched and further food assistance planned for 24 July. Shanti Volunteer Association is providing food assistance to 30 families in coordination with WFP.

Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) is reviewing the assessment findings and plans to support rehabilitation of irrigation canals, provision of livestock feed and other agriculture and livestock recovery interventions.

In Paktika, approximately 122 hectares of agricultural land were reportedly washed away and 37 livestock killed. Further impacts on agriculture and livelihoods in other affected provinces remain under assessment.

Shelter, Land and Site Coordination (SLSC): In Parun, 92 families identified as eligible for humanitarian assistance are receiving coordinated support. IOM is distributing 92 tents, 92 winter kits, 92 blankets and solar kits. UNICEF will distribute 92 non-food item (NFI) kits and hygiene kits each, while Save the Children (SCI) will provide 92 shelter repair kits. Distributions are planned for 23 July.

The extent of shelter damage in Ghazni and Paktia remains under assessment.

Health: The World Health Organization (WHO), in coordination with the Provincial Public Health Directorate (PPHD), the Basic Package of Health Services (BPHS) implementing partner ARSDO and other health partners, has dispatched additional medical supplies, including Emergency Health Kits (EHKs), Essential Health Kits (EH Kits), Trauma Kits and Cholera Response Kits.

Two Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) teams have been deployed, while two Mobile Health Teams (MHTs) remain on standby for rapid deployment. A specialized trauma expert team is scheduled to visit Parun on 27 July.

The United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), through its implementing partners MOVE and AFGA, has deployed a mobile psychosocial support team and two ambulances to facilitate referrals.

Première Urgence Internationale (PU-AMI) has dispatched medicines and medical consumables to the BPHS implementing partner. Handicap International (HI) and the Norwegian Committee for Afghanistan (NCA) have expressed readiness to provide physical rehabilitation services for injured people.

Further information on health needs in other newly affected provinces is expected through ongoing assessments.

Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH): In Parun, one water-supply network, including approximately 500 metres of pipeline, was damaged, disrupting access to safe drinking water for an estimated 1,000 families. One of the two springs feeding the network was destroyed.

Pending rehabilitation, UNICEF and WASH Cluster partners are exploring interim solutions, including water trucking and other emergency water-supply options. UNICEF is also distributing hygiene kits, while hygiene promoters will conduct hygiene awareness and promotion sessions. Humanitarian partners have raised concerns over the heightened risk of waterborne disease outbreaks following the flooding.

Protection: The Protection Coordination Group is coordinating critical protection services, including MHPSS, child- and women-friendly spaces, family tracing and reunification for separated children, and psychosocial counselling for families who have lost loved ones or have missing family members.

UNFPA has initiated prevention and response to gender-based violence (GBV) and MHPSS services and will distribute dignity kits to affected families. UNICEF’s implementing partner HYSO is conducting a child protection-focused needs assessment.

Cash Assistance: The Cash Working Group is coordinating potential Multi-Purpose Cash Assistance (MPCA). To date, Community World Service Asia has confirmed its readiness to provide MPCA to up to 200 affected families.

Coordination

OCHA, together with humanitarian partners and ANDMA, continues to coordinate the humanitarian response in collaboration with the United Nations and national and international non-governmental organization partners. Joint needs assessments have been completed in affected areas, while additional assessments are ongoing or planned to identify needs and inform response planning.

With inter-agency coordination mechanisms activated across affected regions, Operational Coordination Teams (OCTs) continue to meet and coordinate the response across affected provinces. Efforts are ongoing to scale up assistance in the most affected areas while supporting early recovery planning and the restoration of essential services and livelihoods.

This is a flash update based on information available as of 23 July 2026. Figures and other information remain subject to verification and may change as response activities continue.

title: Central African Republic: Situation Report No. 77, as of 21 July, 2026
crisis: Central African Republic: Cholera Outbreak - Jun 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • Am-Dafock: More than 1,800 people receive assistance through mobile clinics
  • 300 returnee households receive essential household items and non-food items in Zémio
  • Bambari: 500 people trained on epidemic risk prevention, alert and response

GENERAL CONTEXT

Mbomou Prefecture – South-East

  • During the night of 20–21 July, armed elements raided Tandjia village, located 12 km from Nzako, and abducted approximately 20 people, including children. 15 adults were released on 21 July, while six boys remained in captivity and were taken towards Ndenguilo village along the Chinko axis. Following the incident, the Central African Armed Forces (FACA) based in Nzako launched search operations. In response to heightened protection risks, particularly the abduction of children, local authorities conducted community awareness-raising activities, urging communities to restrict children's movements to farms, mining sites and hunting areas during the school holiday period.

HUMANITARIAN NEEDS AND RESPONSE

Multi-sector

Haut-Mbomou Prefecture – South-East

  • From 15 to 16 July, COOPI, in partnership with Action Communautaire pour la Reconstruction et le Développement Durable (ACRED), provided multi-sectoral assistance to 300 vulnerable households in Komboli village, near Zémio. The beneficiaries, who are returnees, received shelter kits comprising bamboo sheets, ropes and locally sourced timber, based on their preferences. Non-food items and essential household items were also distributed, including tarpaulins, blankets, sleeping mats, mosquito nets, buckets and kitchen utensils. In addition, each household received cash assistance to help cover costs related to the construction or rehabilitation of their shelters. The intervention forms part of the emergency response for internally displaced persons (IDPs), returnees and host communities in Zémio sub-prefecture, with support from the Central African Republic Humanitarian Fund (CAR HF).

Health

Countrywide

  • Between 10 and 20 July, seven new suspected cholera cases were reported, including four in health facilities and three in communities. No deaths were recorded during the reporting period. Since the outbreak was declared on 26 June, a cumulative total of 650 suspected cases and 44 deaths have been reported, while 595 people have recovered. Under the coordination of the Ministry of Health, response activities continued in affected areas. As part of efforts to strengthen epidemiological surveillance, 40 epidemiologists and data managers were trained to ensure the daily updating of surveillance data at the health district level. In addition, 25 traditional practitioners in Bangui were trained in active case finding and rapid referral of suspected cases to treatment facilities. Of the seven newly reported suspected cases, four are currently receiving treatment, including two at the Community Hospital, one at Bimbo Hospital and one at Maman Elisabeth Domitien University Hospital Center (CHUMED). Infection prevention and control activities continued, with 3,093 people sensitized on household water treatment and 69,120 water purifying tablets distributed. 21 households located around identified cases in Bokassa 1 and Bangui were disinfected. In addition, 125 handwashing stations were installed in the Bimbo and Mbaïki districts, and hygiene staff at the Community Hospital received training on infection prevention and control measures in healthcare settings. Key challenges to the response are data management and the mobilization of the resources required to contain the outbreak.

title: Syria Mine Action AoR Situation Update No.8 (March - July 2026)
content:
Explosive ordnance (EO) contamination remains one of the most significant protection, humanitarian, recovery and development challenges facing Syria. Between 1 March and 1 July 2026, 268 EO-related incidents were recorded nationwide, resulting in 452 casualties — 130 people killed and 322 injured.

Agricultural and grazing areas accounted for the majority of recorded incidents during the reporting period, underscoring the persistent link between contamination, livelihoods, food security, safe movement and recovery. Men and boys remain particularly exposed while farming, herding, travelling through contaminated areas and undertaking other livelihood-related activities, while children continue to be disproportionately affected when they encounter explosive items during play, movement, work or while supporting their families.

Mine action partners continued delivering survey, clearance, explosive ordnance risk education (EORE) and victim assistance (VA) across Syria. These efforts reduced risks to affected communities, enabled safer delivery of humanitarian assistance, and supported access to homes, services, agricultural land, infrastructure, reconstruction and recovery efforts.

The reporting period also saw important strategic developments, including the initiation of National Mine Action Strategy and National Mine Action Standards processes, the Syria Mine Action Partner Conference in Geneva convened by the Syria National Mine Action Centre (SNMAC) and the Geneva International Centre for Humanitarian Demining (GICHD), and the AoR’s successful participation in the National Directors’ Meeting (NDM). These developments helped elevate Syria’s contamination challenges, national ownership, coordination priorities, operational achievements and the need for sustained investment in mine action.

Despite this progress, operational and administrative constraints continued to affect the ability of some partners to scale activities in line with needs. Sustained funding, timely approvals, movement authorisations and the importation of specialised mine action equipment, tools and materials remain essential to enabling partners to respond safely and at the scale required.

Mine action is not optional - it is a necessary step in restoring safety, dignity, and the conditions for recovery across Syria.

This Situation Update was produced by the Syria Mine Action Area of Responsibility (MA AoR) in cooperation with the International NGO Safety Organisation (INSO), whose continued support in verifying EO-related data remains essential to understanding the scale and impact of explosive hazards across the country.

title: Lebanon: Flash Update #45 - Escalation of hostilities in Lebanon (as of 20 July 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • At least 4,328 deaths and 12,230 injuries recorded due to hostilities since 2 March, with 348 fatalities and 226 injuries since the latest ceasefire announcement, according to the Ministry of Public Health.
  • 741,111 people reported returning to their areas of origin, while 412,700 people remain displaced (as of 15 July), including 29,700 Internally Displaced Persons (over 53 per cent women and girls) in 278 collective shelters as of 20 July.
  • As some communities enter their fifth month of displacement, declining resources are placing critical interventions, including food assistance, cash-for-rent, protection services, and operational coordination, at risk of disruption from September 2026 without additional funding.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

Humanitarian and protection needs persist in Lebanon, as people experiencing prolonged displacement and those returning to conflict-affected areas continue to require urgent support. While the latest ceasefire announcement led to significant returns of over 700,000 people, ongoing security incidents in southern Lebanon continue to impede safe and sustainable returns, exacerbate protection risks, and disrupt service delivery and infrastructure rehabilitation. Reports of airstrikes, artillery shelling, demolitions and sonic grenades continued daily across South and Nabatieh governorates, including in Bint Jbeil, Marjayoun and Nabatieh districts in Nabatieh Governorate, and Tyre District in South Governorate.

As of 15 July, 412,700 people remain displaced across Lebanon, according to the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM). Although this represents a decrease of approximately 550,000 people since the ceasefire announcement, return movements have slowed in recent weeks, indicating that displacement levels are stabilizing as obstacles to return persist. The trend is also reflected in collective shelter occupancy, with 29,700 internally displaced persons (IDPs) residing in 278 collective shelters nationwide. While shelter populations have continued to decline gradually since early July, needs remain acute. Communities in collective shelters report deteriorating conditions in some shelters, sustained pressure on services, increasing reliance on debt to meet basic needs, and limited access to livelihood opportunities.

Returns continue, though at a slower pace, as challenges to return persist. As of 15 July, 741,111 people have begun returning to their areas of origin (DTM), including approximately 136,000 people who have returned to Nabatieh Governorate and 104,000 to South Governorate. Since early July, the largest increases in returnee populations were recorded in Saida District, South Governorate (4,875), Tyre District, South Governorate (3,835), and Bint Jbeil District, Nabatieh Governorate (1,841). Humanitarian assistance and protection services remain critical in areas of return, where widespread damage to housing, roads, water and electricity networks, and agricultural land continues to drive needs. Given ongoing insecurity and uneven access to services, returns remain fluid and may be reversible.

Operational pressures are increasing as the response enters its fifth month following the escalation of hostilities on 2 March. Communities in collective shelters report a reduction in the range and frequency of assistance compared with the 2024 response, reflecting the challenges of sustaining support at scale amid protracted displacement and deepening humanitarian needs. Food Security, Nutrition, Shelter and Protection partners anticipate critical funding shortfalls in the next six weeks without additional resources. Anticipated gaps include daily meal provision, cash-for-rent assistance, protection services, nutrition partner capacity, national and regional convoy services.

Humanitarian and protection needs remain acute among displaced populations, returnees, and host communities. Key concerns include explosive ordnance contamination, housing insecurity, economic hardship, civil documentation challenges, psychosocial distress and heightened protection risks, particularly for women, girls, children, older persons, persons with disabilities, and households experiencing prolonged displacement. Declining coping capacities, rising living costs and limited livelihood opportunities continue to deepen vulnerabilities of conflict-affected people.

Access to essential services remains constrained across many conflict-affected areas. Damage to water, electricity, health and public infrastructure continues to disrupt service delivery and increase reliance on temporary solutions. Water and electricity remain among the most frequently reported service gaps in return areas. Several hospitals and primary healthcare centres, particularly in hard-to-reach areas of South and Nabatieh governorates, remain closed or only partially operational due to infrastructure damage, staffing shortages and access constraints.

The Ministry of Public Health reported 4,328 people killed (including 392 women and 253 children) and 12,230 injured (1,450 women and 1,036 children) as of 13 July. 135 health care professionals have been killed on duty and 406 reported as injured since 2 March. Since the 20 June ceasefire announcement, 348 people have been killed and 226 injured.

Funding constraints remain a major challenge to sustaining humanitarian assistance. As of 20 July, the 2026 Lebanon Flash Appeal has received $284.8 million, or 44.5 per cent of the $639.9 million requested.

title: Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar - Bulletin Issue 17, July 2026
content:
Armed conflicts continue to intensify across Myanmar, and the Mechanism is advancing its investigations into indiscriminate or deliberate aerial and artillery attacks on civilians and their homes, schools, hospitals and places of worship. It is also continuing to focus on collecting and analysing evidence of unlawful detention and imprisonment, including physical and sexualized torture, committed by Myanmar security forces. It also continued investigations into ongoing crimes in Rakhine State alongside its long-standing investigations into earlier crimes committed against the Rohingya.

The Mechanism investigates serious international crimes committed by and against all individuals, regardless of the political affiliation, ethnicity or religion of either the perpetrators or the victims. To date, it has collected information and evidence from more than 1,600 sources and information providers, including 756 accounts from witnesses. It has also shared 146 packages of evidence and analysis with national and international investigative, prosecutorial and judicial authorities.

title: UNHCR Ukraine Housing and Winter 2025 Post Distribution Monitoring Report
content:
Overview

This report synthesizes five Computer-Assisted Telephone Interviewing (CATI)-based post distribution monitoring (PDM) assessments covering 2,150 households (HHs), examining humanitarian house repair for both war-affected and internally displaced people (IDPs), construction materials and Rapid Thermal Kit (RTK) assistance delivered in 2025. Sources: Windows Replacement (June 2026, n=290), House Repairs (May 2026, n=561), Construction Materials (May 2026, n=537), IDP Housing Repairs (March 2026, n=454), and Rapid Thermal Kits (April–May 2026, n=308). Service providers: Kyiv Institute of Sociology and Info Sapiens. Target sample sizes for each assessment were determined using a standard statistical sample-size formula (the normal-approximation/Cochran method), applying a 99% confidence level against each programme.

title: UNHCR Ukraine Winter Plan 2026-2027 [EN/UK]
content:
Context and Overview

▪ Winter 2025-2026 was particularly harsh in Ukraine. A report by the UN HRMMU found that Russian Armed Forces systematically and repeatedly targeted energy facilities across Ukraine throughout the 2025-2026 winter months – with electricity generation, transmission and distribution facilities hit at least 423 times between October 2025 and March 2026, including 48 coordinated attacks that targeted three or more regions using multiple types of weapons. These attacks triggered emergency electricity outages, affecting millions of civilians across the country, and disrupted critical utilities to hundreds of thousands of people, leaving many without heating and hot water as temperatures fell below -20°C in the coldest winter in Ukraine since 2010. The impact of these outages was particularly severe for people living in multistory buildings and for people with reduced mobility, including older persons and persons with disabilities.

▪ The REACH Cold Spots Risk Assessment for the 2026-2027 winter season found that the highest levels of risk remain concentrated in the north-east and east of Ukraine, particularly across Kharkivska, Sumska, Donetska, and Kyivska oblasts, where colder winter conditions overlap with war intensity, proximity to active hostilities or the Russian border, displacement, infrastructure disruption, and cumulative damage to electricity, water, and heating systems. Compared to previous years, winter-related vulnerability is increasingly shaped not only by proximity to the frontline, but also by broader energy-system disruption affecting large urban and densely populated areas. The REACH assessment highlights the growing importance of large urban areas – including cities such as Kyiv, Kharkiv, Odesa, and Dnipro – where disruptions to electricity, heating, water, and communication systems may affect large numbers of people. Meanwhile, parts of Khersonska, Zaporizka, and Odeska oblasts in southern Ukraine also demonstrate winter-related vulnerability linked to war exposure, infrastructure disruption, and utility outages.

▪ UNHCR’s border monitoring found that the lack of basic services also influenced people’s decisions to flee abroad last winter. People leaving Ukraine started citing lack of electricity, water, and heating among the top reasons for leaving in September 2025. In December 2025, January and February 2026, around 75% of people who left mentioned either lack of electricity, water or heating. About one-third of respondents who left Ukraine in January and February 2026 said that stabilization of the electricity situation was a main factor influencing a future return decision.

title: Bangladesh: Situation Report #2 - Flash Flood and Landslides (23 July 2026)
content:
Heavy monsoon rains, flash floods, and landslides continue to impact communities across Bangladesh, with an estimated 1.28 million people affected in seven districts, including more than 15,500 persons with disabilities. Approximately 436,000 people are estimated to require humanitarian assistance, while 59 deaths have been reported in the seven most affected districts as of 22 July 2026.

Government assessments indicate widespread damage to housing and essential services. A total of 74,479 houses have been damaged or destroyed, while flooding has fully or partially damaged 29,076 water points and 36,550 latrines, severely affecting access to safe water and sanitation across 42 upazilas in six districts.

The disaster has also had a significant impact on livelihoods and food security. Approximately 27,007 hectares of cropland have been affected, and more than 266,000 livestock have been impacted. Combined losses to the livestock and fisheries sectors are estimated at US$17.3 million across the affected districts.

Despite gradual improvements in some areas, active monsoon conditions continue to pose risks. The Bangladesh Meteorological Department forecast heavy to very heavy rainfall in Bandarban, Chattogram, and Cox’s Bazar and issued moderate- and low-risk landslide advisories for these districts.

Government authorities, humanitarian organizations, and development partners continue to scale up response efforts, providing food assistance, cash support, health services, protection interventions, shelter assistance, and water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) support to affected populations while assessments and recovery planning remain ongoing.

title: Venezuela Earthquakes: Situation Report #8 (July 22, 2026)
content:
Project HOPE continues to expand its humanitarian response across northern Venezuela. The team is significantly increasing access to healthcare for displaced and affected communities by operating eight mobile medical units (MMU), which are providing primary and maternal healthcare services in shelters and underserved communities. Project HOPE also continues to provide additional clinical support at health facilities in Distrito Capital and Miranda, with expansion underway to facilities in La Guaira. To reduce the risk of secondary public health emergencies, Project HOPE is also connecting families to mental health support, providing essential medicines, distributed additional hygiene kits through complementary funding, and recently launched a water trucking initiative.

Situation Overview

Humanitarian needs remain high as communities transition from the immediate aftermath of the earthquakes into a prolonged recovery phase. While debris removal and damage assessments continue, thousands of displaced people remain in temporary shelters with persistent needs for healthcare, safe water, sanitation, and protection services. Overcrowded living conditions, intermittent rainfall, and disruptions to essential services continue to increase the risk of infectious disease transmission. At the same time, health facilities face the pressure of a continued increase in demand for services, including for acute injuries and routine health needs that were interrupted by the disaster. As operations evolve, humanitarian partners are increasingly focused on restoring access to primary healthcare and strengthening local health services to support communities through recovery.

title: Venezuela Earthquake: Flash Update #3 (23 July 2026)
content:
1. Context

Three weeks after the 24 June earthquakes, the death toll and affected population continue increasing. OCHA has formalized the national response into a six-month Humanitarian Response Plan Addendum (July–Dec. 2026).

Toll: 5,278 dead, 16,740 injured, 6,462 rescued alive. Of the confirmed dead, 7% remain unidentified, mainly due to missing fingerprint records and identity system gaps.

Displacement: As of July 21, 107 transitional camps for affected populations have a total capacity of 27,822 people and current occupancy of 23,587 people. As of July 20, 41 camps are in Caracas, 28 in La Guaira, 28 in Miranda, and 10 in Aragua. Of the total camp population, 12,474 people are in La Guaira, 8,554 in Caracas, 1,877 in Miranda, and 682 in Aragua. These numbers are a snapshot, as the population in shelters changes constantly.

Debris: An estimated 1 million tons of debris has resulted from the earthquake. Of this, only 6,700 tons has been cleared in La Guaira so far, representing just 1% of the total.

Humanitarian funding request: OCHA's Humanitarian Response Plan Addendum requests USD 298 million to reach 1.3 million people over six months (JulyDecember 2026). This is in addition to the USD 930 million humanitarian funding appeal required for 6.2 million people in Venezuela prior to the earthquake Limited humanitarian operational presence: OCHA's own access assessment finds that Aragua, Carabobo, and Yaracuy have a relatively limited humanitarian operational presence. These states are accessible; the gap is a lack of resources. Priority needs as per the OCHA Rapid Needs Assessment: health (53%), safe water (52%), food security (50%), psychosocial support (27%), sanitation/hygiene (22%), protection/safety/dignity (18%), shelter (17%).
Economic constraints: June inflation hit 13.8%, more than double May's rate. National reconstruction cost estimates now range from USD 12–15 billion (internal field sourcing).

title: WFP Indonesia Country Brief, July 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Indonesia is an upper-middle-income country, with Gross National Income of USD 4,910 per capita in 2024 (World Bank). While poverty, inequality, and food insecurity have declined, malnutrition remains a concern.

• Indonesia ranked 70th of 123 countries on the 2025 Global Hunger Index. Undernourishment fell from 7.2 percent in 2024 to 6.3 percent in 2025, yet 62 of 514 districts and municipalities remained vulnerable to food insecurity.

• Gross domestic product grew 5.61 percent yearon-year in the first quarter of 2026, while inflation reached 4.76 percent by February 2026. Food price volatility is eroding household purchasing power, and a looming El Niño heightens the risk of drought and reduced rice yields.

• In 2025, Indonesia recorded about 4,691 environmental and extreme weather disasters, 26 percent more than in 2024. Most were linked to climate anomalies and affected more than 12 million people.

• WFP Indonesia supports the Government of Indonesia through policy dialogue and technical assistance on food security, school meals, climate risk, and disaster risk management.

title: Venezuela | Earthquake - Operation Update #1 (MDRVE015)
content:
A. SITUATION ANALYSIS
Description of the crisis

On 24 June 2026, two powerful earthquakes struck north-central Venezuela in rapid succession, with preliminary magnitudes of 7.2 and 7.5. Authorities have reported more than 1,000 aftershocks since the event, creating a high risk of further structural collapse. The epicentres were located near Morón and Yumare, in the states of Carabobo and Yaracuy, west of Caracas. The impact was severe and widespread, with tremors felt across much of the country, including the Capital District, La Guaira, Aragua, Carabobo, Miranda, Falcón, and neighbouring states.

The Government of Venezuela declared a National State of Emergency the same day and designated La Guaira, where the greatest concentration of damaged infrastructure and rescue operations was concentrated, as a disaster zone. According to the Global Disaster Awareness and Coordination System (GDACS), an estimated 9.73 million people have been affected, including approximately 530,000 exposed to extreme earthquake intensity.

The event occurred during the San Juan festivities, a national celebration that attracts large numbers of people to coastal areas; and as many workplaces were closed, this also led to families having many or all members present inside their home when the earthquakes happened. In La Guaira, a popular destination to spend this festivity, this resulted in higher population concentrations in public spaces and along the coastline at the time of the event, increasing the number of people potentially exposed to the impacts of the earthquakes.

As of 15 July, 4,829 people were reported dead, 16,740 injured and approximately 17,907 had lost their homes due to severe damage to housing1. It is expected for these figures to continue to rise in coming days as the Search and Rescue phase focused on extraction of survivors moves towards a focus on recovery, identification and return to family members of bodies retrieved from collapsed structures. Response teams from over 29 countries deployed to Venezuela, including the United Nations Disaster Assessment and Coordination (UNDAC) team and Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) teams operating under the coordination of the International Search and Rescue Advisory Group (INSARAG)2. International search and rescue deployments are progressively concluding, with several Movement teams having completed their missions. A response focused on search, recovery, debris-removal, shelter provision and efforts to bridge emergency relief to recovery and reconstruction efforts continues under national leadership, with a broad range of bilateral and multilateral support focused on humanitarian assistance, restoration of essential services and recovery.

According to OCHA, 2,501 infrastructure assets had sustained some degree of damage, with 856 affected buildings, including 190 that have collapsed.3 A comprehensive technical evaluation of structures is underway by respective authorities to identify homes that can be repaired and those that are too dangerous to return to. Evaluation of safe areas to build permanent housing for those affected is also taking place. Damage to residences, commercial buildings and critical infrastructure also disrupted the functioning of electricity, water-supply, telecommunications and transport systems, as well as public transportation and airport operations. Damaged roads and bridges have also restricted access and affected movement to and within some affected areas. The healthcare capacity has been particularly affected, with limited supply of water systems. More than 400 schools were also reported as affected, while some have been repurposed as temporary shelters until the academic cycle resumes after the summer. Damage to water systems has further affected the availability of basic services.

Moreover, it is important to note that the main affected area, La Guaira, fulfils multiple critical functions for the country. Its proximity to the Capital, Caracas, the presence of the country’s main international airport (Maiquetía) and one of its major ports, makes it a strategic transportation, logistics, trade, tourism, fishing and service hub. Consequently, the incident impacted not only local communities and visitors present, but also essential infrastructure and activities that facilitate connectivity and the supply of goods to the capital and other regions of the country. This increases the number of people and logistical capacity affected.

The physical impacts on affected people remain significant, with thousands of injured, many requiring continued medical care, rehabilitation or referral services, and with families displaced after the destruction or severe damage of their homes. Beyond these physical impacts, the earthquakes have also had significant effects on the mental health and psychosocial well-being of affected people. Many families have experienced loss and grief, injury, displacement, separation from relatives and loss of homes, livelihoods and community support networks. The magnitude of the tragedy on human terms, continued aftershocks, uncertainty regarding housing and recovery, and exposure to damaged environments and recovery operations has contributed to heightened levels of stress, anxiety and sadness among the affected populations.

Notably, La Guaira’s geographical location is prone to various types of emergencies. In December 1999, torrential rainfall triggered catastrophic landslides, flash floods and debris flows across the then State of Vargas—now La Guaira—causing widespread destruction and displacement. The exact death toll remains uncertain; however, the United States Geological Survey estimated that between 15,000 and 30,000 people were killed. The current earthquake has therefore affected communities with lived and intergenerational memories of one of Venezuela’s most severe disasters.

title: DZA: Fire - 07-2026 - Algeria: Wildfires – July 2026 (2026-07-22)
content:
Description

On 18 July 2026, the wildfire emergency in Algeria reached a significant operational peak, with 154 forest, vegetation and agricultural fires recorded within 24 hours across several wilayas. Of these, 138 fires were extinguished, while 16 remained active at the time of reporting.

The fires affected northern, north-eastern, central and western Algeria, including Annaba, Souk Ahras, Skikda, Guelma, Bouira, Médéa, Mila, Mascara, El Tarf, Jijel, Sétif, Béjaïa, Tlemcen, Saïda, Tissemsilt, Biskra and Chlef.

Over the last 24 hours, the Ministry of the Interior, Local Authorities and Transport confirmed six fatalities linked to the wildfires. In Seraïdi, Annaba, more than 100 patients were evacuated from a rehabilitation hospital, while approximately 150 homes were affected or threatened. Preventive evacuations were also carried out in several localities, including El Tarf, Béjaïa, Guelma and Bouira.

The Government of Algeria has led a strong and coordinated national response, ensuring the rapid mobilization of the competent authorities and emergency services. Efforts have focused on protecting lives, supporting affected communities, securing threatened areas and maintaining close operational coordination across the affected wilayas.

The Algerian Red Crescent mobilized its provinces committees, volunteers and logistical resources from the beginning of the emergency. Teams provided first aid, drinking water, food assistance, psychosocial support and essential humanitarian assistance to affected communities and emergency responders.

Response and monitoring activities continue, while high temperatures, dry vegetation, difficult terrain and the risk of fire re-ignition remain important operational considerations.

title: Earthquakes in Venezuela: Situation Report #29 (22 July 2026, Time: 09:00 pm)
content:
Situation Report No. 29
Earthquakes in Venezuela
22 July 2026
Time: 9:00 pm

Highlights

  • Authorities report 1,463 aftershocks since the 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude earthquakes that struck on 24 June.
  • Official toll: 5,398 people dead and 16,740 injured.
  • The United Nations system and its partner organizations continue scaling up the multisectoral response to the emergency. To address the needs of 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months, an additional appeal of US$299 million was launched

Situation overview

Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre located along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). Authorities report 1,463 aftershocks.

Twenty-four days since the earthquakes, authorities report a toll of 5,398 people dead and 16,740 injured since the onset of the emergency. Authorities also indicated that 17,907 people lost their homes.

The Government response remains focused on the management of transitional camps and assistance to affected populations. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination with the authorities, continue implementing multisectoral response activities and scaling up assistance. On 10 July, United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher announced a US$299 million addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan to address the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months. The addendum complements the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, increasing the target population from 5.5 million to 6.2 million people and raising total funding requirements from US$632 million to US$931 million.

title: Shelter Cluster - Palestine Situation Report, June 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

GAZA

• Shelter Cluster partners continued delivering life-saving Shelter and NFI assistance across the Gaza Strip throughout June, responding to urgent needs among affected households through in-kind and voucher modalities. In June 2026, a total of 36,210 households were reached with shelter and NFI support. Distributed items included 17,626 tarpaulins, 14,814 kitchen sets, 12,670 bedding kits, 7,055 bedding items, 1,334 tents, 504 clothing voucher CVA, 50 clothing kits, and 65 sealing off kits. These interventions remained critical in addressing urgent shelter and household needs, supporting vulnerable and displaced populations, improving living conditions, and helping families cope with ongoing displacement and deteriorating humanitarian conditions across Gaza.

• Under the Rapid Joint Distribution Mechanism (RJDM), a significant increase in incident alerts was reported during the reporting period. Recorded incidents included artillery shelling, airstrikes, domestic fires, and forced displacement, affecting thousands of people across the Gaza Strip. Following rapid assessments, partners assisted 587 households with shelter and non-food item (SNFI) support. Of these, 464 households received joint response packages, while 123 households received shelter and NFI assistance tailored to their specific needs.

• Available stocks of essential household items inside Gaza have reached critically low levels, with remaining supplies sufficient to support fewer than 15,300 additional households. The facilitation of Shelter and NFI material entry remains urgently required to sustain response operations and respond to ongoing humanitarian needs, particularly considering increased seasonal requirements during the summer period.

• Shelter partners also reported additional interventions comprising the following:

◦ Emergency repairs and upgrades were completed for 1,837 makeshift shelters, bringing the cumulative number of upgraded makeshift shelters to 2,696.

◦ Emergency Shelter Kits (ESKs) were newly installed for 500 households, increasing the total number of installed ESKs to 867.

• In addition, partners completed emergency repairs to 1,025 partially damaged homes across Gaza’s governorates, bringing the cumulative total of rehabilitated housing units to approximately 1,299 by the end of June.

• During June, the distribution of solar-powered lamps to 7,200 households across the Gaza Strip was underway with support from IOM. The intervention targets 26 displacement sites in both northern and southern Gaza. An update from the implementing partner is still pending and has not yet been received by the Shelter Cluster (SC).

• Pipeline constraints continue to significantly limit the shelter response. The timely release of materials currently in the pipeline—particularly solar lights, timber for framing kits, ropes, and tools—remains essential to enable partners to scale up priority interventions. These include repairs of partially damaged shelters, upgrading makeshift shelters, and supporting a gradual transition toward early recovery activities.

title: Ukraine war situation update | 4 - 10 July 2026
content:
Ukraine strikes dozens of Russian shadow fleet vessels to cripple trade and logistics through the Azov Sea.

Author

Olha Polishchuk

Eastern Europe, Caucasus, and Central Asia Research Manager

Key stats

1,948 political violence events

3% decrease compared to last week

204 incidents of violence targeting civilians

14% decrease compared to last week

At least 110 civilians killed by targeted violence

10% decrease compared to last week

6 Jul.

Kyiv — Russian drones and missiles cause detonations in an unauthorized weapons warehouse in Vyshneve, killing nine civilians

6 Jul.

Kyiv — Russian drones and missiles kill 19 civilians and injure 76 others in Kyiv city

6 Jul.

Omsk, Russia — Ukrainian drones strike an oil refinery in Omsk, around 2,500 kilometers from the Russian-Ukrainian border

Key trends

  • Russian forces occupied two settlements close to the Russia-Ukraine border in the Sumy region and another settlement north of Dvorichna in the Kharkiv region.
  • Ukrainian forces regained control of a village in the Donetsk region, near the boundary with the Dnipropetrovsk region.
  • Russian forces launched at least 64 long-range missile and drone attacks, including on Kyiv city and the surrounding region.
  • Russian strikes reportedly killed at least 95 civilians in the city of Kyiv and across the Donetsk, Kharkiv, Kyiv, Kherson, Zaporizhia, Odesa, Mykolaiv, Sumy, and Dnipropetrovsk regions. Ukrainian strikes reportedly killed at least 15 civilians in the Russian-occupied parts of the Luhansk, Zaporizhia, Kherson, and Kharkiv regions, as well as in the occupied Crimea, and the Azov Sea.

Spotlight: Ukraine intensifies its campaign of targeting Russian vessels to cripple maritime export and supply routes

Beginning on 6 July, Ukraine has embarked on a campaign of targeted drone strikes on Russian and Russian-affiliated vessels, primarily in the Azov Sea, but also in the Black Sea. By 13 July, the number of impacted vessels exceeded 100 and will likely keep growing until maritime traffic to the Russian and Russian-controlled shores in the Azov Sea is effectively crippled. Most of the targeted vessels were Russian and foreign-flagged shadow fleet oil tankers, but Ukrainian drones also struck several tugboats, cargo ships, and ferries. During one of the attacks on 10 July, a crew member of an oil tanker was killed.

These naval attacks are yet another escalation in Ukraine’s campaign of targeting the Russian oil industry and energy sector more broadly, which started with long-range attacks on mainly export-oriented oil infrastructure in Russia back in 2024. The campaign has since expanded to other fuel and power infrastructure, as well as to Russian shadow fleet vessels transporting sanctioned oil. This latest series of strikes completely overshadowed attacks on over 20 Russian shadow fleet vessels recorded since 2025, prior to this escalation.

The choice of the Azov Sea as the area of focus for these strikes seems aimed not just at clogging traffic but also at being symbolic, since the sea is surrounded by a Russian-controlled coast and is treated by Russia as its internal waters. All vessels in the area have either a Russian registration or a Russian authorization to engage in Russian trade or logistics. The attacks also support Ukraine’s recent campaign to isolate Crimea by targeting not only the land logistics network but also maritime supply routes.

Ukraine justified the campaign by claiming that Russian shadow fleet vessels are lawful military targets because they financially sustain the Russian war in Ukraine due to sanction evasion and high profits. The legality of targeting a civilian industry due to its financial contribution to military spending is heavily disputed, particularly in the naval context, where seizure – not the targeting of enemy civilian vessels – is a recognized lawful method of economic warfare. In particular, the Secretary-General of the International Maritime Organization condemned the attacks against civilian merchant ships in the Azov and Black Seas, stating that they were not parties to the conflict. Aside from the legality of targeting the oil industry, Russian shadow fleet vessels have also been used by Russia for hybrid warfare and intelligence gathering, transporting Russian troops, and sailing under military convoys, though it is not clear whether any of the vessels hit during this campaign engaged in this activity.

As a result of Ukraine’s naval campaign, Russia decided to halt shipping through the Don-Azov canal, an important maritime corridor for exporting oil, agricultural products, and other goods, but also an exit route for the Caspian flotilla of the Russian Navy.

title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #15 (20 to 21 July 2026)
content:
The fifteenth Situation Report provides an update on IOM’s response to the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, covering the period from 20 to 21 July.

Highlights

Between 20 and 21 July, IOM continued its multisectoral response in transitory camps and affected communities through interventions in shelter and site coordination, health, protection, WASH and information management.

To date, IOM has reached 8,542 unique individuals through 15,460 instances of assistance and services, mainly in shelter and transitory camp coordination, protection, health and WASH.

IOM and its partner Fundación Vivienda Popular have distributed 3,055 kitchen sets, 2,590 tarpaulins, 2,039 buckets, 1,676 solar lamps and 819 shelter kits to affected households.

IOM activities

IOM continued managing and coordinating five transitory camps in La Guaira and advanced the operational transition of three of them to the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC).

At José María Vargas Sports Complex, IOM maintained essential services for 316 families and supported registration activities. Coordination and registration continued at César Nieves and Playa Grande, while preparations were finalized at Tanaguarena Golf Course for the installation of additional infrastructure.

In WASH, IOM continued expanding access to safe water storage and hygiene items. To date, 1,552 collapsible water containers, 1,009 hygiene kits and 92 semi-collapsible water containers have been distributed.

IOM and its partner Ven Da Tu Mano have provided 5,552 medical consultations, including general and specialized care, medication distribution and psychological support. Mobile health and MHPSS services remained operational at José María Vargas and César Nieves.

IOM continued household registration and population data updates across five camps and conducted a mobility intentions survey in José María Vargas, César Nieves and Playa Grande to identify needs, displacement patterns and intentions to return or relocate.

In protection, IOM continued providing guidance, legal assistance, documentation support and referrals to specialized services, with 130 people assisted and supported to date.

IOM planned response

IOM will continue the operational transition of three camps to NRC, assistance distributions and infrastructure improvements, while strengthening WASH, health, mental health and protection services.

It will also strengthen camp and mobility monitoring, multisectoral assessments inside and outside the sites, and coordination with authorities and partners.
