title: WHO Weekly Situation Update on Ongoing Health Emergency Events in South Sudan - Week #: 29; Date: 13 - 19 Jul 2026
content:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

South Sudan remains in EVD/BVD preparedness and readiness mode, with no confirmed cases to date. National readiness climbed to 65% in July (from 45% in June and 29% in May), above the WHO African Region average of 55%. Transmission stays active in DR Congo 2,124 confirmed cases and 828 deaths across 46 health zones in five provinces, while Uganda entered a 42-day enhanced-surveillance period. Cumulative PoE screening reached 570,599 travellers, and one alert at Nimule is under investigation. Cholera rose 12.7% week-on-week (391 new cases), with a fresh resurgence in Fangak (Juaibor). Polio reported no new isolates; measles remained localized (4 cases pending); and malaria rose 7.3% w/w but remains far below 2025 levels. The Jonglei & Akobo humanitarian situation is deepening GAM at 22.3%, IPC Phase 5 in several counties, and ~620,000 displaced since January.

PRIORITY ACTIONS

  • Deliver the OCV mop-up vaccines to Rubkona, Mayom & Leer (pre-campaign complete) and mount an integrated WASH/case-management response to the cholera resurgence in Fangak (Juaibor).
  • Restore routine immunization in Akobo (0%), Nyirol (25%) & Uror (55%), provide solar-powered vaccine refrigerators, run catch-up campaigns and resolve antigen stockouts to avert a measles outbreak.
  • Deploy 4 State RRT members to Fangak for 7 days and provide cholera response supplies (IPC, IV fluids, ORS); expedite laboratory testing of stool samples.
  • Close remaining EVD readiness gaps before a possible imported case and conduct the Bor County BVD readiness assessment (22 July), training 30 frontline workers.
  • Scale up the nutrition response across Jonglei (GAM 22.3%, IPC Phase 5 in Akobo, Uror, Nyirol & Fangak) for children under five, pregnant and lactating women.

title: WHO Situation Report No. 1: Flash Floods in Eastern Afghanistan (July 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

On 20 July 2026, intense rainfall triggered severe flash floods across Nuristan Province in eastern Afghanistan, with the most significant impacts reported in Parun City, the provincial capital of Nuristan Province. Floodwaters rapidly inundated populated areas, causing widespread damage to homes, public infrastructure, agricultural land and commercial properties. Preliminary reports indicate significant loss of life, injuries and extensive disruption to livelihoods, essential services and local markets.

To date, 23 deaths and 15 injuries have been reported, while additional individuals remain missing across the affected areas. Search and rescue operations are ongoing. Casualty figures are expected to rise as assessment teams gain access to affected locations and rescue efforts continue.

WHO and partners are closely coordinating with local health authorities to support rapid assessments, deploy emergency health supplies and ensure the continuity of essential health services, including care for injured and affected populations.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

Intense rainfall triggered severe flash floods in eastern Afghanistan near Parun City, the provincial capital of Nuristan Province, at approximately 15:00 local time on 20 July 2026. The floods caused significant loss of life, injuries, and widespread damage to homes, public infrastructure, markets, roads and livelihoods in Parun City and surrounding communities.

The situation remains fluid, with search and rescue operations ongoing in Parun City and surrounding areas. Humanitarian partners and de facto authorities are providing emergency health assistance and other life-saving support to affected communities. Mobile Health Teams have been deployed, health facilities placed on heightened alert, and additional medical, nutrition and food supplies mobilized to address immediate needs.

Emergency response operations are ongoing. Health workers, search and rescue teams, and humanitarian partners have been mobilized to provide lifesaving medical care, emergency supplies and mental health and psychosocial support to affected communities.

WHO will continue to coordinate closely with national and provincial health authorities and partners to address the most urgent health needs of affected populations, support ongoing response efforts, and ensure the continuity of essential health services.

title: Yemen — Rapid Displacement Tracking — Quarterly Report (April – June 2026)
content:
During the reporting period (1 April–30 June 2026), IOM Yemen’s Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) recorded 465 newly displaced households (approximately 2,790 individuals) in accessible locations within IRG-administered areas. This represents a 44 per cent decrease compared to Q1 2026 (827 households). Displacement was highest in May (192 households), followed by June (177 households) and April (96 households).

Geographically, displacement was primarily concentrated in Ma’rib (286 households), which accounted for approximately 62 per cent of all recorded movements during the quarter. This was followed by Al Hodeidah (79 households, 17%), Ta’iz (55 households, 12%), and Lahj (27 households, 6%), while smaller numbers were recorded in Ad Dali’ (12 households, 3%) and Shabwah (6 households, 1%).

Among displacement drivers, economic reasons related to conflict emerged as the main trigger, accounting for 236 households (51%) of all recorded movements. Conflict-related insecurity accounted for 175 households (38%), while natural hazard-related events contributed to 53 households (11%). Health-related reasons were reported by one household (less than 1 per cent).

Overall, the findings highlight a decline in displacement levels compared to the previous quarter, alongside a shift in displacement dynamics: economic pressures overtook conflict as the primary reported driver of displacement, while conflict and natural hazard-related events continued to contribute to population movements.

title: Somalia — Emergency Trend Tracking Report — Week 05 (July 2026)
content:
DTM launched a new round of ETT on 14 June 2026 using an updated methodology to monitor displacement driven by conflict, as well as the climatic impacts of the El Niño phenomenon, which is expected to trigger significant displacement toward the end of the year. DTM teams collect data in five districts: Baidoa, Dayniile, Diinsoor, Doolow, and Kahda.

ETT is a crisis-based tool that tracks sudden displacement triggered by specific events or emerging crises. Its objective is to support the prioritization of humanitarian response and enable partners to deliver rapid assistance. It includes information on new arrivals, the number and demographics of IDPs, reasons for displacement, intentions, humanitarian assistance received, and priority needs, among others. Based on previous shock induced displacement patterns, the humanitarian community expects continued movement toward urban areas in search of services. Consequently, ETT coverage focuses on main urban centers and surrounding villages within each assessed district.

title: Zimbabwe Emergency Cholera Response, 2026 - DREF Operation (MDRZW029), 20 July 2026
content:
Date of event

02-07-2026

What happened, where and when?

Zimbabwe is experiencing a renewed cholera outbreak less than two years after controlling its largest cholera epidemic in more than a decade. During the previous outbreak, which occurred between February 2023 and June 2024, Zimbabwe recorded 34,549 suspected cases and 718 deaths, with transmission spreading from Chegutu District to all ten provinces and reaching its peak during June–July 2023.

Following a coordinated multisectoral response, cholera cases declined, and the outbreak was officially declared over on 9 August 2024, after the last reported case was recorded on 30 June 2024. After approximately twelve months without sustained local transmission, cholera re-emerged in 2026, marking the start of a new outbreak.

The current outbreak began on 22 January 2026 in Rushinga District, Mashonaland Central Province, and has since spread to multiple geographically distinct locations across Zimbabwe. Confirmed outbreaks have been reported in Nyanga, Mutasa, Mutare City, Chipinge, and Chimanimani districts in Manicaland Province, as well as Zvishavane District in Midlands Province. The outbreak is unusual because it is occurring during the winter period (May–July 2026) where environmental survival and spread of Vibrio cholerae is reduced. This is outside the traditional rainy-season cholera transmission period when higher temperatures, rainfall, and flooding typically increase contamination of water sources and facilitate disease transmission. The persistence of transmission during the dry season indicates that other drivers, including population mobility, and chronic WASH services deficiencies, are sustaining the outbreak.

The emergence of winter transmission therefore represents a shift in the epidemiology of cholera in Zimbabwe. There is a high likelihood that the outbreak will persist into the next rainy season starting in the next 3 months from October, when environmental conditions become more favourable for accelerated transmission. Also, the outbreak has been affecting mainly non traditional rural hotspots, which increases risk of transmission to neighbouring traditional major hotspots like Harare and Buhera, the major epicentre of the 2023-2024 cholera outbreak where 44 people died from about 2 223 suspected cases recorded. Historical data has shown that once an outbreak reaches major hotspots like Harare, it quickly spreads all over the country. Sporadic outbreaks may thus continue to emerge in geographically distinct districts through repeated importation of cases. This pattern has already been observed since January 2026, with outbreaks successively occurring in Rushinga, Nyanga, Zvishavane and multiple districts within Manicaland Province.

In Zvishavane District, Midlands Province, the outbreak began on 9 May 2026 in a mining setting. By 28 June 2026, a total of 42 suspected cases had been reported, including 13 cases positive by Rapid Diagnostic Test (RDT) and 10 culture-confirmed cases. In Manicaland Province, the outbreak was reported from 14 June 2026, with 24 cases reported by 25 June 2026, including five culture-confirmed cases and one death. Since then, additional cases have been reported in Mutare City (4 cases), Chipinge (1 case), Chimanimani (1 case), and Mutasa (11 cases), demonstrating continued geographical expansion within the province.

title: Venezuela Emergency Response, Situation Report #4 (9 – 20 July 2026)
content:
OPERATIONAL CONTEXT

Nearly one month after the earthquakes, the humanitarian response in Venezuela is rapidly transitioning from the immediate emergency phase to a more structured, large-scale operation. Indeed, humanitarian needs remain immense: over 23,000 people live in transitional camps, thousands more remain displaced in host communities or informal settlements, and damaged housing and basic infrastructure continue to limit access to safe shelter, water, sanitation, healthcare and livelihoods.ii

As aftershocks continue – over 1,300 registered up until now – the humanitarian response continues to expand in scale and complexity. Humanitarian actors are now planning assistance for 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the coming six months, yet significant humanitarian gaps remain, as many communities remain underserved. This requires humanitarian actors that can rapidly identify unmet needs, coordinate effectively with existing response structures and deliver assistance where it is needed most.

Against this backdrop, CESVI has paired rapid operational deployment with early engagement in humanitarian coordination mechanisms, ensuring that field evidence collected from the first days of the emergency directly informed operational planning, strengthened partnerships and supported the targeting of communities that remained outside the initial humanitarian response.

title: Situation Report 3 - Foods and landslides In India - Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Jammu & Kashmir, Nagaland, Sikkim and Uttarakhand (Date: 21st July 2026)
content:
A. Situation Overview :

Heavy monsoon rainfall across multiple regions of India has triggered widespread flooding and landslides, affecting several states including Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Jammu & Kashmir, Nagaland, Sikkim and Uttarakhand. Rivers such as the Brahmaputra, Burhidihing, Disang, Dhansiri (S) and Dikhou are flowing above danger levels, with Dikhou crossing the highest flood level. Continuous rainfall has led to large-scale inundation, erosion, road blockages, and disruption of essential services.

1. Assam Flood - Severe Flooding Across 16 Districts

Assam remains the worst-affected state, with 16 districts impacted and 794 villages inundated. Major rivers—including the Brahmaputra, Burhidihing, Disang, Dhansiri (S)—are flowing above danger levels, with Dikhou (Sivasagar) crossing the highest flood level. Large-scale flooding continues in Sivasagar, Charaideo, Jorhat, Dhemaji, Golaghat, and Tinsukia.

Impact on Humans

A total of 362,933 people were affected across the 16 districts. Sivasagar (157,727 affected), Charaideo (104,415), Jorhat (50,987), and Dhemaji (21,700) reported the highest human impact. 9,606 people were staying in relief camps, including 3,837 men, 3,828 women, 1,924 children, 16 pregnant/lactating mothers, and 1 person with disability.

Animal Husbandry

Loss Animal losses increased sharply, with over 600,000 animals affected across districts. Sivasagar alone reported 512,041 animals impacted, followed by Dhemaji (34,618), Jorhat (24,748), Golaghat (10,140), and Tinsukia (4,992). Poultry losses were extremely high in Sivasagar.

Structural and Property Damages

The report does not list specific house damages for 21 July, but widespread inundation and erosion indicate significant risk to residential and community structures across multiple districts.

Road and Transport Infrastructure

Road connectivity was severely disrupted across Dhemaji, Dibrugarh, Biswanath, Lakhimpur, and Sivasagar due to erosion, dyke breaches, and culvert washouts. Several PWD roads, village roads, and embankment roads were damaged, affecting access to relief and essential services.

Irrigation and Water Supply

Multiple crop areas were submerged—over 19,099 hectares statewide. Irrigation channels in Sivasagar, Golaghat, and Dhemaji were affected due to prolonged inundation, though no major irrigation bund breaches were reported.

Electricity and Power Supply

No major damage to electrical infrastructure was reported, though localized disruptions occurred in inundated pockets.

title: PAK: Pluvial/Flash Flood - 06-2026 - Monsoon Floods, Situation Update #2 (2026-07-21)
content:
Description

Since the onset of the 2026 southwest monsoon on 28 June, intermittent to heavy rainfall has affected several parts of Pakistan, significantly increasing the risk of flash floods, riverine flooding, cloudbursts, landslides, urban flooding, thunderstorms, and Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF)-related incidents, particularly across northern and mountainous regions. Successive monsoon spells have impacted Gilgit-Baltistan (GB), Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP), Punjab, Balochistan, and Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK), resulting in localized flooding, damage to residential houses and critical infrastructure, disruption of transport and communication networks, and humanitarian impacts in vulnerable districts. The National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), Provincial Disaster Management Authorities (PDMAs), and the Pakistan Meteorological Department (PMD) continue to closely monitor the evolving situation and issue regular weather advisories and impact-based forecasts.

Between 28 June and 21 July 2026, multiple weather-related incidents were reported from Gilgit-Baltistan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Punjab, Balochistan, and Azad Jammu and Kashmir. The most affected districts included Diamer, Ghizer, Ghanche, Nagar, Astore, Upper Chitral, Lower Chitral, Shangla, Khyber, Lower Dir, Mardan, Rajanpur, Dera Ghazi Khan, Khuzdar, and Neelum. Reported impacts included flash floods, cloudbursts, landslides, damage to residential houses, schools, roads, bridges, irrigation channels, water supply schemes, electricity infrastructure, standing crops, orchards, and other public facilities, resulting in casualties, injuries, displacement, and disruption of essential services. Provincial Disaster Management Authorities (PDMAs), district administrations, rescue services, and relevant line departments continue to conduct rapid damage assessments, emergency response, and restoration activities in the affected areas.

Among the significant incidents reported during the period, a cloudburst on 19 July in Lari Mengal, Doga Top, and Katha Peeran (Union Council Salkhala, Tehsil Athmuqam, District Neelum, AJK) triggered a flash flood that damaged educational institutions, residential houses, commercial shops, and vehicles. Rescue teams and relevant government departments immediately initiated response operations, rapid damage assessments, and the relocation of affected families to safer locations. On the same day, heavy rainfall triggered flash flooding in Rupal Valley, Sub-Division Shounter, District Astore, Gilgit-Baltistan, where no casualties or damage to residential houses were reported, although minor damage to agricultural crops occurred. Subsequently, on 21 July, another flash flood in Louse Village, District Astore, inundated several residential houses, damaging household belongings and essential assets. According to the initial assessment conducted by the District Disaster Management Authority Astore, number of houses were severely affected, and the Gilgit-Baltistan Disaster Management Authority (GBDMA) initiated arrangements for the distribution of emergency relief items while detailed assessments remain ongoing.

According to the latest PMD and NDMA weather advisories, active monsoon conditions are expected to persist through 24 July 2026. Moist monsoon currents from the Arabian Sea, supported by a shallow westerly wave, are likely to generate widespread rain with isolated heavy to very heavy falls over Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Gilgit-Baltistan, Azad Jammu and Kashmir, northeastern Punjab, and adjoining hilly areas. Localized flash flooding, landslides, cloudbursts, and GLOF-related incidents remain possible, particularly across mountainous and upper catchment areas. Although the Indus, Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, and Sutlej rivers are currently flowing within normal ranges and no significant riverine flooding is anticipated, authorities continue to closely monitor river flows, rainfall patterns, and vulnerable locations due to the possibility of localized high-impact weather events.

Request For Assistance

Government Requests International Assistance

No

NS Requests International Assistance

No

Summary

The National aSociety remains in close coordination with Provincial and District Branches, the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), Provincial/State Disaster Management Authorities (PDMAs/SDMA), district administrations, and other relevant government departments to monitor the evolving monsoon situation, assess humanitarian needs, and support preparedness and response. The PRCS Emergency Operations Centre (EOC) continues to monitor weather forecasts, official advisories, and field updates on a 24/7 basis to ensure timely information sharing and coordination. PRCS remains on operational standby, with Emergency Operations Centres at National and Branch levels operational and District Disaster Response Teams (DDRTs), Community Disaster Response Teams (CDRTs), National Disaster Response Team (NDRT) members, First Aid volunteers, and trained staff ready for deployment. Pre-positioned emergency relief stocks remain available for rapid mobilization based on assessed needs. Following the 19 July 2026 cloudburst in District Neelum, Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK), the PRCS AJK State and District Neelum Branches immediately coordinated with the district administration, shared the initial incident report with NHQ, and supported rapid needs assessments. PRCS NHQ continues to closely coordinate with the AJK Branch, NDMA, SDMA, and district authorities while remaining ready to provide humanitarian assistance, if required. To strengthen Movement coordination and the National Society's preparedness and response, the first Movement Coordination Meeting is being convened on 22 July 2026. The meeting will provide updates on the evolving monsoon situation, review preparedness and response actions, identify operational and resource gaps, and enhance coordination among Movement partners to ensure timely and effective humanitarian support, if required.

title: Colombia: Volcanic Eruption Imminent DREF Final Report (MDRCO033)
content:
Event development

Update regarding the event’s development

On 29 November 2025, the Colombian Geological Service (SGC) announced the change of the Puracé volcano activity level to Orange Alert, following evidence of a sudden and sustained increase in the volcano’s internal activity. This behavior was characterized by a significant rise in the energy and frequency of seismic events associated with fluid movement, as well as continuous gas and ash emissions reaching columns over 1,000 meters high. In addition, the monitoring cameras installed in the area continuously recorded these manifestations, clearly evidencing a scenario of increasing instability and a much more active and complex internal dynamic within the volcanic system than usual.

The phenomenon developed at the Puracé volcano, located approximately 27 kilometres southeast of Popayán, in the department of Cauca. In addition to activity observed at the crater, fine ashfall was reported in several areas of the territory, particularly in the Río Negro village (Paletará district), Mina de Azufre, Agua Hirviendo, the road to Totoró, and northern sectors of Popayán. These reports confirmed that the effects of the volcanic activity extended beyond the immediate surroundings of the volcano, affecting air quality and the daily dynamics of nearby rural and urban communities. Consequently, the Municipality of Puracé declared a state of public calamity in response to the increase in volcanic activity, triggering preparedness actions by emergency response agencies for the evacuation of families located in the highest-risk areas.

The change to Orange Alert status for the Puracé volcano generated a direct and noticeable impact on the communities located within its area of influence. As the volcano’s internal activity increased, emissions of fine ash and volcanic gases began spreading towards populated areas, immediately affecting air quality and the daily routines of local families. Rural sectors such as the Río Negro village (Paletará district), as well as the areas known as Mina de Azufre, Agua Hirviendo, and the road to Totoró, reported ashfall and a strong sulfur odor, raising concern among residents due to respiratory impacts and the contamination of surface water sources.

The impact also extended to the northern area of the city of Popayán, where the presence of airborne particles forced the population to adopt basic protective measures, such as covering water storage containers, reducing outdoor activities, and reinforcing the use of face masks. These atmospheric conditions, combined with the visible increase in gas and ash columns rising between 500 meters and up to 1.7 kilometers above the crater, heightened the population’s perception of risk and created an environment of constant alert.

After nearly two months under Orange Alert status, the Puracé volcano returned to a lower level of instability on 22 January 2026, as the parameters monitored by the SGC indicated a decrease in the probability of a large-magnitude eruption.

title: Earthquakes in Venezuela: Situation Report #28 (21 July 2026, Time: 09:00 pm)
content:
Situation Report No. 28
Earthquakes in Venezuela
21 July 2026
Time: 9:00 pm

Highlights

  • Authorities report 1,405 aftershocks since the 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude earthquakes that struck on 24 June.
  • Official toll: 5,346 people dead and 16,740 injured.
  • The United Nations system and its partner organizations continue scaling up the multisectoral response to the emergency. To address the needs of 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months, an additional appeal of US$299 million was launched

Situation overview

Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre located along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). Authorities report 1,405 aftershocks.

Twenty-four days since the earthquakes, authorities report a toll of 5,346 people dead and 16,740 injured since the onset of the emergency. Authorities also indicated that 17,907 people lost their homes.

The Government response remains focused on the management of transitional camps and assistance to affected populations. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination with the authorities, continue implementing multisectoral response activities and scaling up assistance. On 10 July, United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher announced a US$299 million addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan to address the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months. The addendum complements the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, increasing the target population from 5.5 million to 6.2 million people and raising total funding requirements from US$632 million to US$931 million.

title: Taw Oo District Situation Update: Burma Army activities caused livelihood, fuel, education, and healthcare challenges in Htaw Ta Htoo Township (January to March 2026)
content:
This Situation Update describes events occurring in Htaw Ta Htoo (Htantabin) Township, Taw Oo (Toungoo) District, during the period between January to March 2026. During a Burma Army rotation in Kaw Thay Der village tract, Burma Army soldiers trespassed through villagers’ plantations and forced villagers to walk with them. Additionally, they ate and destroyed villagers’ crops. In March 2026, Karen National Liberation Army (KNLA) soldiers attacked Burma Army soldiers at a garbage dumping site in Kaw Thay Der village tract, injuring five Burma Army soldiers and damaging two lamp posts. Additionally, the presence of Burma Army soldiers at checkpoints between Toungoo Town and Kaw Thay Der village tract caused difficulties for villagers. Burma Army soldiers extorted villagers; looted food and medicines; seized motorbikes and cars; put restrictions on the carrying of foods, oil, petrol, and medicines; and charged merchants high prices to pass through with their goods. Due to the high price of petrol, some hill farmers and motorbike taxi drivers gave up their jobs because they were not making profit from their work. Moreover, flooding and landslides in October 2025 restricted travel to Toungoo Town, leaving villagers unable to sell their harvested crops, causing financial harm. In early 2026, a middle school in Ag--- village faced challenges as teachers submitted resignation letters after hearing derogatory comments from parents and school commission members, leading students to change to a school in town, which caused financial challenges for their parents. The shortage of teachers and inadequate supply of textbooks in Kaw Thay Der village tract undermined the stability of the education system, leaving students with limited education. Finally, Kaw Thay Der village tract is located far away from clinics and hospitals. There were no doctors, and medicines were not easily accessible, causing unnecessary deaths within the village tract.[1]

This Situation Update describes events occurring in Kaw Thay Der village tract,[2] Htaw Ta Htoo (Htantabin) Township, Taw Oo (Toungoo) District, from January to March 2026. Kaw Thay Der village tract has fewer cases of human rights violations [compared to other village tracts] because it is located far away from the SSPC [State Security and Peace Commission[3] also known as Burma Army][4]-controlled area.

Human rights violations occurred when Burma Army soldiers rotated

There are five SAC [State Administration Council][5] camps in Kaw Thay Der village tract: Bu Ser Hkee army camp, Kaw Thay Der army camp, Koe Day army camp, Baw G’Lee army camp, and Tit Say Taung army camp. In Kaw Thay Der village tract, not much fighting has taken place, so SAC soldiers come into the village [tract] to purchase food, and they usually walk around in the village tract. Once a month, the SAC rotates soldiers from one camp to another camp and sends rations to their army camps. When the soldiers were doing their rotation, they trespassed through villagers’ plantations instead of using the village road, and the soldiers plucked and pulled out cardamom trees and ate and destroyed durians and betelnuts from the villagers’ plantation fields. In addition, when the soldiers found villagers in the plantation fields, they forced villagers to walk with them [as human shields] and they also threatened them. Thus, the soldiers’ rotations have become a challenge for the villagers.

In Kaw Thay Der village tract, there are Karen National Liberation Army (KNLA)[6] soldiers administered by the KNU [Karen National Union].[7] Once a month, when the SAC soldiers transport rations into their army camps, the KNLA attacks the SAC soldiers with tripwire mines. [For instance,] on 20 March 2026, the KNLA attacked the SAC soldiers with tripwires [that the KNLA could trigger to detonate] at a garbage dumping site, which is located between Aa--- village and Ab--- village, Kaw Thay Der village tract. A villager reported that, due to the attack, five SAC soldiers sustained injuries, and two lamp posts were damaged. However, there was no intense fighting in Kaw Thay Der village tract.

Economic challenges in Kaw Thay Der village tract

Villagers from Kaw Thay Der village tract regularly purchase their food and goods from Toungoo Town. There are five SAC checkpoints between Toungoo Town and Kaw Thay Der village tract. Villagers from Kaw Thay Der village tract, especially Ac---, Ad---, Ae---, and Af--- villages, are located very far away from towns. [The further the distance, the more tollgates there are that villagers have to cross.] The SAC soldiers at the checkpoints charged more money than they should have from passing merchants. So, the merchants increased the price of their goods [when they arrived at the village] to make a profit. Consequently, it has become more difficult for the villagers who already faced extreme financial issues. Additionally, the SAC soldiers [at the checkpoint] also looted food from the merchants and seized cars and motorbikes. All these factors have resulted in significant difficulties for the villagers. In addition, villagers have to pay tollgate fees to the KNU as well. Thus, the villagers faced livelihood and transportation challenges.

[The issue of tollgates and checkpoints demanding high fees from drivers happened not only in January to March 2026 but also in July 2025.] In July 2025, [on an unknown date,] having bought medicines, a villager from Ag--- village, Kaw Thay Der village tract, was returning from Toungoo Town to Ag--- village. When the villager arrived at the Baya Chay Yin tollgate, which is located on the Thandaunggyi road, [Burma Army soldiers from the gate] looted medicines which were bought by the villager and also threatened him by saying they would put him in jail. Then, they told him that he could pay money if he did not want to go to jail. So, the villager paid 30,000,000 kyats (14,285.71 USD[8]). Following the mid-year of 2025, villagers who travelled within Kaw Thay Der village tract encountered extreme difficulties while traveling. Medicines, oil, petrol, and rice were restricted from being transported [through the gate]. [However,] some drivers [secretly] carried some oil and rice [while driving through the gate]. When the soldiers from the gate found rice and oil in the car, they kept it for themselves. The soldiers also took fish and meats from the drivers without paying the drivers any compensation fee. [This tollgate continued to operate during the reporting period, and villagers remained concerned about crossing it.]

In October 2025, flooding and landslides happened in Toungoo Town and roads to towns were restricted. Most villagers from Kaw Thay Der village tract have durian and mangosteen plantations. These types of fruits have a short shelf life. [When these seasonal] fruits were ready to harvest, villagers did not get the chance to sell them as roads were still restricted for travel [during the reporting period] due to the landslide [and have many checkpoints]. This [transportation challenge] caused shortages of basic food such as rice, oil, and salt. As a result, stealing occurred more frequently within the village tract. It therefore became a challenge for the villagers to support their livelihoods.

Impact of the fuel crisis in Kaw Thay Der village tract

On 3 March 2026, the SAC released an announcement letter ordering a reduction in fuel consumption. The next morning numerous petrol stations shut down completely. However, a few petrol stations remained open and sold limited amounts of fuel. Before the announcement, a litre of fuel cost 3,000 kyats (1.43 USD); however, after the announcement, within a week, the price of a litre of fuel increased from 3,000 kyats to 6,000 kyats (1.43 USD to 2.86 USD), and after, 10,000 kyats (4.76 USD). At the moment [as of March 2026], in mountain areas, a litre of fuel cost 15,000 kyats (7.14 USD). In Toungoo Town, fuel stations sold limited fuel on particular dates, only to licensed motorbikes. The high price of fuel negatively impacted villagers’ livelihoods in Kaw Thay Der village tract. For instance, villagers used machines that required fuel to cut down trees and bushes on their hill farms before they did plantation work. Now [as of March] a litre of fuel cost 15,000 kyats (7.14 USD), and the daily labour fee also cost 15,000 kyats (7.14 USD) per person, excluding three meals a day. Thus, it was not worth it to hire a daily labourer, which caused extreme difficulties for villagers. Moreover, some villagers used to work as motorbike taxis, driving to far places, but after the fuel price changed, they stopped working.

Education challenges in Kaw Thay Der village tract

Before the dictatorship came to power [in the 2021 coup], there were only SAC government schools in Kaw Thay Der village tract. However, after the 2021 coup, KECD [Karen Education and Culture Department][9] schools were established in the village tract. Before, students did not know how to read or write in the Karen language. But now [after the 2021 coup], under the KECD curriculum, the students are able to read and write Karen very well, even though KECD schools have Karen subject classes only up to Grade 5.

Kaw Thay Der village tract has 16 villages, but it only has 11 schools: one high school, three middle schools, and seven primary schools. Those 11 schools’ curriculums were administered by the KECD. The schools received support from the KECD, students’ parents, and village heads. The schools are self-funded schools. When students finish high school in Kaw Thay Der village tract, they continue their education by going to Ah--- Junior College [administered by the KECD] in Ai--- village, Peh Htee village tract, Htaw Ta Htoo Township, and Aj--- school in Maw Nay Pwa village tract, Htaw Ta Htoo Township.

Teachers who work in the [KECD] schools are villagers who finished high school within the village or villagers who attended college. The teachers are volunteer teachers. However, the parents were not pleased with the volunteer teachers. They believed that the teachers who did not finish school would not be able to teach children properly. To illustrate, during the 2025-2026 school year there were 16 teachers at a middle school in Ag--- village. Teachers received 45,000 kyats (21.43 USD) per month from students’ parents; yet the teachers disregarded monetary concerns and continued teaching in schools voluntarily. However, teachers were discouraged to teach when they heard derogatory comments from some school commission members and some students’ parents. One of the school commissioners said that 13 out of 16 teachers submitted resignation letters. This environment had a negative impact on the students’ education. Teachers changed frequently, and it caused difficulties for students to study properly. Furthermore, it was hard for the school to employ 13 [replacement] teachers during the three months of summertime [March to May 2026]. Thus, some parents wanted to send their children to SAC schools, religious schools, and NUG [National Unity Government][10] schools in Toungoo Town. Parents who did not have money or did not have relatives in towns struggled financially to send their children to towns to study.

[Another issue occurred in] Ab--- school located in Ab--- village, Kaw Thay Der village tract, which has classes from Grade 1 to Grade 6, but there were only two teachers, so students did not get to study effectively. Additionally, inadequate books for students have become an obstacle to access education. Villagers could print books in towns; however, villagers were afraid to travel to towns because there are [Burma Army] checkpoints on the way.

Healthcare challenges in Kaw Thay Der village tract

Although there are 16 villages in Kaw Thay Der village tract, there are only two clinics: Ak--- clinic and Al--- clinic. Before the rise of the dictatorship, there was a hospital in Baw G’Lee Town. After the 2021 coup, many healthcare workers from Am--- hospital joined the Civil Disobedience Movement (CDM)[11] causing a staff shortage. Thus, at the moment [as of March 2026], the hospital was closed. There were no doctors in the villages and medicines were not easily available for sale or purchase. Generally, villagers approached other villagers to receive treatment. Villagers who had advanced diseases approached the nearest hospitals in Toungoo Town to receive treatment. Some villagers who should have lived ended up dying because the distance between the villages and the hospitals was too far. In addition, villagers faced financial struggles to receive treatment. It was very challenging to access healthcare.

Further background reading on the situation in Taw Oo District in Southeast Burma/Myanmar can be found in the following KHRG reports:

  • Stolen Childhoods: Violations of children’s rights, urgent needs, and local agency in rural Southeast Burma during the conflict, October 2025.
  • “Taw Oo District Short Update: Burma Army shelling and air strike injured two children, damaged villagers’ houses, and caused displacement in Htaw Ta Htoo Township (July 2025)”, June 2026.
  • “Taw Oo District Short Update: Burma Army air strikes injured a 16-year-old girl and damaged six houses in Daw Hpah Hkoh Township (February to March 2026)”, May 2026.

title: Locust Watch: Seasonal precipitation predictions in the Desert Locust summer and winter breeding areas (August 2026–January 2027) (21 July 2026)
content: El Niño forcing continues to dominate the seasonal precipitation forecasts, and the outlook is nearly unchanged from last month, with minor changes in the predicted precipitation anomalies in a few regions. First, the dry signal has intensified over western India and southeastern Pakistan in August and September, reflecting both the stronger El Niño signal and a slightly less positive Indian Ocean Dipole phase. Wet conditions are still expected to develop across the Horn of Africa in September, extending to northern and eastern Africa and the Middle East in October, with stronger August–October dryness in India and Pakistan, while wetter conditions are expected in western Africa. Another minor shift is a stronger wet signal across the northern Sahel from September through November, with the notable wet anomaly likely indicating a delayed end to the rainy season. Summer breeding will occur in Mauritania and, at a smaller scale, in other Sahelian areas. Breeding should continue in the Western Region during August and September, increasing the risk of outbreaks from September onwards.

title: UNICEF Venezuela Humanitarian Situation Report No.5 (Earthquake Response), 13-20 July 2026
content:
Highlights

  • More than three weeks after the earthquakes of 24 June, official figures report 5,208 deaths, 16,740 people injured, and 17,907 people left without housing.1 Humanitarian needs remain significant, particularly among displaced families residing in transitional camps and communities with disrupted access to essential services.
  • UNICEF continues to scale up multi-sectoral assistance, focusing on health, nutrition, WASH and child protection services for children and families affected by the earthquakes, reaching over 7,519 people in the initial phase of the response. Health services through mobile health teams have reached around 2,108 people, while vaccination campaigns have reached 6,466 people. More than 2,452 children have been screened for acute malnutrition. WASH services are expanding at temporary shelters reaching 7,180 with critical hygiene supplies and 2,861 benefiting from access to safe drinking water. Psychosocial support and recreational activities have reached more than 2,726 children, adolescents and caregivers. Additionally, more than 4,400 people have been reached with hygiene promotion messages and critical information on available life-saving services.
  • UNICEF will reach 150,000 people with critical emergency supplies within the coming weeks, including 49,000 with health supplies, 72,000 with micronutrients, and 29,000 with WASH items. An additional 49 tons of emergency supplies arrived on 14 July to replenish in-country emergency stockpiles.
  • In addition to the US$137.6 million requested under the 2026 Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) appeal and aligned with the addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan 2026, UNICEF requires US$65.7 million to respond to the humanitarian impact of the earthquakes.

This situation report provides updates on the Ebola Bundibugyo Virus Disease (BVD) Outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). It outlines planned and ongoing telecommunications activities of the Logistics & Telecommunications Cluster1 (LTC) Telecoms to support the ongoing humanitarian response.

Summary Points

  • The Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak in the DRC continues to expand, with cases surpassing 2,000 and more than 700 deaths recorded across five affected provinces. The spread of the disease into Haut-Uele and Tshopo increases the likelihood that telecommunications support may need to expand beyond the initial priority areas to support surveillance, coordination, and response operations.
  • Security communications equipment, including Very High Frequency (VHF) radio repeaters and a radio-over-IP gateway, arrived in Bunia between 13 to 17 July. LTC Telecoms and UNDSS will configure and operationalize the equipment to strengthen radio network reliability and support security communications for humanitarian responders across Ituri.
  • A solar backup power solution for Mongbwalu General Hospital, together with equipment needed to repair and set up the NGO security communications channel, is being mobilized from Dubai. The items are expected to arrive in Bunia via UNHAS from Entebbe in early August, strengthening both connectivity resilience and security communications for responders in Ituri.

title: Dengue in the Pacific: Multicountry Situation (As of 20 July 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

• Since 1 January 2025, 12 dengue outbreaks have been reported in the Pacific Islands Countries and areas (PICs).

• The following PICs reported dengue outbreaks in 2025: American Samoa, Cook Islands, Fiji, French Polynesia, Kiribati, Nauru, Samoa, Tonga and Tuvalu. In 2025 there were 21 258 confirmed cases and 21 deaths reported across the Pacific Dengue fatalities were reported in Fiji (n=8), Samoa (n=7), Tonga (n=3), Nauru (n=2) and Kiribati (n=1).

• In 2026 dengue outbreaks were officially declared in New Caledonia, Tonga and Shefa province Vanuatu.

• The most affected countries and areas in 2026 include: Cook Islands, French Polynesia, Samoa, and New Caledonia. These account for 94% of confirmed cases.

• Dengue serotype-1 (DENV-1) and serotype-2 (DENV-2) are currently in circulation.

• Cook Islands declared the end of its outbreak on 25 May 2026.

• As of 20 July 2026: o The dengue outbreak remains ongoing in Shefa Province, Vanuatu, with dengue virus serotype 1 (DENV-1) continuing to circulate. o Low levels of transmission are observed in American Samoa, Kiribati, New Caledonia, Samoa, and Tonga. o Wallis and Futuna is under monitoring, as community transmission has recently been reported in both Wallis and Futuna.

title: UNHCR Afghanistan Situation Regional Update June 2026
content:
Operational Context

In Afghanistan, large-scale returns from Iran and Pakistan continued to strain border reception facilities and humanitarian services. Temporary disruptions at key border crossings, including during Muharram – an important period of religious observance in the Islamic calendar – delayed processing and onward movements for some returnees. The security situation remained volatile amid heightened cross-border tensions and reported incidents in eastern and southeastern border areas. Operational constraints, including restrictions affecting national female United Nations staff and smartphone use, required close coordination with authorities, partners and security colleagues to sustain the humanitarian response. In Iran, the political, security and economic landscape remained challenging. Security incidents heightened uncertainty and protection risks, while rising living costs increased humanitarian needs among refugees and host communities. In this context, UNHCR maintained its presence across Tehran, Mashhad, Isfahan, Kerman and the Dogharoun border, enabling continued monitoring, protection support and the delivery of critical assistance to refugees and other people in need of international protection. In Pakistan, arrests and returns of Afghans declined in June compared to May, largely due to the Ashura holidays (a major religious observance marking the 10th day of Muharram) and temporary border closures. However, a Government directive issued on 28 June requiring the immediate arrest of Afghans without valid visas from 10 July heightened uncertainty among Afghan communities and increased intentions to return although no immediate increase in arrests was observed during the reporting period. The implementation of the Illegal Foreigners’ Repatriation Plan (IFRP), alongside border security concerns and counter-terrorism operations, continued to shape the operational context. Enhanced security measures during Muharram, including increased law enforcement deployments, temporary movement restrictions and periodic communication disruptions in some areas, affected mobility and humanitarian access. These developments heightened protection risks, affected return decisions and constrained humanitarian assistance in parts of the country.

title: Nepal, Western Terai | Flood - Simplified Early Action Protocol Operations Update (sEAP №: sEAP2026NP03) - July 2026
content:
Flood is one of the most severe hazards in Nepal in terms of physical and socioeconomic losses. Major perennial rivers such as Koshi, Karnali, and Narayani often cause flooding across multiple districts of the Southern Terai, while rivers originating in the Mahabharat range, including West Rapti and Babai, frequently generate flash floods that disproportionately impact low-lying floodplains. The Terai’s vulnerable topography and dependence on agriculture further exacerbate flood impacts.

Historically, floods have caused significant devastation. In 2017, prolonged rainfall from 11–14 August affected 31 districts, impacting an estimated 450,000 people and resulting in 43 deaths. According to the Government of Nepal’s National Planning Commission Post Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA) 2017, 41,626 houses were destroyed and 150,510 damaged, over 126,000 hectares of paddy were lost, and livestock—including 812,000 poultry and 9,400 cattle—suffered severe losses. Major flood disasters in 2006, 2008, 2013, 2014, and 2017 repeatedly affected Bardiya, Kailali, and Banke districts, causing widespread infrastructure damage, including roads, bridges, culverts, local markets, and residential areas. Flooding has also occurred outside the monsoon season, such as the October 2022 Babai flood affecting Bardiya district.

Nepal Red Cross Society (NRCS) household surveys conducted in 2021–2022 show that along the Babai River, 25,247 families live in Barbardiya, Thakurbaba, Madhuwan, and Gulariya municipalities, while 21,032 families reside along the West Rapti River in Rapti Sonari, Duduwa, and Narainapur municipalities.

Flooding in these districts has intensified between 2023 and 2025. In Banke district, particularly Rapti Sonari,
Duduwa, and Narainapur, approximately 4,500–5,000 households were affected in 2023, rising to approx. 7,500 households in 2024, with nearly 1,500 displaced, and remaining high at 6,000 households in 2025. Impacts included repeated paddy crop losses, damage to irrigation systems and roads, and riverbank erosion. In Bardiya district, including Rajapur, Geruwa, Barbardiya, Thakurbaba, and Gulariya municipalities, approx. 7,000 households were affected in 2023, rising sharply to around 13,000 households in 2024—including approximately 3,000 displaced households—and 11,000 households affected in 2025. Damage encompassed inundation, extensive crop losses, livestock mortality, and infrastructure damage, alongside urban flooding in low-lying areas.

These trends highlight the increasing severity and frequency of flood impacts in the West Rapti and Babai basins, underlining the continued support of anticipatory action, early warning systems, and community resilience measures.

title: Islamic Relief Pakistan: Humanitarian Situation Report (Period: 26-June to 20-July 2026)
content:
BACKGROUND

Pakistan continues to face severe and compounding risks from both economic fragility and climate-induced disasters. The country remains among the most disaster-prone globally, ranking 18th out of 191 countries in the INFORM Risk Index, reflecting high exposure to hazards, vulnerability, and limited coping capacity. Over the past decade, disaster related damages have exceeded USD 18 billion, significantly constraining economic growth and development progress. More recent climate assessments also indicate that Pakistan is among the top 10 most climate vulnerable countries globally, despite contributing less than 1% of global greenhouse gas emissions.

Pakistan's 2026 monsoon began on 26 June and is forecast by the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) to bring 22–26% more rainfall than the previous season, compounded by accelerated melt across the country's more than 7,000 glaciers. As of the latest NDMA daily sitrep, the cumulative death toll (38) remains far below the same point in the catastrophic 2022 and 2025 seasons — but the situation has escalated in the past 24 hours: NDMA and PDMA Punjab have moved from advisory to an active flood alert for the Chenab, Jhelum and Ravi rivers from 20–24 July, with evacuations already being directed in low-lying and riverbank areas. Current figures should be read as a running total from an in progress, intensifying season, not a final toll.

According to the State Disaster Management Authority (SDMA), a cloudburst in Neelum Valley caused significant damage to infrastructure, including houses, shops, government schools, and bridges. Losses of livestock were also reported in the affected areas. The Azad Jammu and Kashmir State Disaster Management Authority (AJK SDMA) is closely monitoring the situation and has initiated coordination, response, and relief efforts in collaboration with relevant departments and local authorities to support affected communities.

As of 20 July 2026, a total of 47 deaths and 123 injuries have been reported nationwide. The majority of casualties resulted from house collapses and flash floods triggered by heavy rainfall. Additionally, 178 houses have been damaged, either fully or partially, while 179 livestock have perished. These numbers are expected to increase as ongoing rainfall and forecasted precipitation continue to impact affected areas.

title: Weekly Update: Lebanon (14 - 20 July 2026)
content:
Political Context: IDF Escalation Amid Withdrawal Pressure

The 14 to 20 July 2026 period recorded the highest IDF operational tempo of the post-MoU environment: 92 incidents, 57 percent of all activity, a sharp increase from the prior week’s 71. The escalation was concentrated in Nabatieh and included airstrikes, a guided missile strike that killed two on the Ali al-Taher heights on 16 July, and a systematic campaign of burning and demolishing residential properties across southern border communities.

This intensification comes precisely as US pressure on Israel to redeploy from both Lebanon and Syria has become public, with President Trump reported to have urged the Israeli prime minister to withdraw. Israel has still not redeployed from the two Lebanese pilot zones it committed to vacate under the framework agreement, and the US-brokered talks addressing that stalemate produced no announced movement. Against this backdrop, an operational surge and a housing-destruction campaign indicate that Israel is consolidating its southern Lebanon posture rather than preparing to reduce it.

title: Afghanistan: Flash Update #1: Flooding in Eastern Afghanistan (20 to 21 July 2026)
content:
Highlights

  • Heavy rainfall and flash floods affected parts of eastern Afghanistan on 20 July, with the most severe impacts reported in Parun City, Nuristan Province, alongside flooding in Torkham, Nangarhar Province, and Alingar District, Laghman Province.
  • Parun City, Nuristan Province, was severely affected by a sudden flash flood at approximately 15:00 hrs on 20 July. So far 23 people have been confirmed dead, 15 have been injured with others reported missing. Search and rescue operations are ongoing.
  • The flooding caused extensive damage to homes, public infrastructure, markets, roads and livelihoods in Parun. At least 22 houses were completely destroyed and approximately 45 houses were severely damaged according to preliminary assessments. Five markets and some 70 local shops were also damaged. In addition, four bridges, six road sections, 400 metres of protection wall and 450 metres of irrigation canal have sustained damage. Approximately 50 jeribs (10 hectares) of agricultural land were affected.
  • Damage to a water-supply network has disrupted access to safe drinking water for approximately 1,000 families. Twenty-five vehicles, two carpentry workshops and saw machines, one mosque and one private clinic were also damaged or destroyed.
  • In Torkham, Nangarhar Province, flash flooding reportedly killed three Afghan refugees and injured nine others at a returnee transit camp on the Pakistan side of the border. Flooding also temporarily disrupted movement at the Torkham border crossing and damaged or washed away private shops and livelihood-related installations at Zero Point.
  • In Alingar District, Laghman Province, flooding affected agricultural land and irrigation systems. No damage to residential houses had been reported at the time of the latest update.
  • Search and rescue operations are ongoing in Parun, while humanitarian and de facto authority responders are providing emergency health assistance and other initial support. Mobile Health Teams have been deployed, health facilities placed on alert and additional medical, nutrition and food supplies mobilized.
  • Immediate humanitarian priorities include emergency shelter, food assistance, emergency health services and medical supplies, non-food items, mental health and psychosocial support, and comprehensive multi-sector needs assessments.

Situation Overview

Heavy and continuous rainfall on 20 July triggered flash flooding in several areas of eastern Afghanistan. The impacts have varied significantly between locations, ranging from extensive loss of life and destruction in Parun City to damage to livelihoods and irrigation infrastructure in Alingar and disruption to a major border and returnee transit corridor in Torkham.

In Parun City, the sudden onset of flooding rapidly affected residential areas, public facilities and commercial premises. The latest preliminary assessment by the Afghanistan National Disaster Management Authority (ANDMA) in Nuristan indicates that 23 people have been killed, 15 confirmed injured while others remain missing.

The flood damaged the local water-supply network disrupting access to safe drinking water for approximately 1,000 families. Damage to bridges and roads is affecting movement and access, while damage to irrigation infrastructure has increased risks to communities and agricultural livelihoods. Markets, local shops, vehicles, carpentry workshops and saw machines were damaged or destroyed, while agricultural land was flooded.

The flood also caused significant damage to humanitarian and development actors operating in the city. The office of ODESC, a UNESCO implementing partner, was destroyed, while the warehouse and other assets of New Consultancy and Relief Organization (NCRO), including a vehicle and motorbike, were damaged. One national NGO staff member is reportedly missing.

The impact in Torkham extended beyond physical damage to infrastructure and livelihoods. Flooding affected a returnee transit camp on the Pakistan side of the border, resulting in three reported deaths and nine injuries, while movement through the Torkham crossing was temporarily delayed. The flooding also damaged the protection wall of the Directorate of Refugees and Repatriation compound at Zero Point, Torkham, where humanitarian partners are providing basic services to returnees.

In Alingar District, Laghman Province, the reported impact has primarily been on agricultural land and irrigation systems. The damage may affect agricultural production and livelihoods, although no damage to residential houses had been reported at the time of the latest update.

In the southeastern region, flooding has affected communities and infrastructure in several areas, with assessments and verification ongoing.

The full scale of the regional impact remains under assessment. In Parun in particular, search and rescue operations continue and the number of casualties and missing people may change as additional information is verified. Further rainfall and unstable weather conditions also continue to pose a risk of additional flooding.

Humanitarian Response

Humanitarian partners and relevant authorities are working to verify the impact of the floods and identify the most urgent needs in affected areas. Priority response activities include search and rescue, the recovery and identification of people who have died, assistance to injured people and support to affected families.

Initial response priorities include:

  • Emergency shelter and non-food items for families whose homes have been damaged or destroyed;
  • Food assistance for households that have lost access to food stocks, markets or livelihoods;
  • Safe drinking water, hygiene supplies and sanitation support, particularly in areas where water infrastructure has been damaged or contaminated;
  • Emergency health assistance, including support for injured people and the deployment of mobile health services where required;
  • Protection assistance for families affected by loss of life, displacement, unsafe shelter conditions and access constraints;
  • Debris removal and clearance of roads and other access routes;
  • Repair and restoration of damaged irrigation infrastructure and other critical community infrastructure; and
  • Multi-purpose cash assistance, where markets remain functional and cash assistance is feasible, to help affected households meet their most urgent needs.

Response efforts remain constrained by difficult terrain, damaged roads and limited access to some affected communities. Further assessments are required to determine the scale and severity of needs, particularly in remote areas of Nuristan and other mountainous locations.

Coordination

OCHA is coordinating with relevant stakeholders, including disaster-management structures, UN agencies, international and national NGOs and other humanitarian partners to support the assessment and response to the flooding.

In Nuristan, ANDMA provided an updated preliminary assessment to the Nuristan OCT on 21 July. OCHA and SHPOUL coordinated an ad hoc OCT meeting on 21 July to review the evolving situation, coordinate the initial humanitarian response and prepare for inter-agency needs assessments.

A rapid needs assessment is being conducted on 21 July. Three inter-agency needs assessment teams have also been constituted, with surge support from Kunar and Jalalabad, and are scheduled to begin assessments on 22 July.

OCHA’s Eastern Region team remains in close contact with ANDMA, the Nuristan OCT, local authorities and humanitarian partners. Coordination is also ongoing with relevant authorities and partners in Nangarhar and Laghman.

Weather forecasts and early-warning information have been disseminated to humanitarian partners and the OCT network to support preparedness and monitoring of further rainfall and flood risks.

A medical site has been established in collaboration with the Directorate of Public Health and two mobile health teams have been deployed. Medical items and food and nutrition items have also been dispatched with high energy biscuits expected to arrive on 21 July.

At the national level, ANDMA convened a meeting on 21 July to plan the next steps and coordinate response.

Coordination efforts are focused on:

  • Verifying reported casualties, missing persons and the number of affected households;
  • Supporting the deployment of assessment teams to affected areas;
  • Identifying urgent needs and prioritizing assistance to the most severely affected communities;
  • Coordinating search-and-rescue, emergency response and early recovery efforts;
  • Facilitating information-sharing among humanitarian partners and authorities;
  • Identifying access constraints and supporting efforts to restore critical roads and routes; and
  • Monitoring the humanitarian situation, including the potential impacts on food security, livelihoods, health, water and sanitation, and protection.

Further assessments are ongoing. Humanitarian partners continue to coordinate with authorities and affected communities to establish the full scale of the disaster and scale up assistance according to verified needs.

title: WFP Somalia Country Brief - July 2026
content:
• Somalia is facing one of the most complex hunger crises in recent years, driven by drought, insecurity, a sharp drop in humanitarian funding, and the ripple effects of the conflict in the Middle East. The situation is on high alert, with around 2 million people in IPC Phase 4, more than double last year, and a forecasted El Niño event increasing flood risk, indicating a sharp rise in severity.
  • Somalia remains one of the world’s most severe malnutrition crises, with 1.9 million acutely malnourished children. IPC analysis indicates famine risk in Burhakaba, where nearly 40 percent of children under five are acutely malnourished or worse.
  • WFP remains the backbone of Somalia’s humanitarian response, but funding shortfalls are reducing reach. Through August, food assistance reaches only 644,000 people, 34 percent of the IPC Phase 4 population. Urgent funding is needed to prevent further decline.

title: Mozambique Health Cluster Bulletin -June 2026
content:
1. Context Overview

Mozambique continues to face a complex humanitarian situation driven by the combined impacts of climate-related shocks and protracted conflict, with significant consequences for the health and well-being of vulnerable populations. In 2026, severe flooding in the central and southern provinces caused widespread displacement, damaged health infrastructure, and heightened the risk of waterborne disease outbreaks, disrupting access to and continuity of essential health services.

At the same time, insecurity in Cabo Delgado continues to trigger displacement and place additional pressure on already fragile health systems. Humanitarian needs remain acute, particularly among displaced populations, returnees, and host communities, requiring sustained support for primary health care, emergency medical services, mental health and psychosocial support, and outbreak prevention and response.

In response, Health Cluster partners have maintained a coordinated humanitarian effort to ensure the delivery of life-saving and essential health services. Interventions have focused on integrated approaches, including mobile health services, disease surveillance and outbreak response, sexual and reproductive health care, mental health support, and water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) activities. Despite these efforts, considerable challenges remain, particularly related to humanitarian access, funding constraints, shortages of critical resources, and the need to further strengthen health information management, monitoring, and reporting systems.

This bulletin presents a summary of the key activities, achievements, and operational updates of Health Cluster partners during June 2026. It highlights collective efforts to address urgent health needs and support the recovery and resilience of communities affected by conflict in the north and floods in the central and southern regions of Mozambique.

title: Albania | Heatwave - Early Action Protocol Operations Update (sEAP number: sEAP2025AL01 | Operation Number: MDRAL009) (05.06.2026)
content:
EARLY ACTION PROTOCOL
Summary of revisions to the operation

In the Simplified Early Action Protocol for Heatwave, the Albanian Red Cross (ARC) planned the following key interventions:

•Multi-purpose cash assistance for 300 vulnerable households (approx. 825 people) to cover increased costs related to extreme heat (cooling, water, electricity, medicines).
•Health and care support through the Green Line, remote monitoring calls, and mobile team visits targeting 1,500 vulnerable individuals, including older persons and people with chronic conditions.

Implementation Progress (June–December 2025)

•A kick-off and technical workshop (October 2025) brought together ARC, IFRC, Austrian Red Cross, IGEO, ministries, and branch teams. This clarified: roles and responsibilities, trigger mechanism for heatwave activation and coordination and communication procedures.
•Branch-level preparedness planning was initiated to ensure response capacity within the 5-day lead time prior to a heatwave.
•A Memorandum of Understanding with IGEO / Tirana University was finalized to: develop forecasting products and operationalize trigger monitoring systems

Financially, expenditures remained low (approx. CHF 2,183), covering mainly:

•coordination
•travel
•technical meetings

-volunteer training on CVA, KoBo, PGI and CEA basics (2 days in May)

Video no 2 is still in production and will be delivered until 10 July.

title: Costa Rica: Floods - DREF Final Report (MDRCR027)
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event
30-10-2025
What happened, where and when?

On 19 October 2025, the National Meteorological Institute (IMN) reported that Tropical Wave No. 40 was moving towards the Caribbean Sea, with potential for cyclonic development. Between 20 and 21 October, the IMN continued issuing updates on unstable conditions associated with Tropical Waves No. 39 and No. 40 and increased surveillance due to the high probability of cyclogenesis in the Caribbean. On 21 October, Tropical Wave No. 40 evolved into Tropical Storm Melissa.

As Melissa strengthened in the Caribbean, the IMN issued advisories on its indirect influence on Costa Rica, including persistent humidity, activation of the Intertropical Convergence Zone and unstable weather conditions, particularly affecting the South Pacific and the southern coast of the Central Pacific. Advisories issued between 24 and 26 October maintained warnings for intense rainfall, high waves and landslide risks in vulnerable areas.

In response to this situation, on 25 October 2025, the National Emergency Commission (CNE) issued Alert No. 36, declaring an Orange Alert for the Pacific coastal regions, a Yellow Alert for the Central and Northern regions, and a Green Alert for the Caribbean. Municipal and community emergency committees were instructed to monitor local conditions, activate preparedness mechanisms, maintain response capacities on standby and ensure permanent monitoring.

In line with the National Emergency and Disaster Response Plan, the Costa Rican Red Cross activated Response Level 3 for Guanacaste, Puntarenas and the Southern Region. This included concentrating personnel in auxiliary committees, suspending non-essential activities and trainings, activating Regional Operations Coordination Centres (CCOR), deploying National Intervention Teams (ENI) and specialized units, and opening the Emergency Operations Coordination Centre (CECOE) under the National Directorate for Emergency Response
(DINARE).

As rainfall intensified, response operations began on 25 October and continued throughout the week. Activities included rescues in mountainous areas affected by landslides, evacuations from flooded communities, transfers to shelters and pre-hospital care for people affected by incidents related to adverse weather conditions, with the highest impact reported in Guanacaste and Puntarenas. In the early hours of 30 October, intense rainfall also affected northern Alajuela and Cartago, increasing institutional response efforts, including evacuations in areas such as Pénjamo de Florencia and Cartago.

According to consolidated information from the Costa Rican Red Cross Emergency Operations Coordination Centre, 511 emergencies were recorded, including 504 flood-related incidents and seven landslides. The National Society provided pre-hospital care to 250 people, supported the evacuation of 116 people, and reported 540 affected homes.

Given that the forecasted event materialized and generated operational response needs, the National Society requested the transition of the Imminent DREF MDRCR027 to a response operation. Formal approval for this transition was received on 17 November 2025, allowing the operation to continue under an adjusted response framework. The response strategy focused on multipurpose cash assistance, Community Engagement and Accountability (CEA), Protection, Gender and Inclusion (PGI), Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR), National Society strengthening, and the progressive implementation of Health and WASH activities.

Some activities required schedule adjustments due to the overlap with major national and local events, including end-of-year holidays in December, the traditional festivities in Santa Cruz in January, and the presidential elections in February. These factors affected operational coordination, availability of logistical resources and activity planning in the areas of intervention, requiring the rescheduling of some activities to ensure adequate implementation.

title: Greater Horn of Africa Food Insecurity and Health Crisis, Situation Report No. 1 (April - June 2026)
content:
Overview

  • The Greater Horn of Africa (GHoA) Food Insecurity and Health Crisis remains a Grade 2 emergency under the WHO Emergency Response Framework, affecting six countries across the WHO African Region and WHO Eastern Mediterranean Region. The crisis continues to be driven by the convergence of acute food insecurity, conflict, climate shocks, population displacement, recurrent disease outbreaks, economic pressures and fragile health systems.
  • More than 37.8 million people are experiencing or projected to experience acute food insecurity, while over 4.9 million children are projected to suffer acute malnutrition, including more than 1.5 million children requiring treatment for severe acute malnutrition (SAM). The overall regional burden is expected to be higher, as Ethiopia continues to report widespread food insecurity and increasing humanitarian needs, although a comparable national IPC Phase 3+ estimate is not yet available.
  • Acute food insecurity and malnutrition, compounded by recurrent disease outbreaks, conflict, displacement, climate shocks, economic pressures and reduced access to essential health services, continue to increase the risk of preventable illness and death, particularly among children under five years of age, pregnant and lactating women, displaced populations, refugees, returnees, pastoralist communities and people living in hard-to-reach or insecure areas.
  • WHO is providing technical leadership through a coordinated three-level response involving Headquarters, the WHO Regional Offices for Africa and the Eastern Mediterranean, and country offices, working closely with Ministries of Health and Health and Nutrition partners to strengthen emergency coordination, surveillance and early warning, outbreak preparedness and response, management of severe acute malnutrition with medical complications, continuity of essential health services, and integrated health sector coordination.
  • During the reporting period, WHO supported the development of a regional Strategic Response Plan, strengthened surveillance and early warning systems, expanded support to Nutrition Stabilization Centres, reinforced outbreak preparedness and response, deployed technical expertise, pre-positioned emergency medicines and nutrition supplies, and supported integrated health and nutrition service delivery across priority countries.
  • Significant operational challenges continue to constrain the response, including funding shortfalls, insecurity, restricted humanitarian access, overstretched health systems, shortages of trained health workers, supply chain disruptions and limited stabilization centre capacity, affecting the scale and sustainability of life-saving interventions.
  • WHO requires approximately US$25.4 million over the next six months (July–December 2026) to sustain priority life-saving health and nutrition interventions across the six-country response. Funding will support emergency coordination, surveillance and early warning, management of severe acute malnutrition with medical complications, continuity of essential health services, outbreak preparedness and response, and operational support to country-level implementation.

title: Earthquakes in Venezuela: Situation Report #27 (20 July 2026, Time: 09:00 pm)
content:
Situation Report No. 27
Earthquakes in Venezuela
20 July 2026
Time: 9:00 pm

Highlights

  • Authorities report 1,405 aftershocks since the 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude earthquakes that struck on 24 June.
  • Official toll: 5,278 people dead and 16,740 injured.
  • The United Nations system and its partner organizations continue scaling up the multisectoral response to the emergency. To address the needs of 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months, an additional appeal of US$299 million was launched

Situation overview

Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre located along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). Authorities report 1,405 aftershocks.

Twenty-four days since the earthquakes, authorities report a toll of 5,278 people dead and 16,740 injured since the onset of the emergency. Authorities also indicated that 17,907 people lost their homes.

The Government response remains focused on the management of transitional camps and assistance to affected populations. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination with the authorities, continue implementing multisectoral response activities and scaling up assistance. On 10 July, United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher announced a US$299 million addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan to address the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months. The addendum complements the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, increasing the target population from 5.5 million to 6.2 million people and raising total funding requirements from US$632 million to US$931 million.

title: IOM oPt: Site Management Overview (June 2026)
content:
[...]

REDUCING RODENT INFESTATION RISKS: AN INTEGRATED SITE MANAGEMENT APPROACH

At A12 site in Gaza city, Beit Lahia Development Association, with support of IOM, implemented a comprehensive package of site management activities to improve living conditions amidst a severe rodent and insect infestation driven by its proximity to heavily damaged buildings outside the site boundary and overcrowding within the site. These conditions created significant public health and protection risks, particularly for children, women, older persons, and persons with disabilities. A site safety audit identified the infestation as the site’s highest priority concern, informing an integrated response led through site management activities.

The response began with community awareness sessions where residents received information on the pesticides and rodenticides that would be used, the locations where control materials would be placed, and the precautions needed to protect children and other vulnerable groups from exposure. This was followed by a site-wide pest and rodent control campaign covering 196 shelters. Shelters, communal areas, internal pathways, and the site perimeter were treated using insecticides, repellents, and strategically placed rodent bait stations.

Following the intervention, community meetings and additional awareness activities reinforced key prevention messages and encouraged residents to maintain safer environmental practices. A subsequent cleaning campaign removed solid waste and environmental hazards from pathways and communal areas, helping reduce conditions that contribute to rodent infestation. Together, these linked interventions reduced public health and protection risks while creating a cleaner, safer, and more dignified living environment for displaced families.
