General

Damage/Needs assessment

Summary

The IFRC continues to monitor the evolving situation in close coordination with the VNRC and stands ready to provide technical and operational support should humanitarian needs increase or additional assistance be required.

Actions taken by others

Immediately after the disaster, local forces in Mường Than Commune mobilised for rescue operations. Leadership of the Lai Châu Provincial People's Committee formed a working delegation to go directly to the scene and take command of search and rescue efforts. Provincial police and military units were deployed with equipment and support vehicles to focus on disaster relief, search and rescue operations. Lai Châu Provincial Police established a forward command post at Tân Uyên Commune Police station, under the direct command of Colonel Khoàng Văn Thương, Deputy Director of the Provincial Police, to co-ordinate rescue, relief and disaster recovery operations. The Chairman of the Lai Châu Provincial People's Committee issued an urgent directive on July 17, instructing departments, agencies, armed forces and local People's Committees to focus on responding to and recovering from the floods, flash floods and landslides in accordance with the "four on-the-spot" principle, with no room for passivity or unpreparedness. Emergency declarations have been issued for Mường Than Commune and for a landslide site that has severed National Highway 12 within Lê Lợi Commune. Rescue operations in Mường Than Commune are proceeding with urgency. Provincial People's Committee chairman travelled to the scene to inspect and direct recovery efforts and oversee disaster response measures. Provincial and local forces are deploying personnel and equipment to search and rescue operations and disaster relief work, with the aim of restoring stability to residents' lives as quickly as possible.

title: BGD: Flood - 07-2026 - Bangladesh Floods 2026: Nationwide (2026-07-19)
content:
Description

Bangladesh has experienced widespread flooding, flash floods, riverine inundation, and landslides across its south-eastern and north-eastern regions following several days of exceptionally heavy monsoon rainfall. The emergency was initially triggered by a low-pressure system that brought intense rainfall across large parts of the country, resulting in severe flooding, waterlogging, river overflows, and landslides in vulnerable areas. Rainfall totals were particularly high in Chattogram, Teknaf, Bandarban, and Sylhet districts. Chattogram recorded 298.8 mm of rainfall on 9 July and 203 mm on 10 July, while Teknaf received 245 mm on 10 July. On 11 July, the highest rainfall was recorded in Jaflong, Sylhet (156 mm), followed by Lama, Bandarban (155 mm), and Teknaf, Cox’s Bazar (139 mm).

Although weather conditions have gradually improved, the Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD) forecasts that active monsoon conditions will continue through 20 July, bringing light to moderate rainfall accompanied by temporary gusty winds across the country. Maritime ports of Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Mongla, and Payra remain under Local Cautionary Signal No. 3. Hydrological conditions have improved significantly since the peak of the emergency. As of 16 July, only the Kushiyara River remained above the danger level at two monitoring stations, Markuli in Sunamganj and Fenchuganj in Sylhet. Water levels along the Surma River and other major rivers in the north-eastern region have continued to recede, and flood conditions in low-lying areas of Sylhet and Sunamganj are expected to improve further. Similarly, water levels in the Teesta, Dharla, and Dudhkumar rivers in Rangpur Division have fallen and are projected to continue decreasing. Nevertheless, localized flooding, waterlogging, and landslide risks persist in several areas where saturated soils, damaged infrastructure, and access constraints continue to affect communities. The Bangladesh Red Crescent Society (BDRCS) Emergency Operations Centre remains active and continues to monitor the evolving situation.

At the peak of the emergency, flood conditions deteriorated rapidly. Several rivers, including the Sangu, Kushiyara, Monu, and Khowai, exceeded danger levels, with the Sangu River in Bandarban rising more than two metres above its danger threshold. Rising river levels threatened low-lying communities in Chattogram, Feni, Khagrachhari, Sylhet, Sunamganj, Netrokona, Sherpur, Mymensingh, and the northern river basins, causing widespread disruption to livelihoods, infrastructure, transportation networks, and basic services.

The humanitarian impact remains significant. According to the Needs Assessment Working Group (NAWG), an estimated 1,116,174 people have been affected across 10 districts. The Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief (MoDMR) reports that approximately 38,500 people were temporarily displaced, while more than 1,000 evacuation shelters were opened to accommodate affected populations. Government reporting further indicates that 267,918 households were stranded or isolated by floodwaters across seven districts. Media reports citing MoDMR indicate that at least 59 people lost their lives nationwide as a result of floods and landslides.

Housing damage has been extensive across the affected areas. Preliminary government assessments indicate that 15,881 houses were damaged in Bandarban, 13,860 in Chattogram, 1,040 in Khagrachhari, 1,613 in Cox’s Bazar. However, the full extent of housing damage remains unclear as standing water, damaged infrastructure, and access constraints continue to hamper detailed assessments. According to the MoDMR situation update on 18 July 2026, a total of 374 unions and four municipalities across 56 upazilas have been affected by the ongoing floods.

Water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) systems have been severely disrupted across 27 upazilas in 10 districts. In many areas, water supply infrastructure remains submerged, damaged, or contaminated by floodwaters carrying faecal matter, agricultural chemicals, industrial waste, and other pollutants. As of 12 July, the Department of Public Health Engineering (DPHE) reported that more than 12,360 latrines and 3,583 water points had been fully or partially damaged, increasing risks of waterborne disease outbreaks and reducing access to safe drinking water and sanitation facilities.

The floods have also caused substantial damage to agriculture, livestock, and fisheries, threatening household incomes, food security, and rural livelihoods. According to the Department of Agricultural Extension (DAE), approximately 54,470 hectares of cropland and 324,358 farming households have been affected by heavy rainfall and associated hazards. Crop losses alone are estimated at more than 54,409 hectares of agricultural land. The fisheries sector has sustained particularly severe damage, with preliminary assessments from the Department of Fisheries (DoF) indicating losses of 7,613 metric tons of fish and prawns. Floodwaters washed away 21,764 fishponds and 784 commercial enclosures covering 8,966 hectares, resulting in estimated losses of approximately USD 18.3 million.

The livestock sector has also been heavily impacted. Approximately 266,038 cattle and buffalo, 173,592 goats and sheep, 2.85 million chickens, and 62,811 ducks have been affected. Reported animal deaths include 62 cattle, 139 goats, 59 sheep, 154,528 chickens, and 2,063 ducks. Total losses in the livestock sector are estimated at BDT 576.2 million (approximately USD 4.7 million). Combined losses across the fisheries and livestock sectors are estimated at approximately USD 23 million.

The most severely affected districts include Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Bandarban, Rangamati, Khagrachhari, Moulvibazar, and Habiganj, where communities continue to face challenges related to damaged housing, disrupted livelihoods, limited access to essential services, and deteriorated infrastructure.

In Cox’s Bazar, the situation remains particularly concerning due to the combined impact on Rohingya refugee camps and surrounding host communities. Across the 33 refugee camps, flooding and landslides affected more than 28,000 people, damaged over 3,100 shelters, and displaced more than 4,700 individuals. Multiple casualties and injuries were reported as a result of landslides and flood-related incidents. UNHCR has confirmed 15 deaths among Rohingya refugees, while thousands of people have been left homeless following landslides and shelter collapses, further increasing humanitarian needs among already vulnerable populations.

The Government of Bangladesh, led by the Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief (MoDMR), has maintained a coordinated multi-agency response to support flood- and landslide-affected communities. Response measures have included the opening of more than 1,000 evacuation shelters, the distribution of cash assistance, rice, baby food, safe drinking water, and other relief items, as well as the deployment of the Bangladesh Army, Navy, Coast Guard, Fire Service and Civil Defence, and local authorities to support rescue, evacuation, and relief operations. The Government has also mobilised 516 medical teams across 50 affected upazilas to address urgent health needs and reduce public health risks. In addition, the Government has allocated 3,350 metric tons of rice, BDT 23.5 million in cash assistance, and 4,200 bundles of corrugated galvanized iron (CGI) sheets alongside BDT 12.6 million for shelter repair and reconstruction support for affected households across seven districts. National and district-level coordination mechanisms remain active to monitor the evolving situation, facilitate early warning dissemination, support affected communities, and prioritize assistance to the hardest-hit areas. Efforts are ongoing to restore essential services, support displaced populations, and address immediate humanitarian and early recovery needs as floodwaters continue to recede.

Request For Assistance

Government Requests International Assistance: No

NS Requests International Assistance: Yes

Information Bulletin Published

No

Actions taken by National Society

General

Damage/Needs assessment

Search & Rescue

Water & Sanitation

Food aid

Health

Camp management

Psychosocial support services

Evacuation

First Aid

Relief/Supply distribution

Other

Summary

The Bangladesh Red Crescent Society (BDRCS) activated its Central Emergency Operations Centre (EOC) immediately following the onset of the flood emergency and continues to coordinate response efforts across flood- and landslide-affected districts in south-eastern and north-eastern Bangladesh. The EOC remains operational to facilitate real-time information management, situation monitoring, and coordination with district units, government authorities, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), Participating National Societies (PNSs), and other humanitarian partners, ensuring a timely, coordinated, and effective response. To support immediate response operations, BDRCS has mobilized emergency resources through its contingency funds and partner contributions. A total of BDT 2.6 million has been released to district units in Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Bandarban, Rangamati, Khagrachhari, Moulvibazar, and Habiganj to facilitate rapid response activities and assist affected communities. To strengthen evacuation, rescue, and emergency response capacities, BDRCS deployed a wide range of rescue equipment and emergency supplies, including 12 rubber rescue boats, 110 life jackets, 135 rescue helmets, 135 rescue boots, 145 pairs of rescue gloves, five generators, and 5,500 jerrycans, together with rescue ropes, rope bags, float plates, and rescue panels. These assets have enhanced the operational effectiveness of district units and volunteers engaged in life-saving interventions in affected communities. BDRCS has provided emergency food assistance to 6,450 flood-affected households across Bandarban, Khagrachhari, Rangamati, Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Moulvibazar, and Habiganj. Distributed food packages included rice, puffed rice, lentils, edible oil, salt, sugar, biscuits, oral rehydration salts (ORS), soap, sanitary pads, safe drinking water, and other essential household items. These interventions have helped address immediate food security and basic needs among affected populations. To respond to critical health and WASH needs, BDRCS deployed four Mobile Water Treatment Units (MWTUs) and distributed more than 5,114 litres of safe drinking water to affected communities in Bandarban and Chattogram districts. In addition, two emergency mobile medical teams were deployed with essential medicines and relief supplies to provide primary healthcare services and support disease prevention efforts in flood-affected areas. In Cox’s Bazar, BDRCS continues to respond through its Population Movement Operation (PMO), supporting both Rohingya refugees and host communities affected by flooding and landslides. Response activities include early warning dissemination, emergency relocation support, search and rescue operations, and coordination through Camp Disaster Management Committees (DMCs) and humanitarian partners across all 33 refugee camps. PMO teams have provided emergency shelter assistance to 494 affected households in Camps 11 and 12, while WASH volunteers continue to assess damaged facilities and coordinate rehabilitation efforts with sector partners. Health teams remain engaged in community outreach, referrals, household visits, and the provision of essential health services, including outpatient and maternal healthcare. Through its extensive volunteer network and field teams, BDRCS continues to address the urgent needs of flood- and landslide-affected refugees and host communities. Recognizing the scale of the emergency, BDRCS formally requested IFRC support on 8 July 2026 to launch a Disaster Response Emergency Fund (DREF) operation for flood- and landslide-affected populations in the Rohingya camps and adjacent host communities in Cox’s Bazar. In response, IFRC approved and launched a CHF 475,000 DREF operation to support life-saving interventions, including early warning dissemination, evacuation support, search and rescue, emergency shelter assistance, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services, food assistance, cash and voucher assistance (CVA), volunteer mobilization, and operational coordination. The DREF operation complements ongoing efforts by BDRCS, government authorities, and humanitarian partners while strengthening support to the most vulnerable communities. To strengthen Red Cross Red Crescent Movement coordination and review the evolving humanitarian situation, BDRCS convened an emergency coordination meeting on 16 July with IFRC, ICRC, and in-country Participating National Societies (PNSs). The meeting provided updates on the flood situation, damage assessments, response achievements, and operational challenges across affected districts. Given the continued deterioration in humanitarian conditions, extensive damage, emerging needs, and the expansion of affected areas beyond the initial operational scope, BDRCS has developed an enhanced response plan aimed at scaling up humanitarian assistance for the most vulnerable and severely affected households. Planned interventions include the mobilization of additional food parcels, mobile water treatment plants, emergency medical teams, essential household items, cash assistance, and agricultural recovery support. In light of increasing humanitarian needs and widening response gaps, BDRCS has requested IFRC to consider expanding the current DREF operation and has appealed to Participating National Societies to mobilize additional international resources to support a larger-scale response and early recovery effort across the flood-affected districts.

Actions taken by Federation

General

Camp management

Other

Summary

The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) Bangladesh Country Delegation is supporting the Bangladesh Red Crescent Society (BDRCS) in coordinating, strengthening, and scaling up the response to the ongoing floods and landslides across affected areas of Bangladesh. IFRC maintains close coordination with the Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief (MoDMR), the United Nations Resident Coordinator’s Office (UNRCO), humanitarian clusters and working groups, Participating National Societies (PNSs), the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), and other humanitarian partners to facilitate information sharing, operational coordination, resource mobilization, and complementarity of response efforts. IFRC is providing continuous technical and operational support to BDRCS in emergency assessments, response planning, coordination, reporting, information management, and overall operational management. The IFRC Bangladesh Country Delegation remains in close communication with the IFRC Asia Pacific Regional Office to ensure timely technical guidance and surge support as required. Together with BDRCS and Movement partners, IFRC continues to closely monitor the evolving situation, assess emerging humanitarian needs, identify operational gaps, and support the mobilization of additional resources to address the growing needs of affected communities. Following a request from BDRCS, IFRC approved and launched a Disaster Response Emergency Fund (DREF) operation amounting to CHF 475,000 to support flood- and landslide-affected populations in the Rohingya refugee camps and adjacent host communities in Cox’s Bazar. The operation aims to deliver life-saving humanitarian assistance through interventions including early warning dissemination, evacuation support, search and rescue, emergency shelter assistance, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services, food assistance, cash and voucher assistance (CVA), volunteer mobilization, and operational coordination. The DREF operation complements ongoing response efforts led by BDRCS and supports the immediate needs of the most vulnerable affected populations. In addition to the DREF allocation, IFRC has contributed emergency relief support from its Population Movement Operation (PMO) Disaster Preparedness (DP) stocks. Non-food items (NFIs) and emergency shelter materials with an estimated value of CHF 120,000 have been made available to support BDRCS response activities for flood- and landslide-affected populations. These pre-positioned resources are helping to strengthen the timeliness and effectiveness of humanitarian assistance delivered to affected people. In its role as Co-Lead of the Shelter Cluster, IFRC is actively engaging with shelter sector partners to support coordinated assessments, information management, response planning, and gap analysis. Through this engagement, IFRC is contributing to the identification and prioritization of emergency shelter needs, promoting coordinated humanitarian action, and supporting efforts to provide timely shelter assistance to flood- and landslide-affected households across the impacted areas.

Actions taken by RCRC

General

Health

Relief/Supply distribution

Other

Summary

The Red Cross Red Crescent Movement maintains a strong presence in Bangladesh through the Bangladesh Red Crescent Society (BDRCS), the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), and nine in-country Participating National Societies (PNSs), namely the American Red Cross, British Red Cross, Danish Red Cross, German Red Cross, Japanese Red Cross Society, Qatar Red Crescent, Swedish Red Cross, Swiss Red Cross, and Turkish Red Crescent. Throughout the ongoing flood and landslide emergency, Movement partners have remained in close coordination with BDRCS and IFRC, continuously monitoring the evolving situation and consulting with their respective regional offices and headquarters to assess opportunities for additional technical, operational, and financial support. To strengthen BDRCS's response capacity and support the scale-up of humanitarian assistance to affected communities, several Movement partners have confirmed financial contributions to the ongoing response operation. Confirmed contributions include USD 84,166 from the British Red Cross, USD 38,333 from the Danish Red Cross, USD 25,000 each from the American Red Cross, Swedish Red Cross, and the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), and USD 20,833 from the Turkish Red Crescent. These contributions will support BDRCS in delivering essential humanitarian assistance to flood- and landslide-affected populations, including food assistance, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) support, emergency shelter and household items, health services, cash assistance, and other priority interventions. In addition to these confirmed contributions, Participating National Societies continue to engage with BDRCS and IFRC to review evolving needs and identify opportunities for further support. The Red Cross Red Crescent Movement remains committed to supporting BDRCS in addressing immediate humanitarian needs, strengthening response capacities, and assisting affected communities throughout the response and early recovery phases of the emergency.

Actions taken by others

Following the heavy rainfall forecast issued on 5 July, the Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief (MoDMR), the Department of Disaster Management (DDM), the Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD), and the Flood Forecasting and Warning Centre (FFWC) convened a series of coordination meetings to strengthen preparedness and response measures. The National Disaster Response Coordination Centre was activated on a 24-hour basis, and emergency contact information was disseminated to facilitate timely response. At the district level, disaster management committees were mobilized to coordinate early warning dissemination, evacuation efforts, shelter management, emergency feeding, and rescue operations. These efforts were supported by the Bangladesh Army, Bangladesh Navy, Coast Guard, Border Guard Bangladesh, Fire Service and Civil Defence, Bangladesh Police, Bangladesh Red Crescent Society (BDRCS), and local administrations. On 12 July, the Prime Minister’s Office convened a high-level virtual meeting to review the evolving flood and landslide situation, including impacts on infrastructure, shelter conditions, rescue operations, relief distribution, and healthcare services. Relevant authorities were instructed to prioritize the protection of lives and property, expedite the delivery of food assistance, safe drinking water, medicines, and healthcare services, and ensure that evacuation shelters provide adequate safety, sanitation, electricity, communication facilities, and support for vulnerable groups. Government agencies were further directed to strengthen inter-agency coordination, maintain operational readiness, closely monitor weather forecasts and river levels, and ensure transparent and accountable delivery of relief assistance. Led by MoDMR, the Government of Bangladesh activated a comprehensive multi-agency response across the affected districts. Response measures included the opening of more than 1,000 evacuation shelters, the distribution of cash assistance, rice, baby food, safe drinking water, and other relief items, and the deployment of the Armed Forces, Coast Guard, Fire Service and Civil Defence, and local authorities to support search and rescue, evacuation, and relief operations. To address urgent health needs and mitigate public health risks, the Government mobilized 516 medical teams across 50 affected upazilas. National and district-level coordination mechanisms remain active to monitor the situation, facilitate early warning dissemination, and support targeted assistance in the most severely affected districts, particularly Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Bandarban, Rangamati, Khagrachhari, Moulvibazar, and Habiganj. To reinforce response efforts, the Government allocated a cumulative BDT 23 million, 3,350 metric tons of rice, 4,200 bundles of corrugated galvanized iron (CGI) sheets, and BDT 12.6 million for shelter repair support between 7 and 18 July. Chattogram received the largest allocation, comprising BDT 7.5 million, 1,200 metric tons of rice, 1,000 bundles of CGI sheets, and BDT 3 million for shelter repairs. Cox’s Bazar received BDT 4 million, 450 metric tons of rice, 1,000 bundles of CGI sheets, and BDT 3 million for shelter repairs. Bandarban and Khagrachhari each received BDT 2.5 million, 400 metric tons of rice, 500 bundles of CGI sheets, and BDT 1.5 million for shelter rehabilitation. Rangamati received BDT 3 million, 500 metric tons of rice, 500 bundles of CGI sheets, and BDT 1.5 million for shelter repairs. Additional allocations included BDT 1.5 million and 200 metric tons of rice for Moulvibazar, and BDT 1 million and 100 metric tons of rice for Habiganj. Both districts also received 200 bundles of CGI sheets and BDT 600,000 for shelter rehabilitation. These resources were released through successive allocations between 7 and 18 July, enabling the Government to progressively scale up assistance as the situation evolved. The humanitarian community simultaneously strengthened coordination and response efforts. On 11 July, the Inter-Cluster Coordination Group (ICCG) convened an ad hoc meeting to review the evolving situation, anticipatory action activations, and updates from operational partners. The meeting emphasized strengthening information management, consolidating response reporting, identifying priority needs and gaps, and producing the first ICCG Situation Report. Subsequently, the Displacement Management, Health, Logistics, Shelter, and Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) Clusters convened emergency coordination meetings to review field information, identify operational constraints, and coordinate response actions. The Needs Assessment and Information Management Working Group (NA/IMWG) issued Flash Updates on 9 and 12 July and continues consolidating information from affected areas. A multi-sectoral assessment is being planned once access conditions improve. The Anticipatory Action Technical Working Group (AATWG) remains actively engaged with agencies implementing anticipatory action frameworks, monitoring trigger thresholds, sharing operational updates, and supporting coordinated preparedness measures. The ICCG Secretariat continues to coordinate closely with cluster leads, BMD, DDM, MoDMR, the NGO Affairs Bureau, and district administrations to support a coherent and coordinated humanitarian response. In anticipation of peak flooding, the World Food Programme (WFP) activated both Anticipatory Action (AA) and Shock-Responsive Social Protection (SRSP) interventions in Bandarban on 10 July. Through these mechanisms, WFP reached 15,000 households under anticipatory action and an additional 859 households through SRSP, providing multipurpose cash assistance of BDT 5,000 per household alongside early warning messages. These interventions focused on Bandarban Sadar and Lama upazilas. Subsequently, WFP expanded its response, reaching approximately 122,750 people with high-energy biscuits across Bandarban, Rangamati, and Chattogram districts. On 13 July, the Start Fund Bangladesh Project Selection Committee approved GBP 799,890.60 under Alert B075 to support an emergency humanitarian response targeting approximately 55,554 people across six of the most severely affected districts: Bandarban, Khagrachhari, Rangamati, Cox’s Bazar, Chattogram, and Moulvibazar. The allocation supports rapid multi-sectoral assistance to populations affected by floods and landslides. On 18 July, the Food Security Cluster (FSC) Bangladesh published a situation report highlighting priority food security and livelihood needs. Key priorities identified include emergency ready-to-eat food, livestock feed and shelter, emergency agricultural support, storage facilities for seeds and fertilizers, aquaculture and fisheries rehabilitation, multipurpose cash assistance, and the provision of cooking fuel and cooking utensils. Several humanitarian organizations activated anticipatory actions under existing disaster preparedness frameworks. Under the Early Action Protocol for flash floods in the Haor region, CARE Bangladesh mobilized volunteers, assessed evacuation shelters, and pre-positioned four rescue boats in Derai and Gowainghat, targeting approximately 18,500 people. UN Women provided preparedness support to approximately 300 households in Kanaighat, while World Vision disseminated early warning messages to around 50,000 people, pre-positioned 1,000 hygiene kits, validated beneficiary lists for 700 households, and prepared evacuation support for up to 2,000 households. In response to heightened landslide risks, Caritas Bangladesh and Save the Children activated anticipatory actions under the draft National Landslide Early Action Protocol. Save the Children provided BDT 6,000 per household to 400 at-risk households, in line with the 2026 ICCG-endorsed transfer value, while also supporting early warning dissemination and evacuation preparedness activities in Bandarban, Chattogram, and Rangamati. Several NGOs have already initiated direct humanitarian assistance. CARE Bangladesh reached approximately 8,000 people in Matamuhuri and Chakaria upazilas of Cox’s Bazar through the distribution of emergency relief packages, including tents, WASH non-food items, and dignity kits. Caritas Bangladesh provided dry food and non-food assistance to approximately 2,520 people in Bandarban Sadar, Alikadam, and Chakaria upazilas. Islamic Relief Bangladesh allocated GBP 150,000 to support flood-affected communities, including GBP 50,000 dedicated to emergency response activities in Banshkhali and Satkania upazilas of Chattogram District. The intervention is expected to reach approximately 700 households through multipurpose cash assistance, hygiene and dignity kits, and protection messaging. BRAC supported 5,460 families across Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Bandarban, Khagrachhari, and Rangamati through the distribution of dry food packages. In addition, BRAC provided multipurpose cash assistance to 300 families to help meet immediate recovery and basic needs. ActionAid Bangladesh reached approximately 2,500 people in Pekua Upazila of Cox’s Bazar through multipurpose cash assistance and shelter repair support. A further 2,250 people in Teknaf received women-focused protection services and food assistance. Similarly, Dhaka Ahsania Mission (DAM), with support from Start Fund Bangladesh, plans to provide multipurpose cash grants of BDT 8,000 per household to 1,000 households in Chattogram District. The intervention will target 600 households in Baharchara, Chambol, and Chanua unions of Banshkhali Upazila and 400 households in Roypur and Bairag unions of Anowara Upazila, enabling affected families to address their most urgent needs and support early recovery efforts.

title: MWI: Epidemic - 07-2026 - Measles Outbreak (2026-07-20)
content:
Description

The measles outbreak in Nsanje District continues to worsen, affecting several communities, particularly those along the Malawi–Mozambique border. As of 17 July 2026, the district had recorded 188 suspected measles cases, including 76 laboratory-confirmed cases. Children under 15 years of age, particularly those younger than five years, are the most affected. Key drivers of the outbreak include low immunization coverage, delayed health-seeking behaviour, cross-border population movement, and incomplete vaccination records. The situation has escalated in Traditional Authority (T/A) Mbenje, where some members of the Apostolic community do not seek treatment at health facilities due to religious beliefs. Tragically, one child recently died after not being taken to a health facility for medical care. This highlights the urgent need for intensified community engagement, risk communication, and efforts to promote timely healthcare seeking and measles vaccination. The outbreak is placing considerable pressure on the health system through increased demand for disease surveillance, case investigation, laboratory testing, case management, and community outreach. Response efforts continue to be constrained by shortages of essential medical supplies, inadequate transport and fuel, and limited resources to support active surveillance and rapid response activities. The affected population remains at high risk of severe illness, complications, and death, particularly among unvaccinated children. Urgent interventions are needed to strengthen routine and outbreak-response immunization, enhance community awareness, improve cross-border coordination, and ensure timely access to quality healthcare services.

Request For Assistance

Government Requests International Assistance: No

NS Requests International Assistance: No

Information Bulletin Published

Planned

Actions taken by National Society

Health

Community-based surveillance (CBS)

Contact tracing

Psychosocial Support Services (PSS)

First aid

General

Community Engagement and Accountability (CEA) and community feedback mechanisms

Volunteer Support

Summary

Since the onset of the measles outbreak, the Malawi Red Cross Society (MRCS), through its volunteers, has continued to support the Ministry of Health in implementing community-based outbreak response activities in the affected areas. Volunteers continue supporting Community Engagement and Accountability (CEA) activities, including community awareness sessions on measles prevention, early healthcare seeking, the importance of vaccination, and the collection of community feedback to address concerns and rumours. Volunteers also strengthen Community-Based Surveillance (CBS) by identifying and referring suspected measles cases, supporting active case finding, and participating in contact tracing to limit further transmission. In addition, MRCS volunteers provide First Aid services where required and deliver Psychosocial Support Services (PSS) to affected people and their caregivers to help address the emotional and psychological impacts of the outbreak. The National Society also continue to provide operational support to volunteers through coordination and supervision facilitate effective implementation of response activities in the affected communities.

Actions taken by others

The District Rapid Response Team (DRRT), in collaboration with partners, has implemented several measures to control and contain the outbreak. Key interventions include: Conducting active case search and strengthening community-based surveillance in affected areas. Carrying out case investigations, line listing, and contact tracing of suspected cases. Collecting, transporting, and facilitating laboratory testing of specimens for confirmation. Enhancing cross-border surveillance and coordination with neighbouring communities in Mozambique to monitor potential transmission. Conducting community sensitization and risk communication activities to promote early health-seeking behaviour, disease prevention, and vaccination uptake. Holding coordination meetings with the Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) and other response partners to review progress and strengthen response strategies. Providing supportive case management, including treatment of secondary infections with antibiotics, vitamin A supplementation where available, and health education for affected communities. Following the recent increase in cases in Traditional Authority (TA) Benje, where some Apostolic faith communities have limited engagement with formal health services, the Ministry of Health is planning to intensify community engagement and awareness activities. These efforts aim to address misconceptions, promote timely care-seeking, and increase acceptance of vaccination, particularly after the reported death of a child who was not referred to a health facility for treatment. Additional operational support, especially fuel and other logistics for field-level response activities, is urgently required to sustain active surveillance, community engagement, and outbreak control measures.

title: WHO Situation Report No.1: Health emergencies in the Eastern Mediterranean Region (June 2026)
content:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

• While the conflict in the Middle East showed signs of de-escalation at the end of the June reporting period, renewed hostilities in early July reversed this trend and significantly increased the risk of wider regional escalation. Renewed strikes in the Islamic Republic of Iran and several Gulf countries, together with attacks on commercial shipping and disruptions to navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, increased risks to civilians, medical and humanitarian supply chains, and continuity of essential health services.

• In the Islamic Republic of Iran, programme implementation and field support remained constrained by logistical and security challenges, while disruptions to domestic flights and high-risk areas continued to limit access for WHO teams. In Lebanon, insecurity, repeated population movements and damage to critical infrastructure, particularly in South Lebanon and Nabatiyeh, continued to constrain the humanitarian response.

• Sudan remained the Region's largest humanitarian emergency, with 30.4 million people requiring humanitarian assistance, 13.5 million displaced, multiple concurrent disease outbreaks and severe funding shortfalls threatening continuity of health services. Across other graded emergencies, humanitarian conditions continued to deteriorate in the occupied Palestinian territory and Somalia, while conflict, funding constraints, disease outbreaks and climate-related hazards continued to strain health systems in Yemen and the Syrian Arab Republic.

• The food insecurity and health crisis continued to deteriorate across the Greater Horn of Africa, driven by conflict, climate shocks, displacement, recurrent disease outbreaks and fragile health systems. More than 37.8 million people are experiencing, or are projected to experience, acute food insecurity across the six affected countries, including nearly 26 million in Sudan, Somalia and Djibouti. Children under five, pregnant and lactating women, displaced populations, refugees and communities in hard-to-reach areas remain among the most vulnerable.

• WHO's Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean is appealing for US$6.42 million to sustain critical health and nutrition interventions in Sudan, Somalia and Djibouti. The funding will help sustain primary health care and lifesaving nutrition services, strengthen surveillance and early warning, maintain outbreak detection and response capacities, expand nutrition screening and referral pathways, strengthen community engagement, and pre-position essential medicines, diagnostics and therapeutic supplies.

• WHO accelerated regional preparedness for Bundibugyo virus disease through strengthened surveillance, rapid response capacity, contact tracing, infection prevention and control, water, sanitation and hygiene, laboratory preparedness, community engagement and contingency planning. In Somalia, WHO supported national preparedness planning, readiness assessments and pre-positioning of viral haemorrhagic fever and laboratory supplies. A multidisciplinary mission to Sudan identified preparedness strengths and critical operational gaps, while additional technical support missions to Somalia and Djibouti are planned for July.

• WHO sustained emergency health operations across the Region through country-specific support. In the occupied Palestinian territory, partners delivered 708,600 health consultations during the first two weeks of June. In Sudan, WHO supported 13 hospitals, four primary health care facilities and 35 stabilization centres, while strengthening cholera preparedness and response. In Somalia, WHO trained 144 health workers and 73 community leaders to strengthen surveillance across 50 health facilities, distributed 6 tonnes of essential medicines and supplies, and pre-positioned 400 pallets of emergency medical commodities. In Yemen, Health Cluster partners supported 809 health facilities and 116 mobile medical teams, reaching approximately 690,000 people. In the Syrian Arab Republic, WHO expanded EWARS, active case finding and community-based surveillance in flood-affected areas while supporting restoration of essential health services. In Lebanon, WHO continued supporting hospitals, primary health care centres, emergency referral services and health services for displaced and conflict-affected communities.

• At regional level, WHO strengthened emergency preparedness and operational readiness through technical support for chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear emergencies, national Emergency Medical Team development, and a global simulation exercise involving more than 600 health emergency experts from 26 countries. Targeted technical missions to Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia strengthened all-hazards preparedness, public health intelligence, emergency operations centres, health security, emergency logistics and continuity of essential health services across the Gulf Cooperation Council.

title: Bangladesh Red Crescent Society Situation Report 4: Monsoon Flood & Landslide Response (16 July 2026, 16:00 hrs)
content:
Chattogram, Cox's Bazar, Bandarban, Rangamati, Khagrachhari, Cumilla, Moulvibazar, Habiganj, Sunamganj, Sylhet

Current situation, 16 July 2026:

Heavy rainfall has caused flash floods and landslides in Chattogram Division, the Chattogram Hill Tracts, Cox's Bazar, and parts of Sylhet Division. The Bangladesh Meteorological Department forecasts that active monsoon precipitation will persist across the country through 20 July, bringing light to moderate rain and temporary gusty winds. Maritime ports at Chattogram, Cox's Bazar, Mongla, and Payra remain under Local Cautionary Signal No. 3. As of 16 July at 9:00 AM, hydrological conditions indicate that only one river (the Kushiyara) remains above the danger level at two stations: Markuli in Sunamganj and Fenchuganj in Sylhet. The Someshwari River at Kalmakanda has receded below the danger level. In the north-eastern region, the Surma river has decreased and flood conditions in the low-lying areas of Sylhet and Sunamganj are expected to improve over the next 24 hours. Additionally, water levels for the Teesta, Dharla, and Dudhkumar rivers in Rangpur Division have decreased and are projected to fall further over the next three days. BDRCS's Emergency Operations Centre remains open and active.

title: Situation Report 1 - Flood Situation in Assam and Mizoram (Date: 18th July 2026)
content:
A. Situation Overview : Assam Flood

Flood conditions continued across Assam on 18 July 2026, with 7 districts affected—Biswanath, Dibrugarh, Dhemaji, Sivasagar, Jorhat, Tinsukia, and Lakhimpur. A total of 154 villages across 14 revenue circles remain impacted. 21,274 people are affected, with Dhemaji and Tinsukia reporting the highest numbers. No human deaths or missing persons were reported, and displacement remains limited, with only 2 relief camps opened in Tinsukia.

Impact on Humans

The flood affected 21,274 people, including 7,725 men, 7,312 women, and 6,237 children. Tinsukia reported 5,765 affected people, while Dhemaji recorded 14,981 affected individuals in Sissiborgaon alone. No casualties or missing persons were reported across all districts.

Animal Husbandry Loss

A total of 7,347 animals were affected across districts, including 3,884 big animals and 3,463 small animals, with Dhemaji reporting the highest livestock impact (6,690 animals). No animals were washed away.

Structural and Property Damages

No houses—fully or partially—were reported damaged across any district on this date. Similarly, no huts or cattle sheds were reported damaged, indicating minimal structural impact on residential assets.

Road and Transport Infrastructure

Road damage increased significantly, with multiple breaches and erosion reported in Dhemaji, Biswanath, and Lakhimpur. Key roads such as Nigam Baikunthapur PWD Road (Biswanath) and multiple PWD roads in Dhemaji suffered culvert washouts, berm erosion, and carriageway damage. Several stretches of Brahmaputra Dyke roads and Krishnapur–Khajua Patir Road in Lakhimpur were severely eroded, disrupting connectivity.

Irrigation and Water Supply

No irrigation bund breaches or water supply failures were reported on 18 July, indicating stable conditions in these sectors.

Electricity and Power Supply

No damage to electrical infrastructure was reported across any district.

title: Earthquakes in Venezuela: Situation Report #25 (18 July 2026, Time: 09:00 pm)
content:
Situation Report No. 25
Earthquakes in Venezuela
18 July 2026
Time: 9:00 pm

Highlights

  • Authorities report 1,350 aftershocks since the 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude earthquakes that struck on 24 June.
  • Official toll: 5,119 people dead and 16,740 injured.
  • The United Nations system and its partner organizations continue scaling up the multisectoral response to the emergency. To address the needs of 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months, an additional appeal of US$299 million was launched

Situation overview

Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre located along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). Authorities report 1,350 aftershocks.

Twenty-four days since the earthquakes, authorities report a toll of 5,119 people dead and 16,740 injured since the onset of the emergency. Authorities also indicated that 17,907 people lost their homes.

The Government response remains focused on the management of transitional camps and assistance to affected populations. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination with the authorities, continue implementing multisectoral response activities and scaling up assistance. On 10 July, United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher announced a US$299 million addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan to address the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months. The addendum complements the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, increasing the target population from 5.5 million to 6.2 million people and raising total funding requirements from US$632 million to US$931 million.

title: Islamic Republic of Iran: Humanitarian Update No. 06 | As of 30 June 2026
content:
This Humanitarian Update is produced by OCHA Regional Office for the Middle East and North Africa (ROMENA) on behalf of and in collaboration with UN agencies and humanitarian organisations. It covers the period from 1 to 30 June 2026.

HIGHLIGHTS

  • The ceasefire remained in effect throughout June, although localized incidents between 8 and 11 June reportedly injured 20 people and damaged civilian infrastructure, according to authorities.
  • Humanitarian needs continue to be driven by the impacts of the February–April escalations, particularly damage to health, water, housing and education infrastructure, alongside broader recovery needs.
  • Recovery efforts continue across affected sectors. More than 1,100 schools have been restored, while national and humanitarian partners support debris clearance, restoration of essential services, protection assistance, and recovery planning for cultural heritage and environmental assets.

KEY FIGURES

3.4K+ Civilians killed (figure is for the period 28 February-9June, as reported by WHO Middle East Conflict Situation Report #9, 11 June 2026)

33K+ Civilians injured (figure is for the period 28 February-9June, as reported by WHO Middle East Conflict Situation Report #9, 11 June 2026)

149K+ Civilian units damaged (figure is for the period since 28 February as reported by the Iranian Red Crescent Society on 7 June 2026)

SITUATION OVERVIEW

The ceasefire remained in effect throughout June, though localized incidents between 8 and 11 June injured 20 people and damaged civilian infrastructure.

Humanitarian needs continue to stem largely from the February–April escalation, while ongoing recovery assessments, inflation, and rising living costs further strained vulnerable households. Agricultural facilities had sustained an estimated US$205 million in direct damages, however domestic food production and supply chains remained largely resilient.

Emergency operations continue in affected areas, focusing on access improvements and response readiness, while additional rescue and life-support equipment is needed to strengthen capacities.

HUMANITARIAN IMPACT AND NEEDS

Health

According to the Ministry of Health and Medical Education (MoHME), as of 7 June, 52 health workers had been killed and 718 injured during the 2025 and 2026 escalations. Damage to health and power infrastructure continued to disrupt services, with outages threatening hospital operations and vaccine and medicine cold chains, particularly for children under five and patients requiring emergency or referral care. Key needs include backup power for health facilities and cold-chain warehouses, rescue and life-support equipment, and restored access to priority health facilities. Funding and health commodity procurement constraints continue to limit the response.

Water, Sanitation and Hygiene

Damage to water and power infrastructure continues to limit access to safe drinking water, increasing public health risks, particularly in areas dependent on chlorinated systems and brackish groundwater. Priority needs include water disinfection, restoration of pumping and transmission capacity, temporary water storage and trucking, provision of safe drinking water, and debris clearance to enable repairs.

Food Security

Food remains available in markets; however, rising prices continue to undermine affordability. Between June 2025 and June 2026, food prices increased by 133.9 per cent, while the cost of the minimum food basket rose by more than 35 per cent since February 2026. Lower-income households have experienced the highest inflationary pressures, increasing the need for targeted food and cash assistance.

Protection

Internal movements remained largely temporary, localized, and economically driven, with no large-scale displacement observed. However, a deterioration in conditions could trigger broader population movements. Afghan nationals in Iran continued to face socio-economic hardship, high documentation costs, and uncertainty over mandatory health insurance, while rising living costs, debt, and housing pressures eroded coping capacities. Along the Iran–Pakistan border, extreme heat, difficult travel conditions, financial constraints, and insecurity heightened protection risks for irregular migrants, with increasing family arrivals indicating growing vulnerability.

Education

As of 30 June, the Ministry of Education reported that 1,195 schools had been fully restored, while damage to education and sports facilities was estimated at US$25.1 million, with a further US$2.4 million in losses to equipment, including school supplies, sports resources, and camp facilities. Public education continued to be delivered partly online during the reporting period.

Shelter and Non-Food Items

As of 7 June, the Iranian Red Crescent Society (IRCS) reported that 149,528 civilian units had sustained damage during the escalation, including 123,647 residential units and 24,450 commercial units. The Tehran Municipality assessed that 51,000 residential units had sustained various degrees of damage, expecting most of the reconstruction to be completed by the end of June.

Early Recovery

Debris clearance and recovery activities continue in affected areas. Environmental assessments have identified direct impacts on 16 protected areas, affecting wildlife habitats and ecosystems. Partners continue to advocate for environmental recovery efforts, which remain underfunded compared to other recovery priorities.

Cultural Heritage

Since February 2026, more than 100 cultural heritage sites and institutions have reportedly been affected. The United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO) confirmed damage to two World Heritage sites and impacts on 628 museums, cultural institutions, and heritage assets, threatening cultural preservation, identity, and heritage-based livelihoods. Recovery remains constrained by limited funding, specialized expertise, and restoration materials.

RESPONSE

Health

The United Nations Children’s Agency (UNICEF), in partnership with MoHME and a private-sector partner, is supporting routine immunization through the procurement of 200,000 rotavirus vaccine doses and two million doses of Diphtheria, Tetanus, and Pertussis (DTP) vaccine. UNICEF received 294 Rapid Response backpacks expected to reach 310,000 people, and is procuring and delivering five prefabricated health units, five primary healthcare tents, and equipment for 25 walk-in cold rooms. WHO is procuring diagnostics, medicines, vector-control supplies, generators, trauma and emergency kits, and non-communicable disease kits for affected provinces. Mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) for health workers continues in 23 cities; as of 23 June, over 5,900 people attended in-person sessions, 3,000 joined webinars, and 594 health workers received individual support, including 94 referrals for specialized care. The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) is planning to provide 142 units of emergency backup generators to provincial cold chain warehouses. The International Organisation for Migration (IOM) provided MHPSS to 31 beneficiaries and will support procurement of trucks, generators, and air conditioners for MoHME. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) delivered medical humanitarian assistance for trauma care and other specialized supplies.

Water, Sanitation and Hygiene

UNDP is supporting water service restoration through the procurement of 100 chlorination and disinfection units, rehabilitation of priority pumping systems, deployment of temporary water storage and water trucking, and installation of five reverse osmosis desalination units in affected communities. The support includes on-the-job training for local operators in system maintenance and water quality monitoring, in partnership with provincial water authorities.

Food Security

National efforts to maintain essential commodity supplies and stabilize markets continued nationwide. The World Food Programme (WFP) provided food and cash assistance to 35,542 refugees, including daily bread through supported bakeries and wheat flour distributions, while school feeding continued via take-home rations for about 9,000 refugee students.

Protection

UNICEF is training frontline workers and caregivers to support children affected by conflict-related distress through the Teaching Recovery Techniques Plus Parenting package. The United Nations Refugee Agency (UNHCR) continues reception, registration, protection and legal counselling, case management, psychosocial and child protection services, and protection risk assessments. IOM assessed 128 vulnerable households, initiated cash assistance for 260 households, and is procuring 59 wheelchairs for migrants with disabilities for direct distribution.

Education

Education partners are supporting learning continuity through online and offline learning, educational packages, and TV-based education while beginning rehabilitation activities. UNESCO has secured funding to provide MHPSS to conflict-affected children and families in partnership with the Tehran Disaster Mitigation and Management Organization.

Shelter and Non-Food Items

IRCS announced plans to construct 20 relief warehouses across Tehran Province to strengthen emergency preparedness and response capacity. The facilities will store essential relief supplies and rescue equipment to ensure faster response during crises.

Early Recovery

National partners continued debris clearance and recovery efforts. According to Tehran Municipality, 1,704 machines were deployed, 603 debris-clearing missions conducted, and 4,032 transport operations completed during the escalation, with about 20 per cent of the estimated 20,000 tonnes of conflict-generated debris cleared. The Government continued efforts to strengthen energy resilience, including adding nearly 5,000 MW of solar power capacity. UNDP is supporting debris removal and emergency response capacity through heavy machinery and rescue equipment for IRCS, while UNESCO is mobilizing resources for environmental assessment and post-conflict ecosystem recovery.

Cultural Heritage

UNESCO is supporting assessments and recovery planning for conflict-affected cultural heritage sites, including Golestan Palace and Chehel Sotoun, while mobilizing resources and strengthening capacities across the museum and heritage sectors. Assessments of museums and intangible cultural heritage have been completed to guide recovery interventions, and coordination for implementation of secured funding is ongoing.

title: PAHO Regional Situation Report No.7: Measles in the Region of the Americas (17 July 2026)
content:
Situation Overview

Between epidemiological week (EW) 1 and EW 27 of 2026(ending on 11 July 2026), the Region of the Americas reported 43,559 confirmed measles cases from 17 countries and territories, representing a 3.8 fold increase compared to the same period in 2025. Guatemala (27,145), Mexico (12,052), the United States (2,231) and Canada (1,097) accounted for the majority (98%) of confirmed cases (Map 1). Additionally, 44 deaths have been reported (1). The substantial increase in the regional cumulative total compared with Situation Report No.6 is primarily attributable to a retrospective update from Guatemala, which added 20,078 cases. Guatemala’s reported total increased from 7,067 to 27,145 cases following the inclusion of cases confirmed by epidemiological linkage and clinical criteria, in addition to laboratory-confirmed cases. This change in case reporting should be considered when interpreting regional totals and trends.

During EW 25 and EW 26 of 2026, the Region of the Americas reported 1,818 new confirmed measles cases across eight countries and territories, representing a 38.4% decrease compared with the previous two-week period (EW 23-24; 2,949 new cases)2 (Figure 1). The decrease was driven mainly by fewer cases reported in Guatemala, Mexico, Peru, and the United States. In contrast, Canada reported an increase, driven primarily by a rise in cases in Quebec.

Following the earthquakes, the risk of measles introduction and spread in Venezuela remains a concern due to suboptimal vaccination coverage, surveillance gaps, and gathering of displaced population in temporary camps related with emergency response and early recovery activities. Given the risk of possible imported cases, particularly in areas receiving humanitarian personnel, strengthening early detection, laboratory confirmation capacity, active case finding, and vaccination of displaced populations remain a priority to reduce the risk of importation and onward transmission.

The following sections describe the Pan American Health Organization’s (PAHO) ongoing operational response to the regional measles situation. The Operational Snapshotsummarizes the status of priority countries and the technical cooperation underway with each. The PAHO Response by Strategic Pillar consolidates regional actions across the four operational pillars guiding the Organization's response: epidemiological surveillance and laboratory diagnosis; immunization and vaccine operations; risk communication and community engagement; and operational readiness and partnerships.

title: Situation Report No.6: Earthquakes in Venezuela 2026 (M7.2 and M7.5), 17 July 2026

HIGHLIGHTS

• More than three weeks after the two earthquakes struck north-central Venezuela on 24 June 2026, affecting at least seven states, the emergency response remains active. While the most acute phase of rescue, trauma care and immediate postdisaster surgery has eased, priorities are now focused on sustaining essential health services, strengthening referral pathways, supporting temporary camps and preventing public health risks.

• Referral hospitals remain operational, though service delivery is still under strain, most notably in La Guaira, where limited bed availability, structural damage, and a high volume of referrals persist. Emergency Medical Teams (EMTs) remain integrated into the national response, providing more than 14,000 consultations while strengthening clinical capacity, referral pathways and continuity of care in the affected states.

• Integrated epidemiological surveillance has been strengthened across affected states through expanded reporting, laboratory support, event-based surveillance and vaccination activities. No large-scale outbreaks have been confirmed to date despite ongoing public health risks in transitional camps.

• The rise to 107 transitional camps heightens protection and public health risks, requiring coordinated action on WASH, mental health, GBV mitigation, and outbreak prevention, alongside stronger support for host communities.

• PAHO/WHO continues supporting the Ministry of Popular Power for Health (MPPS) through the deployment of its Regional Response Team, covering health emergency coordination, logistics, information management, epidemiology, risk communication and community engagement, and EMT coordination. In coordination with the MPPS, PAHO/WHO is also supporting the virtual CICOM and EMT mobilization, with sixteen EMTs now operational across La Guaira, Caracas, Miranda, and Aragua, increasing clinical capacity in the affected areas.

• PAHO/WHO has shipped a total of 33.5 metric tons (MT) of critical medical equipment and supplies to support the response in Venezuela. Of this, supplies have already been distributed to 10 health facilities, with an additional distribution to 18 health facilities and 36 shelters planned in the coming days, including Interagency Emergency Health Kits (IEHK) and Trauma and Emergency Surgery Kits (TESK).

title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #13 (15 to 16 July 2026)
content:
The thirteenth Situation Report provides an update on IOM’s response to the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, covering the period from 15 to 16 July.

Highlights

Between 15 and 16 July, IOM expanded its multisectoral response in transitory camps and affected communities in La Guaira, with interventions in shelter and site coordination, health, protection, water, sanitation and hygiene, and information management.

To date, IOM has reached 7,290 unique individuals through 11,277 instances of assistance and services, mainly in health, shelter and site coordination, WASH and protection.

At the José María Vargas Sports Centre, IOM maintained essential services for 347 families and supported the relocation of 40 households to other sites in Caracas. At Mare Abajo II, the installation of 200 new bunk beds increased total availability to 350.

IOM Activities

IOM continues to support transitory camps and affected communities in La Guaira through shelter, site coordination, WASH, health and mental health, protection, registration, mobility monitoring and inter-agency coordination.

At Mare Abajo II, IOM installed 200 bunk beds with mattresses, prepared a module to partition family spaces and continued works on showers, drainage and site preparation. At Tanaguarena Golf Course, it coordinated service delivery and the distribution of supplies.

At César Nieves Stadium, IOM supported water provision, the cleaning and maintenance of toilets, the installation of showers, waste management and the distribution of sanitation supplies. It also distributed 30,000 litres of water in Mare Abajo II and nearby communities.

At the José María Vargas Sports Centre, 16 mobile health and mental health sessions have been conducted, providing a cumulative total of 1,377 consultations. In Playa Grande, 108 medical consultations were carried out, while dental, internal medicine and psychological support services were strengthened.

Registration reached 536 families and 1,605 people at César Nieves Stadium; 153 families and 463 people in Playa Grande; and 20 families and 65 people at Tanaguarena Golf Course. Progress was also made in designing a household survey and monitoring post-earthquake displacement.

IOM Planned Response

IOM will continue strengthening the management and improvement of transitory camps, including the installation of toilets, showers, water systems, lighting and internal partitions, as well as health and mental health care, protection screening and referrals, and measures to prevent sexual exploitation and abuse.

It will also continue updating registration records, conducting multisectoral assessments and monitoring mobility, while consolidating information on services, actors and gaps to improve the coordination of interventions.

title: oPt: Humanitarian Situation Report | 16 July 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Continued military operations, new displacement and deteriorating access further limited humanitarian assistance and heightened protection concerns across Gaza.
  • Agricultural recovery is at risk as animal feed shortages and soaring prices threaten livestock survival across the Gaza Strip.
  • Engine oil shortages continue to disrupt essential water and sanitation services, increasing the risk of sewage overflows and public health hazards.
  • Settler attacks have become a leading cause of Palestinian injuries in the West Bank, accounting for 55 per cent of all Palestinian injuries in 2026.
  • Israeli settlers demolished the abandoned Al Yanoun School, while Ar Rifa'iyya School became at imminent risk of demolition following an Israeli court ruling. Overall, 84 schools in Area C and East Jerusalem remain under pending demolition or stop-work orders.
  • Jabal al Aqra'a became the 47th Palestinian community to be fully displaced following recurrent settler attacks and related access restrictions since January 2023.

Overview

Across the OPT, insecurity, access restrictions, repeated displacement and funding gaps continue to deepen humanitarian needs while constraining response efforts. In the Gaza Strip, ongoing military operations, movement restrictions and insecurity are driving new displacement, disrupting humanitarian operations and limiting access to food, water, shelter, health care and other essential services. Shortages of critical supplies, including engine oil and animal feed, are further undermining water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services, food security and agricultural recovery.

In the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, Israeli forces’ operations, demolitions, settlement expansion, settler violence and movement restrictions continue to drive displacement, heighten protection risks and undermine access to housing, livelihoods, education and other essential services. Settler attacks have emerged as a leading driver of Palestinian injuries and displacement in 2026, with Bedouin and herding communities in Area C particularly affected.

Gaza Strip

This section covers 6 to 12 July unless otherwise specified.

The humanitarian situation across Gaza remains dire amid ongoing military activity, recurring security incidents, and increasing movement restrictions. These conditions continue to fuel new displacement, disrupt humanitarian operations, limit access to essential services, and heighten protection risks for affected populations. Critical funding gaps are further compounding these challenges, constraining the ability of humanitarian partners to sustain and scale up responses despite growing needs across the Strip.

According to the Ministry of Health (MoH) in Gaza, which operates under the de facto authorities, 40 Palestinians were reported killed, including those who died of wounds and had their bodies retrieved from under the rubble, and 127 people were injured between 8 and 15 July. This brings the overall reported casualty toll since the announcement of a ceasefire agreement on 10 October 2025 to 1,123 fatalities and 3,616 injuries. Another 96 fatalities were retroactively added to the total number after their identification details were approved by MoH.

On 13 and 14 July, reported Israeli military strikes on police positions in North Gaza resulted in 12 fatalities, reflecting the volatile security environment and the continued impact of military operations on civilian infrastructure and public-service capacity. Further south, an airstrike on 10 July reportedly destroyed shelters in displacement sites in Al Mawasi area in Khan Younis. As a result, 78 families were displaced and another 130 families had their shelters damaged, significantly increasing emergency shelter needs and heightening protection concerns, particularly for women, children, older persons, and persons with disabilities.

Humanitarian operations were also affected by interference and insecurity. On 12 July, humanitarian workers were forced to halt food distributions after armed personnel affiliated with the de facto authorities forcibly entered the Abu Rashid food distribution point in Jabalya, North Gaza. The forces also entered a warehouse belonging to the World Food Programme (WFP) and reportedly assaulted two truck drivers who were delivering humanitarian supplies. In a statement issued on 13 July, the Humanitarian Coordinator, who also serves as the Deputy Special Coordinator and Resident Coordinator, condemned these incidents, stressing that they are not isolated and reflect an increasingly dangerous pattern of intimidation, violence and obstruction, including smuggling attempts, targeting and abusing humanitarian operations. He added that this is happening as the expansion of areas under Israeli control is further reducing the space available to civilians, making it imperative that humanitarian assistance is able to move safely and reach people in need without interference.

In southern Gaza, access constraints are particularly acute for communities located near the “Yellow Line” in northern Rafah. Between 6 and 13 July, 11 displacement sites in the Al Mawasi Fish Fresh area became inaccessible due to continued daily movement of Israeli military tanks in the vicinity, placing approximately 1,600 displaced people at heightened risk of secondary displacement. Humanitarian services in the affected displacement sites were suspended due to insecurity and access constraints, significantly reducing partners’ ability to monitor conditions and deliver assistance. The situation was further aggravated by the loss of access to the primary water source serving these sites, raising serious concerns over access to safe drinking water, hygiene conditions, and public health risks.

Following reports of movements of Israeli forces and disruptions to humanitarian services in the area, the UN and its humanitarian partners began conducting joint missions to affected communities. On 13 July, OCHA and its humanitarian partners consulted representatives from 17 displacement sites hosting approximately 3,000 families near the “Yellow Line” in northern Rafah. Community representatives reported that the yellow blocks marking the line had moved northward. They also described daily movements of Israeli tanks, the construction of sand embankments and recurrent gunfire. Families reported remaining inside their tents for much of the day due to fear of injury from gunfire or stray bullets.

Insecurity has significantly disrupted humanitarian access, particularly water trucking, food assistance, hygiene activities, and routine site-management support. Many communities reported severe water shortages and limited access to emergency medical transportation. Some families expressed concerns that they had few viable relocation options due to overcrowding elsewhere, shortages of tents and non-food items, and inadequate access to services.

Similar concerns were observed in Deir al Balah. On 15 July, the Deputy Humanitarian Coordinator led a joint humanitarian mission to a school-turned-shelter in Bureij to assess emerging needs and gaps in humanitarian services. The shelter hosts 18 displaced families and is located about 50 yards from the “Yellow Line.” Families reported living there for more than a year and a half, with access constraints hampering the delivery of humanitarian assistance. Their living conditions are severely undermined by insecurity, the absence of alternatives, and severe gaps in access to drinking water, food, healthcare, sanitation and education.

Humanitarian partners have started mobilizing responses to address the most pressing needs and gaps identified in these visited areas. In parallel, they continue to respond to the needs of newly displaced families in various areas across the Strip (See the Intersectoral Support section in Annex 1 below) and maintain support for those in protracted displacement.

title: Afghanistan: Weekly Market Report: Issue 303: Week 2 – July 2026
content:
Key Highlights

Exchange Rate and Trade Dynamics:

• Exchange Rate: During the second week of July, the Afghani remained broadly stable at AFN 65.7/USD. However, the Afghani remained 5% stronger than last year and 13% stronger than the three-year average, continuing to help moderate imported inflation despite ongoing external market pressures.

• Trade: Market supply remained generally adequate, supported by domestic harvests and continued regional trade. However, Afghanistan's heavy reliance on imported goods continues to expose domestic markets to fluctuations in the exchange rate, fuel prices, and regional trade conditions, contributing to price volatility and maintaining the country's vulnerability to external shocks.

Food Items:

• National average food prices remained relatively stable during the second week of July, with only modest weekly movements across most staple commodities.

• Wheat and Flour: Wheat grain prices declined slightly (-0.7%) during the week, while both high-price and low-price wheat flour remained broadly stable. Compared to last year, wheat grain (+12%), high-price flour (+7%), and lowprice flour (+11%) remained above their year-ago levels, reflecting sustained production and transportation costs.

• Rice: Both rice categories declined slightly during the week. Nevertheless, high-price and low-price rice remained 26% and 33% higher than last year, respectively, and above their three-year average levels.

• Other Staples: Cooking oil increased by 1.4% during the week, while pulses (-0.2%) and salt (-0.1%) declined marginally. Sugar increased by 0.8%. Compared to last year, cooking oil (+3%), sugar (+10%), and salt (+8%) remained higher, whereas pulse prices were 13% lower than a year earlier. • Vegetables: Vegetable prices showed mixed seasonal movements. Potato prices increased by 3.3%, while tomato and onion prices declined by 1.9% and 7.1%, respectively. Compared to last year, tomato (+34%) and potato (+51%) prices remained significantly higher, while onion prices were 10% lower, reflecting improved seasonal availability.

Non-Food Items:

• Fuel: Diesel prices continued its upward momentum and increased by 5.3% during the week, reflecting higher International oil prices and continued supply constraints from Russia. Compared to last year and the three-year average, diesel prices remained 15% and 18% higher, respectively.

• Fertilizers: Fertilizer prices remained largely stable during the week, with DAP declining (-0.3%) and Urea increasing slightly (+0.1%). Compared to last year, DAP (+17%) and Urea (+49%) remained considerably higher, while improved seed (-2%) and animal feed (-7%) remained below last year's levels.

• Livestock: The price of a one-year-old live female sheep declined marginally (-1.0%) during the week and remained 6% below last year's level and 3% below the three-year average, contributing to weaker pastoralist ToT.

Labour Market:

• Labour market conditions remained weak. The unskilled labour wage declined marginally (-0.8%), while labour availability improved to 2.0 days/week (+3.0%). Despite this improvement, labour availability remained 15% below both last year and the three-year average, indicating continued pressure on household income opportunities.

title: Attacks on Health Care in Myanmar: 24 June - 07 July 2026
content:
Data collected by Insecurity Insight shows that since the military coup on 01 February 2021 and 23 June 2026 at least 1,948 incidents of violence against or obstruction of access to health care took place across Myanmar:

  • equivalent to one attack on health care every day for more than five years
  • 65% of these attacks were attributed to the Myanmar Armed Forces (MAF)
  • 175 health workers were killed and 932 arrested
  • health facilities were damaged on at least 510 occasions

During the first year following the February 2021 military coup, most incidents affecting health care were linked to political protests. Health workers were routinely arrested and MAF frequently raided health facilities in search of pro-democracy health workers or injured protesters. Although these types of incidents have become less frequent since the initial post-coup period, health workers continue to face arrest and detention due to alleged links to the Civil Disobedience Movement (CDM), Health facilities are also still raided, in some cases, forcibly closed by the authorities, disrupting access to care and limiting the availability of health services. These incidents demonstrate that political targeting of health care remains an ongoing feature of the conflict despite changes in its overall dynamics.tion text here.
