24% increase compared to last week

At least 118 civilians killed by targeted violence

18% increase compared to last week

Key events

29 Jun. Dnipropetrovsk — A Russian missile strike kills seven civilians and injures 28 others in Dnipro city

1 Jul. Kherson — Russian drone strikes kill three civilians and wound 31 others in Kherson city

3 Jul. Sumy — Russian aerial bombs kill five civilians and injure 49 others in Sumy city

Key trends

  • Russian forces continued their advances in the Kharkiv region, claiming two settlements near Vovchansk and Kupiansk. In the Donetsk region, they advanced west of the Slovyansk-Kramatorsk agglomeration, occupying two villages. Despite local Ukrainian counteroffensives at the Dnipropetrovsk-Zaporizhia administrative line, Russia’s infiltration and flag-planting operations allowed it to claim advances and occupy a village northwest of Huliaipole.
  • Russian forces launched at least 65 long-range missile and drone attacks, including on Kyiv city and the surrounding region, but mostly on the Chernihiv and Dnipropetrovsk regions.
  • Russian strikes reportedly killed at least 96 civilians in the city of Kyiv and across the Sumy, Kharkiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zaporizhia, Kherson, Mykolaiv, and Odesa regions. Ukrainian strikes reportedly killed at least 20 civilians in the Russian-occupied parts of the Zaporizhia, Donetsk, Kherson, and Luhansk regions.

Spotlight: Russia resumes its air campaign on Kyiv to bend Ukraine’s will to fight

A combined attack of Russian drones, ballistic missiles, and cruise missiles launched during the night of 1 and 2 July at the city of Kyiv and its suburbs killed at least 31 civilians and injured over 100 others. The strikes also damaged over 100 residential buildings, as well as educational institutions, a Red Cross warehouse, and oil and energy infrastructure. Russia followed these attacks with a similar mass round of strikes on Kyiv and the Kyiv region on 6 July. Preliminary data point to at least 26 fatalities and tens of injured civilians. The strikes mark a new high of civilian targeting in population centers. ACLED records the third-highest fatality count in Kyiv following the 1 and 2 July overnight strikes since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, on par with the strikes it carried out on 31 July 2025.

During the week, Russian forces also struck the regional capitals of Sumy, Kharkiv, Dnipro, Zaporizhia, Kherson, Odesa, and Mykolaiv, killing at least 34 civilians and injuring over 250 others. They also targeted civilian infrastructure, including apartment buildings and gas stations. The urban centers in front line regions are particularly vulnerable to Russian strikes due to their proximity to Russian launchpads and importance in military logistics and humanitarian service provision. While these strikes highlight Ukraine’s critically low air defense missile stock, they also suggest Moscow’s intent to intensify targeting of civilians and civilian infrastructure behind the front lines, at the cost of breaking civilian casualty records. This intent relies on Vladimir Putin’s presumed theory that continuing deep strikes into Ukraine and their disastrous consequences will be sufficient to break the will of Ukrainian society to fight back. However, this has resulted in little change despite the Ukrainians’ openness to negotiations to end the war.

title: Zimbabwean Returnee Influx Situation Report #1 (July 15, 2026)
content:
FAST FACTS

  • Escalating anti-migrant sentiments and localized violence in South Africa since April have triggered a large-scale return of Zimbabwean migrants.
  • The government on July 14 said that almost 100,000 Zimbabweans had returned so far.
  • More than 20,000 Zimbabweans are reportedly awaiting transportation support at Zimbabwean diplomatic missions and assembly points across South Africa. Returns are likely to continue in the coming weeks.
  • Women and children account for approximately 70% of returnees, highlighting significant protection and reintegration concerns.

OUR RESPONSE

  • We are coordinating with government and humanitarian partners to identify and address response gaps.
  • We are leading the response around water, sanitation and hygiene needs at Beitbridge Reception Center.
  • As part of these efforts, we have so far provided safe drinking water to 15,792 returnees and supplies for approximately 400 bacteriological water-quality tests.
  • We have installed two 5,000-liter water tanks, four water points, a storage platform and a new pipeline. We also have rehabilitated two ablution blocks and installed five mobile toilets.
  • We have installed two high-capacity floodlights to improve site safety and security.

International Medical Corps is closely monitoring the evolving situation and coordinating with government authorities, as well as with UNICEF, UN agencies and other humanitarian partners to support a coordinated response to the influx of returning Zimbabwean migrants. With UNICEF support, International Medical Corps is leading key WASH interventions at Beitbridge Reception Center. We have already begun providing safe drinking water through water trucking and water-storage infrastructure, and have procured water-quality testing reagents to support routine monitoring and to ensure safe drinking water. In addition, we have completed assessments to identify critical sanitation gaps and priority rehabilitation needs.

We have so far provided safe drinking water to 15,792 returnees and supplies for approximately 400 bacteriological water-quality tests; installed two 5,000-liter water tanks, four water points, a storage platform and a new pipeline; rehabilitated two ablution blocks and installed five mobile toilets; and installed two high-capacity floodlights to improve site safety and security.

International Medical Corps will continue to expand its WASH response by rehabilitating existing ablution facilities, installing additional mobile toilets and ablution units, strengthening handwashing and waste-management systems, and providing cleaning materials, disinfectants and other essential commodities to support hygiene promotion and infection-prevention and control measures.

The humanitarian situation remains fluid, with additional returns from South Africa expected in the coming weeks. Continued pressure on reception capacity, health services, WASH infrastructure and transportation systems is likely unless additional resources are mobilized. Immediate priorities include expanding sanitation infrastructure, strengthening health services, addressing protection risks and supporting the safe transportation and reintegration of returnees. International Medical Corps will continue to coordinate closely with the DCP, IOM, UNICEF and other humanitarian partners to monitor emerging needs and support a coordinated humanitarian response.

title: UNHCR Tanzania Operational Update - June 2026
content:
As of 30 June 2026, Tanzania hosts 131,034 refugees and asylum seekers, mainly from Burundi and the DRC. Of these, 89,808 live in Nyarugusu Camp, while 41,226 (mostly Burundian) refugees live in urban areas, villages, and old settlements in Dar es Salaam, Kigoma, Katavi, and Tabora regions.

In collaboration with the Government, UNHCR, and partners, have been receiving asylum seekers fleeing violent clashes in the DRC. In June 2026, a total of 62 new arrivals were received in Tanzania, bringing the total number of arrivals to 4,391 since renewed violence in eastern DRC in January 2025.

UNHCR continues to provide protection and assistance to persons of concern. Some services, including primary health care and education, are also extended to the host community. In addition, UNHCR seeks durable solutions for refugees.

title: Global Weather Hazards Summary, July 16, 2026 - July 22, 2026
content:
Global Overview: El Niño is present. Flood risk exists in parts of Central Africa, northern and eastern Central Asia, areas of Central America, and parts of Northern South America.

Africa Weather Hazards

Recent and upcoming heavy rains maintain an elevated flood risk along the Gulf of Guinea coast. Hot and abnormally dry conditions continue over much of East Africa.

1) Inundation continues in the Sudd wetlands of South Sudan.

2) Over the last 30 days or more, poor rainfall caused significant deficits and abnormal dryness in northern, central, southwestern, eastern Ethiopia, northern Eritrea, South Sudan, eastern Central African Republic (CAR), northeastern DRC, Uganda, and western Kenya. Continued rainfall deficits have caused drought in southern South Sudan.

3) Below-average rainfall since the beginning of the rainfall season has led to negative SPI values and abnormal dryness in dryness in the southern parts of Mali, and central and eastern Liberia.

4) Compounding recent wet conditions and forecasted heavy downpours during the upcoming week, maintain an elevated risk of flooding across coastal areas of Guinea, Sierra Leone, Liberia, Nigeria, and western Cameroon.

5) Forecasted much above-average temperatures greater than 35°C will lead to abnormal heat in coastal regions of northern Morocco and Algeria, Tunisia, Uganda, western Kenya, eastern South Sudan, northern Eritrea, and Ethiopia's western, northern, and eastern regions.

6) Ongoing heavy downpours extending from last week into the current period continue to drive high runoff, sustaining an active threat of flash floods in parts of western Ethiopia.

title: WFP Guatemala Country Brief, July 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• In June, WFP provided assistance to 2,411 people (93 percent women) through a combination of emergency assistance, capacity strengthening, and malnutrition prevention activities.

• In parallel, WFP prepared and prepositioned over 322,300 food rations (January-June) to enable a rapid, Government-led emergency response.

• Guatemala faces a convergence of acute food insecurity and malnutrition, seasonal stress and heightened climate risk, making early action critical to protect livelihoods, safeguard food consumption and prevent further deterioration in nutrition outcomes.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• In June 2026, The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) announced the onset of El Niño, with forecasts pointing to a 63 percent likelihood of a very strong event by the end of 2026, heightening the risk of climaterelated shocks.

• In Guatemala, the onset of El Niño is typically associated with irregular rainfall, prolonged dry spells, higher temperatures, soil moisture deficits and agricultural drought, particularly in rain-fed areas. These conditions could place additional pressure on staple crops such as maize and beans, particularly among rural households that rely on subsistence agriculture.

• These climate-related risks are unfolding against an already severe food security situation, with more than 3 million people projected to face acute food insecurity through to April 2026 (while the 2026–2027 IPC results are expected to be published in July 2026).

• Nutrition vulnerabilities remain equally persistent and structural. Chronic malnutrition affects around 42 percent of children under five nationwide, while more than 11,400 cases of acute malnutrition and 16 associated deaths among children under five had been reported from January to June 2026. This convergence of seasonal climate stress, food insecurity and persistent nutrition vulnerabilities heightens the risk of longer-term human capital losses.

title: UNHCR Ukraine Operational Update - 10 July 2026 [EN/AR]
content:
OPERATIONAL CONTEXT & HIGHLIGHTS:

• The Russian Federation has significantly intensified aerial attacks against Ukraine, with Kyiv and other cities subjected to multiple large-scale strikes. The UN HRMMU reported that civilian casualties in Ukraine were higher in June 2026 than in any other month since April 2022, with at least 293 civilians killed and 1,990 injured. This concerning trend appears to be continuing into July. A massive attack on Kyiv overnight on 1-2 July killed 31 people. Only a few days later, another attack on 5-6 July killed 19 people in Kyiv city and ten people in the Kyiv region. So far this year, Russian Armed Forces launched over 520 ballistic missiles at Ukraine, more than twice as many as in the same period in 2025, according to Ukraine air force data.

• The Ukraine Recovery Conference (URC) took place in Gdańsk, Poland, on 25 and 26 June. UNHCR’s Representative Bernadette Castel-Hollingsworth attended, joining key discussions with partners, UN agencies and Government counterparts. The Representative also spoke at a side event on recovery and future returns of displaced Ukrainians – highlighting the need for people-centered investments in housing, jobs and services in Ukraine.

• Marking the 75th anniversary of the 1951 Refugee Convention and the 65th anniversary of the 1961 Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness – and ahead of World Refugee Day in June – UNHCR together with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs launched a photo exhibition in Kyiv highlighting the stories of refugees and stateless people in Ukraine.

• In the fifth year since the start of the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and more than 12 years since the war began, UNHCR’s programme in Ukraine increasingly aims to help war-affected people and communities to recover, and displaced people to find durable solutions, particularly through housing and strategic protection advocacy.

title: WFP Aghanistan Country Brief, July 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• After a prolonged pipeline break, more than 1,600 mt of the approximately 6,000 mt of nutrition commodities expected in the country have arrived, enabling WFP to reach 80,000 children and 25,000 mothers.

• Since early July, funding shortfalls have forced WFP to suspend famine-prevention programmes in hotspot areas, putting 1.5 million people at risk of life-threatening hunger.

• Funding constraints have also forced WFP to suspend cash assistance at all border crossings, leaving vulnerable returning families without critical support.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Regional conflicts are exacerbating the humanitarian crisis in Afghanistan, with staple food prices at elevated levels and transport costs tripling due to prolonged border closure with Pakistan, re-routed supply chains due to the conflict in the Middle East, and increased fuel prices. These supply chain pressures are particularly acute for imported specialized nutritious foods (SNFs), with most WFP-supported health clinics currently facing a stock out of these commodities.

• At the same time, Afghanistan is experiencing record levels of acute malnutrition, with 3.7 million children under five and 1.2 million pregnant and breastfeeding women affected in 2026. The shortage of nutrition supplies, combined with funding constraints, means that one million malnourished children will be unable to receive life-saving assistance this year.

• Since early July, WFP's famine-prevention programmes in hotspot areas have been suspended, putting 1.5 million people at heightened risk of life-threatening hunger. Overall, WFP is now forced to turn away 13 million acutely hungry Afghans.

• In addition, funding constraints have compelled WFP to suspend cash assistance for returnees from Iran and Pakistan at all border crossings, leaving vulnerable families without critical support upon arrival.

title: Yemen Agrometeorological Update: Food Security and Early Warning Information System (01 - 30 June 2026) [EN/AR]
content:
HIGHLIGHTS:

  • Precipitation: Rainfall across Yemen remained generally low throughout June 2026, with localized convective activity over the southern uplands. Despite this, the monthly mean was slightly above the five-year average.
  • Rainfall anomalies: Compared to the long-term average and June 2025, June 2026 showed mixed rainfall patterns across Yemen, with most areas experiencing drier-than-average conditions and some localized wetter-than-average zones.
  • Temperature: Elevated temperatures persisted across Yemen during June 2026, with daytime temperatures reaching 35–40°C in eastern and coastal regions, while highland areas remained relatively cooler with nighttime temperatures of 15–20°C.
  • Vegetation: Vegetation conditions across Yemen remained generally favorable in June 2026, with 76% of cultivated areas showing fair-to-good performance. Time-series change analysis using NDVI indicated stable or improving conditions in cultivated areas, particularly in Al Hudaydah.
  • Crop season: As the growing season advances, slight agricultural water stress (ASI: 25–40%) was observed in parts of Dhamar, Al Bayda, and Sana'a governorates, indicating localized soil moisture deficits.
  • Livelihoods and food security: Below-average rainfall combined with above-average temperatures reduced soil moisture levels, disrupting crop establishment, increasing water demand, intensifying livestock stress, and further undermining agricultural livelihoods across Yemen.

title: Attacks on Health Care in the occupied Palestinian territory (24 June - 07 July 2026)
content:
Data collected by Insecurity Insight shows that between 07 October 2023 and 23 June 2026, at least 3,354 incidents of violence against or obstruction of access to health care took place across the occupied Palestinian territory. 95% of all incidents were attributed to Israeli forces.

  • Gaza: 2,339 attacks on health care were recorded during which health facilities were damaged 448 times, 770 health workers were killed and 398 arrested. Patient access to medicine was obstructed on 303 occasions.
  • West Bank and East Jerusalem: 947 attacks on health care were recorded during which health facilities were damaged 30 times, 12 health workers were killed and 190 arrested. Patient access to medicine was obstructed on 585 occasions.

title: Agrometeorological 10 days Bulletin for 11–20 July 2026 Across the Northern Tonle Sap Basin of the PEARL Project
content:
Flood Early Warning

With floods forecasted during the next 10 days, protect roots from standing water and secure the orchard. On low ground, raise soil mounds around young trees 30-50 cm (about knee height) but do not bury the graft union. Open diversion channels one hand wide and one palm deep to lead water to safe outlets; keep inlets free of trash. Move tools, fertilizers, and crates to higher shelves (about one palm above floor). Mulch 10-15 cm (about a palm to a palm-and-a- half) with dry rice straw or chopped prunings, keeping a hand-width gap at the trunk. Harvestable fruit in very low plots should be picked early and stored above floor level. After floods recede, remove (rogue) trees that do not recover and dispose of plant waste away from the orchard; wash tools with soapy water.

title: WHO Weekly Situation Update on Ongoing Health Emergency Events in South Sudan - Week #: 28; Date: 06 - 12 Jul 2026
content:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

South Sudan remains in EVD/BVD preparedness and readiness mode with no confirmed cases to date, despite sustained regional risk; DR Congo has now reported 1,926 confirmed cases and 702 deaths (CFR 36.5%). Cumulative PoE screening rose sharply from 394,410 to 552,071 travellers (157,661 additional), and the National Master Training of Trainers was completed, producing a pool of 90 trainers. Two EVD alerts (Yambio and Tambura) were investigated and discarded. Cholera declined 23.7% week-on-week (347 new cases), with the OCV mop-up campaign set for 10 July. Polio detected a new cVDPV1 environmental isolate in Juba; measles and rubella reported no new cases this week, and Guinea Worm remains at zero cases for 2026.

title: Jordan Operational Update - April-June 2026
content:
OPERATIONAL CONTEXT

In April, the Ministry of Planning and International Cooperation of Jordan initiated the planning phase of its 2026–2028 Strategic Framework for the Refugee Response. With UNHCR’s close engagement in the process, the framework aims to deliver an integrated and results-oriented approach in a context of constrained funding, while addressing refugee returns as a key strategic priority. In June, UNHCR released findings from the 2026 Socio-Economic Survey on Refugees in Jordan, conducted in collaboration with the World Bank and WFP. The survey, carried out every two years, covered a representative sample of 4,905 refugee households across camps and host communities, representing 24,752 registered refugees. Findings indicate persistently high levels of economic vulnerability, with an estimated 66 per cent of refugees living below the poverty line of 89 JOD per person per month.

title: Situation report on Bangladesh Flash Flood, July 2026
content:
Since 4 July 2026, continuous heavy rainfall associated with an active monsoon and a persistent low-pressure system over the north-west Bay of Bengal, combined with upstream runoff, has triggered widespread flash floods, severe waterlogging, and landslides across southeastern, eastern, and northeastern Bangladesh.

The disaster has affected more than 1.11 million people across 10 districts: Chattogram, Cox's Bazar, Sunamganj, Khagrachhari, Rangamati, Bandarban, Cumilla, Moulvibazar, Sylhet and Feni that resulting in 53 fatalities and 39 injuries as of today.

While Chattogram District has experienced the highest level of impact in terms of the affected population. Exceptional rainfall has been recorded across the affected areas. Chattogram city received 412.3 mm of rainfall within 24 hours till date, marking the highest single-day July rainfall recorded in the past 42 years.

The major rivers, including the Matamuhuri, Sangu, Surma, and Kushiyara, exceeded their danger levels, leading to embankment breaches, extensive flooding, and prolonged waterlogging.

Several lowlying areas were completely inundated, including the entirety of Banshkhali Upazila in Chattogram District. In the hill districts of Chattogram Division, saturated slopes triggered multiple landslides, causing casualties, damaging homes and infrastructure, and disrupting road connectivity.

Bangladesh’s flood threat is shifting from the country’s southeastern districts to the north and northeast, with forecasters warning that continued heavy rainfall and upstream runoff could trigger fresh flooding in Sylhet,
Sunamganj and Rangpur over the coming days.

The Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD) has forecast moderate to very heavy rainfall across much of the country over the next several days, raising concerns that the existing flood situation could worsen before improving

title: Africa Region | Ebola (BVD) Epidemic - Operation update #2 (MDRS1007)
content:
A. SITUATION ANALYSIS

Description of the crisis

Over the last seven weeks following the declaration of the Bundibugyo Virus Disease (BVD) epidemic on 15 May 2026, the situation in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) remains concerning, characterized by persistent community transmission, geographic transmission expansion, and escalating strain on response capabilities. As of 10 July 2026, the DRC recorded 1,873 confirmed cases and 672 fatalities, resulting in an overall case fatality ratio of 35.9%. Transmission has impacted 41 out of 140 health zones in Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uele and Tshopo provinces in DRC. Uganda has 20 confirmed cases and two fatalities, with incidents documented in Kampala and Wakiso. The Bundibugyo Ebola virus has an incubation period of between 2 and 21 days according to the WHO.

According to the Centre des opérations d’urgences de sante publique (DRC COUSP), two new provinces in DRC have confirmed cases, namely the Haut-Uele province and Tshopo province. Ituri Province continues to be the epicentre, as of 10 July, reporting 1,705 cases and 577 fatalities. Bunia, Mongbwalu, and Rwampara Health Zones are the primary transmission hubs, collectively accounting for nearly 65% of all confirmed cases nationwide. The weekly incidence rose from 259 cases between 18–24 June to 305 cases between 25 June to 1 July 2026. The growth was predominantly attributed to Ituri Province. Despite an overall reduction in weekly incidence in North Kivu Province, transmission escalated in Katwa Health Zone. Focused increase of cases was also noted in Mangala, Bambu, Nia-Nia, and Tchomia Health Zones.

North Kivu Province recorded 165 cases and 94 fatalities, resulting in a case fatality ratio of 57%, which is more than double the national rate. South Kivu reported three cases and one fatality, with no additional verified cases since 26 May. Nevertheless, the low alert-investigation performance reported in South Kivu on 4 July, only 4.4%, means that the absence of recently confirmed cases should be interpreted cautiously and does not yet exclude undetected transmission.

A surveillance report from the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) Continental Incident Management Support Team on 6 July forecast that the cumulative confirmed cases in the DRC are expected to continue increasing beyond, reflecting ongoing transmission. Although the projected epidemic curve suggests a gradual slowing in the rate of increase, the number of confirmed cases is still anticipated to rise in the coming weeks. There is currently no evidence of a sustained decline in transmission, indicating that the outbreak has not yet reached its peak. Furthermore, the wide upper bound of the 95% confidence interval highlights continued uncertainty in the epidemic trajectory and suggests that substantially higher case numbers remain possible if transmission is not effectively contained.

The evolving epidemiological context is generating urgent operational needs, including increased ambulance capacity to strengthen surveillance activities, facilitate rapid case investigations, and support timely emergency response efforts. Reduction of the transmission rate opportunities remains through prevention, strengthened surveillance, community engagement, risk communication, infection prevention and control, and cross-border coordination. With rapid and coordinated action, neighbouring countries can strengthen preparedness, support early detection, and help prevent wider regional spread.

Notably, the crisis is unfolding in a complex context marked by armed conflicts, other situations of violence and heightened insecurity, high population mobility, porous borders, limited access to affected communities, and constrained contact tracing, particularly in eastern DRC. These factors continue to increase the risk of undetected transmission and further geographic spread. The community aggression is heavily driven by mistrust and misinformation which has undermined ongoing humanitarian and public health operations.

Spontaneous and orchestrated violence directed against Ebola treatment centres, Safe and Dignified Burial (SDB) and other volunteers have included; attack of the Ebola Treatment Centres in Bunia (16 June) and Bafwabango (30 June) alongside verbal threats against DRC Red Cross volunteers conducting community engagement activities.

As a background security context, since the beginning of 2026, a total of 19 serious security incidents involving volunteers in the East of DRC have been reported by DRC RC, including the incident of 16 June when two Red Cross volunteers were killed while carrying out duties on a non-Ebola project in Walungu Territory, South Kivu. These incidents underscore the growing security threats facing aid workers and highlights the dangerous consequences of misinformation and declining community acceptance across the region. Meanwhile, in Mongwalu, there is a temporary improvement in the security situation following the deployment of additional police forces. Notwithstanding, there are risks for the Red Cross (and others) associated with a further militarization of the Ebola response.

Countries neighbouring DRC continue to be at high-risk of cross-border transmissions driven by sustained population mobility, the risk is mostly concentrated in those border areas closer to the outbreak zones. At the regional level, governments of countries at risk continue to strengthen infection prevention and control efforts, cross-border surveillance at border entry points for early detection. In the spirit of shared responsibility and collective effort, the Red Cross has mobilised its footprint of national staff, volunteers and experts to directly support the response. Resource mobilisation for various public health activities in emergency is ongoing while supporting and reinforcing Red Cross Red Crescent movement capacity.

title: UNRWA Situation Report #229 on the Humanitarian Crisis in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem [EN/AR]
content:
All information updated for 1 - 7 July 2026 [1]
Days 997 - 1003 since the start of the war in the Gaza Strip

Highlights

The Gaza Strip

  • The latest WASH Cluster monitoring, conducted in June, indicates a continued deterioration in water security, with 84 per cent of assessed households experiencing moderate-to-high water insecurity. Access to water for domestic use declined between May and June, and drinking water was identified as the most pressing humanitarian concern, reported by 62 per cent of households.
  • Sanitation and hygiene conditions also remain concerning. Eighty-six per cent of households reported barriers to accessing toilets and latrines, due to lack of water, privacy concerns, and poor cleanliness, among others. Environmental health risks persist, with 52 per cent of households reporting sewage or sludge near shelters and 43 per cent reporting nearby solid waste accumulation. More than half of households reported lacking hygiene items, while health concerns remain widespread, including skin diseases or scabies (64 per cent), bedbugs (31 per cent), and lice (22 per cent).

title: Earthquakes in Venezuela: Situation Report #21 (14 July 2026, Time: 09:00 pm)
content:
Situation Report No. 21
Earthquakes in Venezuela
14 July 2026
Time: 9:00 pm

Highlights

  • Following the 24 June earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 (18:00 local time), authorities report more than 1,200 aftershocks.
  • Official toll: 4,734 people dead and 16,740 injured.
  • A total of 6,462 people have been rescued.
  • An additional appeal for US$298 million was launched to scale up the earthquake response and address the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people over the next six months.
  • The United Nations system and its partner organizations, in coordination with the Government, are responding with multisectoral actions and will continue to scale up assistance to affected people.

Situation overview

Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre located along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). Authorities report 1,275 aftershocks.

Twenty days since the earthquakes, authorities report a toll of 4,734 people dead, 16,740 injured and 6,462 rescued since the onset of the emergency. Authorities also indicated that 17,907 people lost their home.

The Government response remains focused on search operations, the management of transitional camps and assistance to affected populations. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination with the authorities, continue implementing multisectoral response activities and scaling up assistance. United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher announced a US$298 million addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan aimed at addressing the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people over the next six months. This is in addition to the 5.5 million people already targeted under the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, which requires US$632 million in funding.

title: Dooplaya District Incident Report: Burma Army soldiers arrested and beat four villagers, including a 16-year-old, in Noh T’Kaw Township (March 2026)
content:
Excerpt

Part 3 – Complete Description of the Incident

Describe the Incident(s) in complete detail.

Seik Gyi [Kyainseikgyi] Town in Dooplaya District is under the control of the SAC [State Administration Council]. Villagers from both nearby and distant areas were travelling through Seik Gyi Town. Some villagers from distant areas did not know the alternative routes to avoid the town, so they passed through it. Police in Seik Gyi Town, along with SAC soldiers and immigration officers, were operating and conducting checks at the entrance of the town on the main road. This checkpoint is located in the Seik Gyi Town–Kyon Kone area, where multiple groups [of the Burma Army] are involved in the checking.

On 20 March 2026, at around 10 am, Saw A---, Saw B---, Saw C---, and Saw D--- accompanied two friends, both women, from Aa--- village, Lay Wah Hka village tract, Noh T’Kaw (Kyainseikgyi) Township, Dooplaya District, who were travelling to another village via Seik Gyi Town. When they arrived at the checkpoint, the SAC stopped them but did not stop the two women. The SAC asked questions in Burmese, but the young people only spoke Karen, so they did not understand what they were being asked. When they [the Burma Army] checked Saw A---’s phone, they saw a picture of his friend wearing camouflage trousers. Then, the SAC [soldiers] punched each of them [the four men] in the face at least three times. After that, they were handcuffed and forced to kneel with their hands raised. They were then hit with a stick at least 30 times each.

As the two women were not stopped by the SAC at the checkpoint, they went to Ab--- village, Noh T’Kaw village tract, Noh T’Kaw Township. They informed one of their friends in Ab--- village about the incident. Then, their friend asked for help from a BGF [Border Guard Force][7] checkpoint authority in the village. The BGF checkpoint authority contacted the SAC and informed them that those young people were civilians, not enemies [members of an armed group]. Therefore, on 20 March 2026, at about 11 am, the SAC released them. After they were released, they returned to the village and did not continue their journey. [After release, they did not seek formal treatment at a medical facility.]

In March 2026, [a KHRG researcher conducted an interview with Saw A--- and] he explained that after he returned home, he could not move his body easily or sleep well at night because of his injury. He even needed to take medicine to reduce the pain. Saw A--- added: “I could not breathe well and felt dizzy when they hit me. I could not bear the pain, and I thought it would be better if they shot me dead. Last night, I could not sleep well. I cannot lie on my back for long, so I sometimes have to sleep lying prone.”

Saw A---'s injury had worsened, and he was experiencing more pain when the KHRG researcher asked him about his injury again [later] in March 2026.

title: WHO EMR Polio Bulletin Issue No. 1449, Week 27 (ending on 12/07/2026)
content:
Wild poliovirus type 1 (WPV1)

Cases: Four new WPV1 positive cases in 2026 from Afghanistan reported this week. The new WPV1 cases are: 2 from Nangarhar province (Behsud and Rodat districts), 1 each from Hilmand province (Musaqalah district) and Hirat province (Shindand district) noting that the Hirat/Shindand case was identified by positive contacts. In total, 52 WPV1-positive cases have been confirmed in 2025 (21 from Afghanistan and 31 from Pakistan in 2025) and 14 WPV1 cases reported in 2026 (11 from Afghanistan and 3 from Pakistan).

Environment: Thirteen new WPV1 positive environmental samples in 2026 were reported this week, 12 from Afghanistan and 1 from Pakistan. The new WPV1 environmental samples of Afghanistan are: 5 from Kandahar province (all from Kandahar district), 4 from Nangarhar province (2 from Behsud, and 1 each from Batikot and Jalalabad districts), 2 from Kabul province (both from Kabul district), and 1 from Hilmand province (Lashkargah district), with dates of collection on 20th and 24th May 2026, while the new WP1 environmental sample from Pakistan was reported from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province (Peshawar district) with collection date on 11th June 2026. In total, 745 WPV1-positive environmental samples have been reported in 2025 (94 from Afghanistan and 651 from Pakistan) and 146 WPV1-positive environmental samples reported in 2026 (46 from Afghanistan and 100 from Pakistan).

Vaccine-derivedpoliovirus (VDPV)

Cases:

• cVDPV2: No new positive cases reported this week. The cVDPV2 case count to date in 2026 is 6 (5 from Somalia and 1 from Sudan) and in 2025 is 47 (31 from Yemen, 13 from Sudan, 2 from Somalia and 1 from Djibouti).

Environment

• cVDPV1: No new cVDPV1 isolates were reported this week. cVDPV1 were confirmed from 10 environmental samples in 2025 (all from Djibouti).

• cVDPV2: No new cVDPV2 isolates were reported this week. To date, cVDPV2 was confirmed in 11 sewage water samples in 2026 (8 from Somalia and 3 from Sudan), and In 2025 from 58 samples (17 from Djibouti, 15 from Yemen, 13 from Somalia, 7 from occupied Palestinian territory, and 6 from Sudan).

title: BGD: Flood - 07-2026 - Bangladesh Floods 2026: Nationwide (2026-07-14)
content:
Description

Bangladesh is experiencing widespread flooding, flash floods, riverine inundation, and landslides across the south-eastern and north-eastern regions of the country. Although the low-pressure system that triggered the initial period of extreme rainfall has weakened and moved towards Uttar Pradesh, India, the Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD) continues to forecast intermittent heavy to very heavy rainfall through 13 July across the divisions of Chattogram, Sylhet, Rangpur, Rajshahi, Dhaka, Khulna, and Barishal. While rainfall intensity is expected to gradually decrease in the coming days, the risk of further flooding and landslides remains elevated.

Rainfall has remained exceptionally high. Chattogram recorded 298.8 mm on 9 July and 203 mm on 10 July, while Teknaf recorded 245 mm on 10 July. On 11 July, the highest rainfall was recorded in Jaflong, Sylhet (156 mm), followed by Lama, Bandarban (155 mm) and Teknaf, Cox’s Bazar (139 mm). Additional rainfall of 100–300 mm was forecast through 12 July, maintaining a high risk of flooding, waterlogging and landslides.

Flood conditions continue to evolve. As of 11 July, several river stations remained above danger level, including the Sangu, Kushiyara, Monu and Khowai rivers. By the evening of 11 July, seven stations on five rivers across six districts were flowing above danger level. The Sangu River in Bandarban exceeded danger level by more than two metres at its peak, while rising river levels continue to threaten low-lying areas in Chattogram, Feni, Khagrachhari, Sylhet, Sunamganj, Netrokona, Sherpur, Mymensingh and northern river basins.

The humanitarian impact remains significant. According to the Needs Assessment Working Group (NAWG), an estimated 1,074,534 people have been affected across 10 districts. The Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief (MoDMR) reports that approximately 38,500 people have been temporarily displaced, while more than 1,000 evacuation shelters have been opened.

Government reporting indicates that more than 267,918 households have been stranded or cut off by floodwaters across seven districts, while media reports citing the Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief indicate that at least 51 people have died nationwide due to floods and landslides. Preliminary Government reports indicate that 15,881 houses were damaged in Bandarban and 13,860 in Chattogram. The full extent and severity of housing damage remain unclear, as standing water and access constraints continue to delay detailed assessments. Water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services have been disrupted across 27 upazilas in 10 districts. In several areas, infrastructure remains submerged, while water sources have been damaged or contaminated by floodwater carrying faecal matter, agricultural chemicals, industrial waste and other pollutants. As of 12 July, the Department of Public Health Engineering (DPHE) reported that more than 12,360 latrines and 3,583 waterpoints had been fully or partially damaged.

The most affected districts include Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Bandarban, Rangamati, Khagrachhari, Moulvibazar and Habiganj.

In Cox’s Bazar, the situation remains particularly concerning due to the combined impact on Rohingya refugee camps and host communities. Across the 33 camps affected more than 28,000 people, damaged over 3,100 shelters were damaged, more than 4,700 individuals were displaced, and caused multiple fatalities and injuries associated with landslides and flooding. UNHCR has reported 15 deaths among Rohingya refugees and thousands of people left homeless following landslides and shelter collapse.

The Government of Bangladesh, led by the Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief (MoDMR), has activated a multi-agency response to support flood- and landslide-affected populations across the impacted districts. Emergency measures include the opening of more than 1,000 shelters, the allocation and distribution of cash assistance, rice, baby food, safe drinking water and other relief items, and the deployment of the Army, Navy, Coast Guard, Fire Service and local authorities to support rescue, evacuation and relief operations. The Government has deployed 516 medical teams across 50 affected upazilas. Government authorities continue to monitor the evolving situation through national and district-level coordination mechanisms, while prioritizing assistance to the most severely affected areas, including Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Bandarban, Rangamati, Khagrachhari, Moulvibazar and Habiganj. Efforts are ongoing to maintain access to essential services, support displaced populations, and address immediate humanitarian needs in affected communities.

Request For Assistance

Government Requests International Assistance: No

NS Requests International Assistance -

Information Bulletin Published

No

Actions taken by National Society

General

Damage/Needs assessment

Search & Rescue

Water & Sanitation

Food aid

Camp management

Evacuation

First Aid

Relief/Supply distribution

Human remains management and identification

Summary

The Bangladesh Red Crescent Society (BDRCS) has activated its central Emergency Operations Centre (EOC) and is coordinating response efforts across flood- and landslide-affected districts in south-eastern and north-eastern Bangladesh. Continuous information collection, situation monitoring, and coordination with district units, government authorities, IFRC, and humanitarian partners are ongoing. BDRCS has mobilized emergency resources through a combination of internal funds and partner support. A total of BDT 1.8 million has been released to district units in Chattogram, Cox's Bazar, Bandarban, Rangamati, Khagrachhari, Moulvibazar and Habiganj to support immediate response activities. To strengthen evacuation and rescue capacity, BDRCS mobilized emergency rescue equipment and non-food items including: 12 rubber boats, 110 life jackets, 135 rescue helmets, 135 rescue boots, 145 pairs of gloves, 5 generators, 5,500 jerrycans, Rescue ropes, rope bags, float plates and rescue panels. BDRCS has provided emergency food assistance to 2,220 flood-affected households across Bandarban, Khagrachhari, Rangamati, Chattogram, Cox's Bazar, Moulvibazar and Habiganj. Food packages included rice, puffed rice, lentils, oil, salt, sugar, drinking water, biscuits, ORS, soap, sanitary pads and other essential items. In Cox's Bazar, through the Population Movement Operation (PMO), BDRCS continues to support Rohingya refugees and host communities through supporting early warning dissemination, emergency relocation, search and rescue, and coordination through Camp Disaster Management Committees (DMCs) and humanitarian partners across all 33 camps. BDRCS PMO has provided emergency shelter assistance to 494 affected households in Camps 11 and 12, while WASH volunteers are assessing damaged facilities and coordinating with sector partners. Health teams continue community outreach, referrals, household visits, and essential health services, including outpatient and maternity care. Through its volunteers and field teams, BDRCS remains actively engaged in addressing the immediate needs of flood- and landslide-affected refugees and host communities, BDRCS called an emergency coordination meeting on 12 July with IFRC, ICRC and in-country Participating National Societies to update about the overall flood situation and response by BDRCS. Based on needs, BDRCS is also planning to scale-up operation by mobilizing: Mobile Water Treatment Plants, emergency medical teams, essential household items and cash assistance. Based on the initial damage and needs assessments, BDRCS requested IFRC on 8 July 2026 to support the launch of a Disaster Response Emergency Fund (DREF) operation targeting populations affected by floods and landslides in the Rohingya camps and adjacent host communities in Cox’s Bazar. The proposed operation aims to address urgent humanitarian needs through life-saving interventions, including early warning dissemination, evacuation support, search and rescue, emergency shelter assistance, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services, food assistance, cash and voucher assistance (CVA), volunteer mobilization, and operational coordination. The DREF operation is intended to complement ongoing response efforts by BDRCS and humanitarian partners while strengthening support to the most vulnerable and affected communities.

Actions taken by RCRC

Summary

Nine Participating National Societies (PNSs) maintain a presence in Bangladesh: the American Red Cross, British Red Cross, Danish Red Cross, German Red Cross, Japanese Red Cross Society, Qatar Red Crescent, Swedish Red Cross, Swiss Red Cross and Turkish Red Crescent. All PNSs are closely monitoring the evolving flood and landslide situation and are coordinating with their respective regional offices and headquarters to assess potential support to BDRCS. To support the scale-up of the ongoing humanitarian response, the American Red Cross has confirmed USD 25,000 through its Quick Action Fund (QAF), while the Swedish Red Cross has committed an additional USD 25,000 through its Initial Response Fund (IRF). These contributions will support BDRCS response activities for flood- and landslide-affected communities.

Actions taken by Federation

Summary

The IFRC Bangladesh Country Delegation is supporting BDRCS in coordinating and scaling up the response to the ongoing floods and landslides. The delegation is maintaining close coordination with the Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief (MoDMR), the United Nations Resident Coordinator’s Office (UNRC), humanitarian clusters and working groups, Participating National Societies (PNSs), and the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) to ensure effective information sharing, operational coordination, and resource mobilization. IFRC is also providing technical support to BDRCS in assessment, planning, coordination, reporting, and operational management. The IFRC Bangladesh Country Delegation remains in regular contact with the IFRC Asia Pacific Regional Office. IFRC along with BDRCS and Movement partners continue to closely monitor the evolving situation, assess emerging humanitarian needs, identify response gaps, and mobilize additional resources to support affected communities. As Shelter Cluster Co-Lead, IFRC is engaging with shelter sector partners to facilitate coordinated assessments, response planning, and information management to address the shelter needs of affected populations.

Actions taken by others

Following the heavy rainfall forecast issued on 5 July, the Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief (MoDMR), the Department of Disaster Management (DDM), the Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD), and the Flood Forecasting and Warning Centre (FFWC) convened a series of coordination meetings to strengthen preparedness and response measures. The National Disaster Response Coordination Centre was activated on a 24-hour basis, and emergency contact information was disseminated to facilitate timely response. At the district level, disaster management committees were mobilised to coordinate early warning dissemination, evacuations, shelter management, provision of emergency meals, and rescue operations. These efforts were supported by the Bangladesh Army, Bangladesh Red Crescent Society (BDRCS), Border Guard Bangladesh, Fire Service and Civil Defence, Bangladesh Police, and local administrations. On 12 July, the Prime Minister’s Office convened a high-level virtual meeting to review the impacts of flooding and landslides, including waterlogging, infrastructure damage, shelter conditions, rescue operations, relief distribution, and health service provision. Relevant authorities were instructed to prioritise the protection of lives and property, expedite the delivery of food assistance, safe drinking water, medicines, and healthcare services, and ensure that evacuation shelters provide adequate safety, sanitation, electricity, communication facilities, and support for vulnerable groups. Government agencies were further directed to strengthen inter-agency coordination, maintain operational readiness, closely monitor weather forecasts and river levels, and ensure transparent and accountable delivery of relief assistance. Led by MoDMR, the Government of Bangladesh has activated a comprehensive multi-agency response across flood- and landslide-affected districts. Emergency measures have included the opening of more than 1,000 evacuation shelters, the distribution of cash assistance, rice, baby food, safe drinking water, and other relief supplies, and the deployment of the Bangladesh Army, Navy, Coast Guard, Fire Service and Civil Defence, and local authorities to support search and rescue, evacuation, and relief operations. To address urgent health needs and reduce public health risks, the Government has mobilised 516 medical teams across 50 affected upazilas. National and district-level coordination mechanisms remain active to monitor the evolving situation, support early warning dissemination, and facilitate targeted assistance in the hardest-hit districts, particularly Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Bandarban, Rangamati, Khagrachhari, Moulvibazar, and Habiganj. To reinforce response efforts, the Government allocated a cumulative BDT 17.5 million (approximately US$142,276) and 3,250 metric tons of rice between 7 and 12 July for seven flood- and rainfall-affected districts. Chattogram received the largest allocation, comprising BDT 6.5 million and 1,200 metric tons of rice, followed by Cox’s Bazar with BDT 3 million and 450 metric tons of rice. Bandarban and Khagrachhari each received BDT 2 million and 400 metric tons of rice, while Rangamati received BDT 2.5 million and 500 metric tons of rice. Additional allocations included BDT 1 million and 200 metric tons of rice for Moulvibazar, and BDT 500,000 and 100 metric tons of rice for Habiganj. These resources were released through successive general and flood-response allocations on 7, 9, 10, and 12 July, enabling the Government to progressively scale up assistance as the situation evolved. The humanitarian community has also significantly strengthened coordination and response efforts. On 11 July, the Inter-Cluster Coordination Group (ICCG) convened an ad hoc meeting to review the evolving flood situation, anticipatory action activations, and initial updates from clusters and operational partners. The meeting agreed to strengthen information management, consolidate reporting on response activities, identify priority needs and operational gaps, and produce the first ICCG Situation Report. Subsequently, the Displacement Management, Health, Logistics, Shelter, and Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) Clusters convened emergency coordination meetings to review field-level information, identify operational constraints, and coordinate follow-up actions. The Needs Assessment and Information Management Working Group (NA/IMWG) issued Flash Updates on 9 and 12 July and continues to consolidate available data from affected areas. Preparations are underway for a multi-sectoral assessment once access conditions improve. Meanwhile, the Anticipatory Action Technical Working Group (AATWG) remains closely engaged with agencies implementing anticipatory action frameworks, monitoring trigger thresholds, sharing operational updates, and supporting coordinated preparedness actions. The ICCG Secretariat continues to liaise with cluster coordinators, BMD, DDM, MoDMR, the NGO Affairs Bureau, and district administrations across the affected areas to support a coordinated humanitarian response. In anticipation of peak flooding, the World Food Programme (WFP) activated both anticipatory action (AA) and shock-responsive social protection (SRSP) interventions in Bandarban on 10 July. Through these mechanisms, WFP reached 15,000 households under anticipatory action and an additional 859 households through SRSP, providing multipurpose cash assistance of BDT 5,000 per household alongside early warning messages. Interventions focused on Bandarban Sadar and Lama upazilas to support vulnerable households before conditions deteriorated further. On 13 July, the Start Fund Bangladesh Project Selection Committee approved GBP 799,890.60 under Alert B075 to support an emergency humanitarian response targeting approximately 55,554 people across six of the most severely affected districts: Bandarban, Khagrachhari, Rangamati, Cox’s Bazar, Chattogram, and Moulvibazar. The allocation will support rapid multi-sectoral assistance to flood- and landslide-affected populations. Several agencies also activated anticipatory actions under existing disaster preparedness frameworks. Under the Early Action Protocol for flash floods in the Haor region, CARE Bangladesh mobilised volunteers, assessed evacuation shelters, and pre-positioned four rescue boats in Derai and Gowainghat, targeting approximately 18,500 people. UN Women reached around 300 households in Kanaighat with preparedness support, while World Vision disseminated early warning messages to approximately 50,000 people, pre-positioned 1,000 hygiene kits, validated beneficiary lists for 700 households, and prepared evacuation support for up to 2,000 households. In response to heightened landslide risks, Caritas Bangladesh and Save the Children activated anticipatory actions under the draft National Landslide Early Action Protocol. Save the Children provided BDT 6,000 per household to 400 high-risk households, in line with the 2026 ICCG-endorsed transfer value, while also supporting early warning dissemination and evacuation preparedness activities in Bandarban, Chattogram, and Rangamati districts. Islamic Relief Bangladesh allocated GBP 150,000 to support flood-affected communities, including GBP 50,000 dedicated to emergency response activities in the Banshkhali and Satkania upazilas of Chattogram District. The intervention is expected to reach approximately 700 households through multipurpose cash grants, hygiene and dignity kits, and protection messaging designed to address immediate humanitarian needs and enhance community awareness. Similarly, Dhaka Ahsania Mission (DAM), with support from Start Fund Bangladesh, plans to provide multipurpose cash grants of BDT 8,000 per household to 1,000 households in Chattogram District. Assistance will target 600 households in Baharchara, Chambol, and Chanua unions of Banshkhali Upazila and 400 households in Roypur and Bairag unions of Anowara Upazila, helping affected families meet their most urgent recovery and basic needs.

title: WFP Palestine Emergency Response External Situation Report #92, 14 July 2026 (Reporting period: 1-30 June 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

The UN Humanitarian Country Team has warned of the intensifying risks such expansion poses to civilians.

title: Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak: Democratic Republic of the Congo | Uganda Weekly External Situation Report 09, Data as of 12 July 2026
content:
Event description

The Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo intensified during the past week, with epidemiological indicators suggesting sustained and increasing transmission. The outbreak was characterized by a rising incidence of reported cases, increasing mortality and continued geographic expansion into additional provinces and health zones, indicating ongoing propagation across affected areas. Outside the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the epidemiological situation remained unchanged, with no new cases reported in Uganda or France and no evidence of secondary transmission. Nevertheless, continued geographic expansion and increasing transmission intensity within the Democratic Republic of the Congo elevate the likelihood of cross-border spread and reinforce the need for sustained regional surveillance, preparedness and response measures.

Democratic Republic of the Congo

Since the last update of 5 July 2026 (Situation Report #8), the epidemiological situation in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has further deteriorated with sustained transmission and continued geographic expansion. An additional 339 confirmed cases and 198 confirmed deaths have been reported, representing increases of 20.9% and 38.0% in cumulative confirmed cases and deaths, respectively. The crude case fatality ratio (CFR) among confirmed cases increased from 32.1% to 36.6%, likely reflecting delayed case detection, late presentation for care, and the persistently high proportion of deaths occurring in the community, rather than increased disease severity. Geographic spread also continued during the reporting period, with the outbreak expanding from three to five affected provinces following the confirmation of cases in Haut-Uélé and Tshopo provinces. The number of affected health zones increased from 36 to 42, with Wamba (Haut-Uélé Province), Ariwara and Boga (Ituri Province), and Lubunga, Makiso-Kisangani, and Mangobo (Tshopo Province) reporting their first confirmed cases.

Daily reported confirmed cases have continued to increase over the course of the outbreak, although substantial day-to-day variability is observed. A log-linear model fitted to the daily incidence data estimates an average daily growth rate of 2.3% (95% CI 2.0% - 2.5%), indicating that the outbreak continues to expand and transmission remains above the threshold required for sustained epidemic expansion.

Despite this continued geographic expansion, recent transmission remains concentrated in a subset of affected areas. Of the 42 affected health zones, 33 have reported at least one confirmed case within the past 21 days. During this period, 869 confirmed cases and 441 confirmed deaths were reported. Ituri Province continues to bear the overwhelming burden of the outbreak, accounting for 775 cases (89.2%) and 382 deaths (86.6%), while the remaining four affected provinces together reported 94 cases (10.8%) and 59 deaths (13.4%). In contrast, nine previously affected health zones have now surpassed 21 consecutive days without reporting a confirmed case, suggesting an absence of recent transmission while enhanced surveillance remains in place. These include Miti-Murhesa (53 days) in South Kivu Province; Aru (38 days), Aungba (23 days), and Gety (52 days) in Ituri Province; and Goma (48 days), Kalunguta (49 days), Mabalako (29 days), Oicha (26 days), and Vuhovi (31 days) in North Kivu Province.

The highest levels of recent transmission were recorded in Bunia (207 cases), Rwampara (159), Mongbwalu (92), and Nizi (80) in Ituri Province, reaffirming the Bunia–Rwampara–Mongbwalu transmission corridor while highlighting Nizi as an increasingly important hotspot. Transmission also intensified in Mangala (36 cases) and Nia-Nia (33), the latter serving as the epidemiological source of the newly affected provinces of Haut-Uélé and Tshopo. In North Kivu Province, Katwa (39 cases) remained the principal hotspot, followed by Butembo (16) and Beni (10). Collectively, these health zones accounted for 77.3% of all confirmed cases reported during the past 21 days.

A similar pattern was observed for mortality. Bunia reported the highest number of confirmed deaths (108), followed by Mongbwalu (71), Rwampara (52), Nizi (30), Katwa (28), Mangala (23), Nyankunde (14), Lita (13), Nia-Nia (11), Beni (8), and Butembo (7). Together, these health zones accounted for 365 (82.8%) of the 441 confirmed deaths reported during the same period.

he confirmation of cases in Haut-Uélé and Tshopo provinces marks a significant geographic expansion of the outbreak beyond its original focus in Ituri and North Kivu. Although relatively few cases have been reported in these newly affected provinces, the detection of cases in three health zones in Tshopo, including Makiso-Kisangani in the provincial capital, raises concern because of its large urban population and its role as a major transport hub connecting northeastern DRC with other parts of the country. Epidemiological investigations indicate that the cases in Tshopo and Haut-Uélé are linked to transmission originating in Nia-Nia Health Zone in Ituri, suggesting geographic extension of an existing transmission chain rather than the emergence of independent outbreak foci. The recent confirmation of the first case in Ariwara Health Zone represents a further northward expansion of the outbreak towards the borders with South Sudan and Uganda, increasing the potential for cross-border spread through frequent population movement and trade.

The expanding geographic footprint of the outbreak has also continued to pose risks beyond affected communities. During the reporting period, a United States humanitarian worker infected with Bundibugyo virus disease while working in the Democratic Republic of the Congo was medically evacuated to a specialized high-level isolation unit at Frankfurt University Hospital, Germany. The patient, a logistics staff member with a humanitarian organization supporting the Ebola response in Bunia, Ituri Province, was reported to be in stable condition following early diagnosis and treatment. The case highlights the continued occupational risk faced by frontline humanitarian personnel responding to the outbreak.

Since the beginning of the outbreak, the Democratic Republic of the Congo has reported 1963 confirmed cases, including 719 confirmed deaths (CFR 36.6%). Ituri Province remains the epicentre of the outbreak, accounting for 90.3% (1,772) of all confirmed cases and 84.6% (608) of all reported deaths nationwide. The most affected health zones continue to be Bunia (503 cases, 156 deaths), Rwampara (384 cases, 89 deaths), Mongbwalu (329 cases, 171 deaths), Nizi (110 cases, 36 deaths), Nyankunde (97 cases, 23 deaths), Mangala (50 cases, 29 deaths), and Lita (45 cases, 19 deaths), all located in Ituri Province, together with Katwa (71 cases, 47 deaths), Butembo (44 cases, 20 deaths), and Beni (30 cases, 20 deaths) in North Kivu Province. Collectively, these health zones account for approximately 84.7% of all confirmed cases and 84.8% of all confirmed deaths reported nationally.

Investigation of 430 confirmed deaths as of 05 July 2026 showed that 397 (92.3%) occurred in the community or before admission to a treatment facility, highlighting persistent delays in case detection, referral, isolation, and access to clinical care. Only 33 deaths (7.7%) occurred after patients had been admitted to treatment centres or healthcare facilities. During the current reporting period, 205 additional confirmed deaths were reported, including 139 (67.8%) community deaths and 66 (32.2%) deaths among patients admitted to treatment facilities, indicating that delayed presentation for care continues to contribute substantially to mortality.

As of 12 July 2026, a total of 12,370 contacts were under follow-up, of whom 10,156 (81.5%) were successfully seen within the previous 24 hours. Ituri Province accounted for the majority of contacts under follow-up, with 9,866 contacts, including 7,830 (79.4%) successfully seen during the reporting period. In North Kivu, 2,152 of 2,377 contacts (90.5%) were successfully followed up, while all contacts in South Kivu had completed the required 21-day monitoring period. Contact follow-up data for the newly affected provinces of Haut-Uélé and Tshopo were not reported. The overall follow-up rate remains below the operational target for effective contact tracing. The marked disparity between provinces is of particular concern. While North Kivu achieved a follow-up rate exceeding 90%, Ituri, the epicentre of the outbreak and home to more than 80% of contacts under follow-up, reached only 79.4%. This leaves a substantial number of contacts in the highest transmission setting unreached each day, increasing the risk of undetected infections and sustained community transmission.

title: UNICEF Côte d’Ivoire Humanitarian Situation Report No. 2, 1 April - 30 June 2026
content:
Highlights

  • As of May 2026, an estimated 85,630 refugees and asylum seekers, including 49,666 children, have fled to northern Côte d’Ivoire due to the worsening security situation in Burkina Faso and Mali. Since the beginning of 2026, 2,844 new arrivals have been registered.
  • On May 2026, strong winds and heavy rainfall affected the Bounkani region, impacting more than 120 households, 32 schools, 5 health centers and causing significant damage to homes and community infrastructure.
  • Between May and June 2026, more than 4,600 households were affected by eviction operations across several municipalities in Abidjan, generating significant humanitarian needs in the areas of shelter, food assistance, essential household items, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), and protection.
  • Côte d’Ivoire continues to face the mpox outbreak declared on 1 July 2024. To date, a total of 1,114 suspected cases have been identified, including 170 reported in 2026. Of these, 269 cases have been confirmed across 48 health districts, with three deaths reported among the confirmed cases.
  • During the second quarter of 2026, UNICEF continued to work closely with the Government of Côte d’Ivoire to meet humanitarian needs, including through the following interventions:
    • 1, 608 children under five were screened for wasting, and 352 severely malnourished children received treatment.
    • 23,810 children were vaccinated against measles in the two main regions (Tchologo and Bounkani) hosting refugees and asylum seekers.
    • 16,000 people, including 7,865 children, were provided with safe water for drinking and domestic needs, while 400 households were reached with hygiene and Kitchen set.
    • UNICEF supported the delivery of alternative early childhood education through the Preschool on Wednesdays and Saturdays (PréMS) programme, reaching 763 children, including 441 girls.

title: GEO: Flood - 07-2026 - Flash Flooding in Kakheti #2 (2026-07-14)
content:
Description

During the early hours of 12 July 2026, exceptionally heavy rainfall triggered flash floods and mudflows in Telavi Municipality, Kakheti Region. The Telaviskhevi River overflowed its banks after intense precipitation, causing widespread flooding across urban areas, significant damage to public infrastructure, residential buildings, businesses, and agricultural land. The event also generated large volumes of mud, rocks, and woody debris that overwhelmed sections of the river channel.

title: Sri Lanka Cyclone Ditwah 2025 - DREF Operational Update (MDRLK023), 14 July 2026
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event

28-11-2025

What happened, where and when?

A low-pressure system that developed over the southwest Bay of Bengal near Sri Lanka on 25 November 2025 rapidly intensified into a deep depression by 26 November 2025, bringing heavy rains and strong winds across the island. The Department of Meteorology, along with the Disaster Management Centre (DMC), issued early warnings as the system began to track north-northwestwards, positioning itself approximately 100 kilometres south of Sri Lanka's eastern coastline. On the morning of 27 November 2025, the Department of Meteorology escalated its alert to a "Red" Level Warning, the highest meteorological threat level as the deep depression intensified into Cyclonic Storm "Ditwah".

Cyclone Ditwah made landfall on the eastern coast of Sri Lanka on 28 November 2025, triggering what has since been described as the most extensive flooding and landslide damage the country has experienced in the past two decades. The storm's trajectory carried it across the Eastern, North-Central, Central, and Northwestern provinces, cutting through major population centres and historically vulnerable terrain, including Batticaloa, Polonnaruwa, Badulla, Kandy, and the central highlands. The cyclone brought exceptionally heavy rainfall, with several districts recording more than 200 mm within 24 hours and localised rainfall exceeding 500 mm in the worst-affected areas. These conditions precipitated widespread flooding, flash floods, and more than 200 landslides across the country in the immediate aftermath of the storm.

In response and based on the request of the Sri Lanka Red Cross Society (SLRCS), the IFRC launched an Emergency Appeal (EA) on 2 December 2025, with Secretariat funding of CHF 5 million for 18 months, targeting 500,000 people. Following the approval of a DREF allocation of CHF 1 million on 4 December 2025 to provide immediate life-saving and early recovery support to 268,180 people, the EA was revised on 5 January 2026 to reflect a 24-month timeframe, with a total funding requirement of CHF 12 million from the Secretariat and CHF 14 million Federation-wide, targeting 597,365 people, alongside an updated Operation Strategy outlining key sectoral interventions.

title: Yemen Floods 2024 - Final Report (MDRYE014)
content:
A. SITUATION ANALYSIS

Description of the crisis

During 2024, Yemen’s rainy season (April-June and July-September) were marked by unprecedented rainfall, resulting in severe flooding that caused widespread destruction and displacement. These floods further exacerbated Yemen’s already dire humanitarian situation, which is shaped by protracted conflict, recurrent disasters, and disease outbreaks.

Following the cessation of heavy rains in October-November 2024, no additional flooding was recorded, and no major changes happened in the situation on the ground were observed during the reporting period from November 2024 to June 2025. Consequently, the overall impact and figures remained unchanged. According to the Yemen Red Crescent Society (YRCS), more than 688,000 people across 98,300 households were affected by the floods, with 240 deaths and 635 injuries reported.

In total, 20 of Yemen’s 22 governates were affected, including Abyan, Ad Dali’, Al Bayada, Al Hodeidah, Al Jawf, Al Maharah, Al Mahwit, Amran, Dhamar, Hadramawt, Haijah, Ibb, Lahj, Ma’rib, Raymah, Sa’dah, Sana’a, Sana’s City, Shabwah and Ta’iz. Among these, Sa'dah, AJawf, Hajjah, Marib, Taiz, Al Hodaidah and Al Mahwit were the most severely affected. Overall, the floods resulted in the destruction or damage of more than 34,700 houses and shelters, including tents used by displaced populations. In addition, 126 health facilities were damaged, numerous water sources and roads were destroyed, livelihoods were disrupted, and approximately (99,000 hectares of agricultural land were submerged. Significant losses to livestock were also reported, further intensifying the already critical food security situation.

While no additional flooding was recorded after October–November 2024, the impacts of the floods occurred within one of the world’s most protracted humanitarian crises. Prolonged conflict, displacement, and recurring climate shocks have significantly eroded coping capacities, leaving millions of people unable to recover without assistance.

By mid-2025, the Yemen Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan estimated that 19.5 million people required humanitarian assistance, including 4.8 million internally displaced people, with persistent needs across health, WASH, food security, nutrition, and shelter/NFI, underscoring the sustained relevance of flood response and early recovery interventions in addressing both immediate flood-related impacts and underlying vulnerabilities.

title: WFP Tajikistan Country Brief, July 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• With support from the Russian Federation, WFP delivered 384.2 mt of food commodities to strengthen Tajikistan’s School Feeding Programme ahead of the new school year.

• WFP and the Government launched fortified wheat flour production in Kulob, strengthening national efforts to improve nutrition and reduce micronutrient deficiencies through locally produced fortified foods.

• Ahead of the Republic of Korea–Central Asia Summit, WFP showcased its partnership with KOICA to promote modern agriculture, youth empowerment and resilient rural livelihoods in Tajikistan.

title: WFP Burkina Faso Country Brief, June 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• In May, WFP assisted 278,373 people and distributed 2,809 mt of food assistance, reaching 90 percent of the planned assistance. School feeding and emergency food assistance recorded strong results, while nutrition treatment remained below target.

• In June, WFP demobilized its airlift fleet, including the Chinook helicopter, shifting to a cost-efficient, data-driven approach centered on road convoys and negotiated access.

• WFP launched the rainy season resilience package, supporting vulnerable communities with integrated resilience activities aimed at strengthening livelihoods, restoring productive assets, and enhancing climate adaptation ahead of the agricultural season.

• WFP continues an integrated response requiring USD 72 million for Jun–Nov 2026 to sustain operations and avoid further deterioration in food security.

title: Somalia — Emergency Trend Tracking Report — Week 04 (July 2026)
content:
DTM launched a new round of ETT on 14 June 2026 using an updated methodology to monitor displacement driven by conflict, as well as the climatic impacts of the El Niño phenomenon, which is expected to trigger significant displacement toward the end of the year. DTM teams collect data in five districts: Baidoa, Dayniile, Diinsoor, Doolow, and Kahda.

ETT is a crisis-based tool that tracks sudden displacement triggered by specific events or emerging crises. Its objective is to support the prioritization of humanitarian response and enable partners to deliver rapid assistance. It includes information on new arrivals, the number and demographics of IDPs, reasons for displacement, intentions, humanitarian assistance received, and priority needs, among others. Based on previous shock induced displacement patterns, the humanitarian community expects continued movement toward urban areas in search of services. Consequently, ETT coverage focuses on main urban centers and surrounding villages within each assessed district.

title: Attacks on Health Care in Sudan, 24 June - 07 July 2026
content:
Data from Insecurity Insight shows that since fighting started between the SAF and RSF in April 2023 and 09 June 2026 at least 768 incidents of violence against or obstruction of access to health care took place across Sudan:

  • Over two-thirds of these 768 attacks were attributed to the RSF
  • 213 health workers were killed, 15 kidnapped and 129 arrested
  • Health facilities were damaged 218 times

During the reporting period, 42 incidents affecting health care were reported in Nyala in South Darfur where a cholera outbreak was declared on 23 June 2026, following a period of ongoing insecurity. Health facilities were damaged on 13 occasions and four health workers killed and 30 were arrested. The cumulative impact of these incidents likely weakened the capacity of the local health system before the outbreak, reducing the availability of health infrastructure and personnel needed for clinical care, disease surveillance, and infection prevention and control. Protecting health facilities, health workers and patients is essential to ensuring an effective cholera response and safeguarding civilians' access to health care.
