title: Burundi: Monthly update - DRC Situation - June 2026
content:
Operational highlights

• The Governments of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Burundi, together with UNHCR, convened the second Tripartite Commission in Kinshasa (2-4 June 2026) to discuss the facilitated voluntary returns. Parties reaffirmed their commitment to ensuring that returns remain voluntary, safe and dignified, while agreeing to strengthen registration, intention surveys, cross-border coordination, sensitization, and resource mobilization to support return and reintegration efforts. The next tripartite meeting will be hosted by Burundi.

• The World Refugee Day was commemorated on 23 June in Bujumbura, providing an opportunity to also mark the 75th anniversary of the 1951 Refugee Convention. The event brought together government representatives, partners, donors and refugees to recognize the contributions, resilience and aspirations of refugee communities. Other events took place in the refugee-hosting areas during the reporting period.

• During the reporting period, the biometric registration exercise at Busuma was concluded. The total population in Busuma stands now at 54,343 refugees (Document - COMMUNIQUE CONJOINT - Achevement de l'enregistrement biometrique des refugies congolais sur le site de Busuma).

• The facilitated voluntary return to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) continued with 3,773 during the month, bringing the cumulative number of returnees to 8,233 since the operation began on 23 April 2026. Children accounted for more than 60 per cent of returnees, while women slightly outnumbered men.

• As of the reporting period, the Cishemere Transit Centre hosts 3,163 individuals (1,003 households), while the Makombe Transit Centre hosts 617 individuals (209 households). Humanitarian conditions in both transit centres remain challenging, with significant protection concerns and limited access to basic services.

title: Bangladesh Red Crescent Society Situation Report 3: Monsoon-Triggered Landslides and Flooding in Cox's Bazar, Bandarban, Chattogram, Rangamati, Khagrachari, Moulvibazar and Habiganj, Bangladesh (12 July 2026, 16:00 HRS)
content:
The emergency has now entered its second week and continues to widen in scope. While the low-pressure system that drove the initial spell of extreme rainfall has weakened and moved on over Uttar Pradesh, India, the Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD) continues to forecast heavy to very heavy rainfall in spells through 13 July across Chattogram, Sylhet, Rangpur, Rajshahi, Dhaka, Khulna and Barisal divisions. Flooding has spread to new areas, including a breach of the Dhalai river embankment in Kamalganj upazila, Moulvibazar, and rising river levels in Habiganj, while conditions have deteriorated in Satkania, Lohagara, Banshkhali and Chakaria. According to the latest consolidated figures, over 1 million people are now affected nationally across 10 districts, with more than 40 casualties recorded, around 36,500 people temporarily displaced, and more than 1,700 shelters activated.

BDRCS continues to monitor the situation through its central Emergency Operations Centre (EOC) and remains in close coordination with its district units, the Population Movement Operation (PMO) in Cox’s Bazar, district administrations, BMD, NAWG and other humanitarian partners. Confirmed funding from the American Red Cross Quick Action Fund, Initial response Fund supported by Swedish Red Cross, Locally Led Disaster Response Fund supported by British Red cross, and a pending IFRC DREF request are supporting an expanded response, with cash allocations now released to Nine district units and Chattogram City Unit. Further rounds of emergency water jerrycans and search-and-rescue items dispatched to twelve units, including newly affected north-eastern districts. Response efforts currently include volunteer mobilization, search and rescue support, public awareness campaigns, evacuation assistance, first aid, emergency food and cash assistance, and preparedness measures in high-risk communities.

title: VNM: Flood - 07-2026 - Flash Floods and Landslides in Northern Viet Nam #4 (2026-07-10)
content:
Description

Despite the weakening of Typhoon Maysak, its circulation, combined with prevailing weather conditions, has continued to bring heavy rainfall across northern Viet Nam, particularly affecting the mountainous provinces of Dien Bien, Lao Cai and Thai Nguyen. Continued rainfall has maintained the risk of flash floods, landslides and localised flooding, causing damage to housing, agriculture and critical infrastructure while disrupting transportation and local livelihoods. Authorities remain on high alert as additional rainfall is forecast over the coming days.

According to rapid reports from the Provincial Departments of Agriculture and Environment of Lai Chau, Dien Bien, Lao Cai, Son La, Tuyen Quang, and Thai Nguyen, heavy rainfall and landslides between the afternoon of 8 July and 9 July caused widespread damage to housing, agriculture and infrastructure. One person was injured in Son La Province after falling rocks struck a vehicle. Four houses were destroyed, 141 houses were damaged, 36 additional houses were affected by flooding and landslides, and 45 households were evacuated due to landslide risks.

Agricultural losses continued to increase, with approximately 243 hectares of rice fields, crops and other cultivated land flooded or damaged across six provinces. Floodwaters also killed or swept away 24 head of livestock and 350 poultry, primarily in Dien Bien and Thai Nguyen provinces.

Transportation infrastructure was significantly affected as landslides and flooding disrupted traffic at 17 locations along National Highways 6, 4H, 12, and 32, as well as at 75 locations on provincial roads across Lai Chau, Dien Bien, Lao Cai, and Son La provinces. Damage was also reported to irrigation infrastructure, with 137 metres of irrigation canals damaged in Dien Bien and Tuyen Quang provinces.

Preliminary economic losses have been estimated at approximately VND 14.99 billion (around CHF 490,000), with damage assessments continuing in Lai Chau Province.

title: ZMB: Epidemic - 07-2026 - Measles outbreak (2026-07-10)

title: Earthquakes in Venezuela: Situation Report #19 (12 July 2026, Time: 09:00 pm)
content:
Situation Report No. 19
Earthquakes in Venezuela
12 July 2026
Time: 9:00 pm

Highlights

  • Following the 24 June earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 (18:00 local time), authorities report more than 1,200 aftershocks.
  • Official toll: 4,490 people dead and 16,740 injured.
  • A total of 6,462 people have been rescued.
  • Tom Fletcher, the United Nations humanitarian chief, concluded his four-day visit to the country and called for sustained international support for the Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP).
  • An additional appeal for US$298 million was launched to scale up the earthquake response and address the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people over the next six months.
  • The United Nations system and its partner organizations, in coordination with the Government, are responding with multisectoral actions and will continue to scale up assistance to affected people.

Situation overview

Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre located along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). Authorities report 1,222 aftershocks.

Eighteen days after the earthquakes, authorities report a toll of 4,490 people dead, 16,740 injured and 6,462 rescued since the onset of the emergency. Authorities also indicated that 17,907 people remain without housing. According to official reports of 11 July, 315 of those who died have yet to be identified.

The Government response remains focused on search operations, the management of transitional camps and assistance to affected populations. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination with the authorities, continue implementing multisectoral response activities and scaling up assistance. United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher concluded his visit to Venezuela this week and called on the international community to sustain support for the humanitarian response. In this context, he announced a US$298 million addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan, aimed at addressing the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people over the next six months.

title: Tunisia: Flood 2026 - DREF Operational Update (MDRTN012)
content:
Description of the Event

19-01-2026

What happened, where and when?

In January 2026, Tunisia experienced exceptionally heavy and sustained rainfall that triggered widespread flooding, flash floods, and river overflows across large parts of the country. According to meteorological authorities, rainfall levels reached records not seen since the 1950s. Particularly intense precipitation on 19 and 20 January rapidly overwhelmed drainage systems and saturated soils, resulting in extensive damage to housing, critical infrastructure, and public services.

The floods caused five confirmed fatalities, while several individuals were reported missing during the emergency phase. Flood risks were further aggravated by increased flows in rivers originating from Algeria following the cyclone’s movement across the border, contributing to the scale and duration of the flooding.

The event affected 15 governorates across eastern and northern Tunisia, including Tunis, Ariana, Manouba, Ben Arous, Bizerte, Nabeul, Sousse, Monastir, Mahdia, Sfax, Béja, Jendouba, and Kef. Impacts were reported in urban, peri-urban, rural, coastal, and mountainous areas. Low-lying neighbourhoods, flood-prone settlements, and communities with inadequate drainage infrastructure were particularly affected. Flooded roads and inundated residential areas disrupted access to essential services, markets, and livelihoods, while some remote communities became temporarily isolated.

An estimated 25,000 people were affected nationwide, including households cut off by floodwaters. Continued rainfall on 20 and 21 January compounded the effects of already saturated ground conditions and increased the extent of flooding in several areas. By the end of January 2026, although water levels had gradually receded in most locations, significant humanitarian needs remained due to damage to homes, infrastructure, livelihoods, and basic services.
The scale of the impacts required continued response efforts and recovery support from national authorities and humanitarian partners.

title: BGD: Flood - 07-2026 - Situation Report-5, Monsoon Depression in Cox’s Bazar #4 (2026-07-10)
content:
Sources for data marked as Other

The well-marked low persists over Northwest Madhya Pradesh & adjoining area. It is very likely to move north-northwestwards and recurve northeastwards thereafter. Under its influence steep pressure gradient persists over North Bay and adjoining area. The axis of monsoon trough runs through Rajasthan, the center of the wellmarked low, Bihar, West Bengal to Assam across southern part of Bangladesh. Monsoon is active over Bangladesh and strong over North Bay. According to the Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD), active monsoon conditions are expected to continue until at least 11 July, with heavy to very heavy rainfall forecast across Cox's Bazar and the Chattogram Division. The five-day rainfall forecast indicates that very heavy rainfall (≥88 mm/day) is expected across several sub-districts of Cox’s Bazar between 9–12 July, with Ukhiya forecast to receive the highest and most persistent rainfall. Teknaf, Maheshkhali, Kutubdia, Ramu, Cox’s Bazar Sadar, and Chakaria are also expected to experience very heavy rainfall on multiple days. Rainfall is expected to decrease significantly across all sub-districts on 13 July, reducing light to moderate levels. The prolonged period of intense rainfall during 9–12 July may increase the risk of flash flooding, waterlogging, landslides, and localized disruptions, particularly in the highly affected areas. A BMD landslide warning forecasts 200–500 mm of rainfall between 9 and 11 July, maintaining a high landslide risk in Teknaf, Ukhiya, and Cox's Bazar Sadar. The Needs Assessment Working Group (NAWG) Anticipatory Impact Analysis continues to identify Cox's Bazar as highly vulnerable to flash flooding. Continued rainfall is expected to increase the risk of flooding, landslides, infrastructure damage, access constraints, and displacement. Humanitarian partners should maintain heightened preparedness, monitor weather advisories and high-risk locations, disseminate early warning messages, support relocations where necessary, and exercise caution during field movements.

Across the 33 Camps: Between 5 and 9 July 2026, a total of 304 weather-related incidents were reported, affecting 5,863 households (28,091 people) across the 33 camps. The incident caused damage to 3,127 shelters and displaced 4,732 individuals. To date, *15 fatalities and 18 injuries have been recorded. These figures underscore the significant humanitarian impact of the ongoing monsoon conditions and highlight the need for continued monitoring, preparedness, and response efforts, particularly in areas at heightened risk of flooding, water logging, and landslides. Additionally, 7 deaths (47%) have been reported within these camps due to landslide. Floodwaters have inundated 54 unions and 3 municipalities, affecting an estimated 80,000 people. During the past 24 hours, temporary flooding has also been reported across most parts of the district, disrupting mobility, communication, access to essential services, and daily livelihoods. To date, 6 fatalities have been reported in the host communities, including 4 deaths caused by landslides in Cox's Bazar Sadar and Chakaria, 1 death resulting from the collapse of a mud wall in Pekua Upazila, and 1 death caused by drowning in Maheshkhali. title: oPt: Humanitarian Situation Report | 10 July 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Across the Occupied Palestinian Territory, Israeli access restrictions, insecurity and funding shortfalls continue to constrain humanitarian operations.
  • In the West Bank, successive movement restrictions have effectively isolated approximately 12,000 Palestinians in communities west of Ramallah, where the transfer of a four-month-old Palestinian baby to hospital was delayed at an Israeli-staffed road gate. The infant was later pronounced dead at the hospital.
  • In 2026, over 3,200 Palestinians have been displaced across the West Bank by settler attacks and demolitions for lack of Israeli-issued building permits – an average of 17 people per day, double the daily rate over the preceding three years.
  • In Hebron's H2 area, Israeli forces installed a gate restricting one of the last remaining access routes to the Old City, further expanding an increasingly institutionalized system of movement restrictions affecting about 7,000 Palestinians.
  • In Gaza, with most people already displaced, new displacement along the “Yellow Line” continues amid ongoing military operations.
  • Aid work is increasingly exposed to insecurity and delays as external actors exploit humanitarian shipments to smuggle high-value items into Gaza, where the de facto authorities attempt to locate and confiscate them.
  • The number of families receiving shelter assistance in Gaza fell by 37 per cent from May to June due to funding shortfalls.

Overview

Across the Occupied Palestinian Territory (OPT), humanitarian space continues to shrink as insecurity, expanding movement and access restrictions, repeated displacement and funding shortfalls increase humanitarian needs while constraining humanitarian operations. In the Gaza Strip, military activity, expanding access-restricted areas and repeated displacement continue to expose civilians to heightened protection risks and deteriorating living conditions despite sustained humanitarian assistance. In the West Bank, expanding movement restrictions, Israeli forces' operations, demolitions, settlement expansion and recurrent settler violence are increasingly driving displacement, restricting access to essential services and livelihoods, and isolating Palestinian communities. Together, these developments are increasing humanitarian needs while making it more difficult for humanitarian partners to reach affected people and sustain assistance across the OPT.

title: BGD: Flood - 07-2026 - Situation Report-7, Monsoon Depression in Cox’s Bazar #6 (2026-07-12)
content:
Sources for data marked as Other

Overall Situation DATE: 12 JULY 2026 | TIME: 06:00 PM SITUATION REPORT-7, MONSOON DEPRESSION IN COX’S BAZAR Population Movement Operation Needs Assessment & Information Management Working Group Anticipatory Impact Analysis Mapping on Potential Flash Flooding in the Northeast and Hilly Areas in Chattogram Division as of 11 July 2026. According to the latest analysis by the Needs Assessment and Information Management Working Group (NAIM WG) and the Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD), Cox's Bazar remains among the districts at the highest risk of flash flooding. BMD forecasts indicate an additional 100–300 mm of rainfall through 12 July 2026, while elevated river water levels and saturated soil conditions continue to increase the likelihood of flash floods and landslides, particularly across the Chattogram Hill Tracts and Cox's Bazar District. The analysis estimates that approximately 139,081 people across all Upazilas of Cox's Bazar could be affected by flash floods, including 65,564 children, 73,512 adults, and 1,989 persons with disabilities. The risk of further landslides remains particularly high in Cox's Bazar Sadar, Ukhiya, and Teknaf due to persistent rainfall and unstable slope conditions. Within the Rohingya camps, where soil remain saturated following consecutive days of heavy rainfall and recent landslides, additional precipitation is expected to further increase the risk of flash floods, slope failures, and landslides, particularly in low-lying areas and settlements located on steep hillsides. Humanitarian operations may experience temporary access constraints due to inundated roads, damaged pathways, and collapsed retaining walls. Disruptions to WASH services, shelter conditions, and humanitarian supply chains may further increase the vulnerability of affected populations. The evolving situation underscores the importance of continued monitoring, timely dissemination of early warning messages, rapid damage and need assessments, preparedness for the temporary relocation of households from high-risk areas, and close coordination among humanitarian partners and government authorities. In the host communities, the Government of Bangladesh has continued its response by distributing cash assistance, rice, and dry food packages in affected areas while pre-positioning additional relief supplies to support ongoing emergency operations. However, continued rainfall and access constraints remain significant operational challenges, highlighting the need for sustained preparedness and humanitarian assistance in the coming days. Heavy to very heavy rainfall (44–88 mm or more per 24 hours) scenario is still likely at places over the Rangpur, Rajshahi, Mymensingh, Dhaka, Chattogram, and Sylhet divisions during the next 24 hours commencing from noon on 12 July 2026. Looking ahead, BMD/RIMES Integrated Forecast Dissemination Portal forecasts that from 12–16 July 2026, a gradual improvement in weather conditions across Cox's Bazar District may occur, with light to moderate rainfall expected in most upazilas. Amont these, Teknaf is expected to receive the highest rainfall, with up to 74 mm on 13 July, while rainfall elsewhere is expected to remain below critical thresholds. Although the overall rainfall intensity is projected to decrease, localized waterlogging and isolated flash flooding may still occur in lowlying areas, particularly on 13 July, warranting continued monitoring and preparedness.

Risk Analysis

Impact Across the 33 Camps Between 5 and 12 July 2026, a total of 473 weather-related incidents were reported, affecting 9,449 households (42,934 people) across the 33 camps. The incident caused damage to 4,334 shelters and displaced 9,707 individuals. To date, 15 fatalities and 20 injuries have been recorded. These figures underscore the significant humanitarian impact of the ongoing monsoon conditions and highlight the need for continued monitoring, preparedness, and response efforts, particularly in areas at heightened risk of flooding, waterlogging, and landslides. Impact on BDRCS Priority Camps In BDRCS Priority Camps (11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 17, 18, 19), approximately 163 incidents (34%) with 2,841 Households or 1,3666 Individuals (32%) are affected. These incidents have caused significant impacts to infrastructures inside the camp including 2,005 damaged shelters (46%), and 124 damaged WASH facilities (water points, latrines) which is 27% total. Additionally, 7 deaths (47%) have been reported within these camps due to landslides. Impact in Host Communities According to reports from the Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief (MoDMR) district and sub-district administrations, monsoon floods have inundated approximately 49% of the administrative jurisdictions across Cox's Bazar district, amongst them Pekua (95%), Matamuhuri (85%), and Chakaria (80%) sub-districts are the most sufferer. As of 12 July 2026, monsoon-related incidents have resulted in 15 fatalities, 19 injuries, and 1 missing person. A total of 2,566 people has been temporarily evacuated and are currently being accommodated in emergency evacuation centers. Preliminary damage assessments indicate that 1,195 houses have been affected. Critical infrastructure has also sustained significant damage, with 81 bridges and extensive sections of the road network affected across multiple upazilas, disrupting access and constraining response operations. Based on rapid assessments, the priority humanitarian needs include rice, cash assistance, dry food, and household kits. Continued rainfall, combined with damaged roads and transport infrastructure, continues to hamper humanitarian response efforts and is expected to delay early recovery activities. title: UNICEF Cameroon Cholera Outbreak Flash Update No. 1, 3 July 2026
content:
Overview

Historical data show that the Far North Region has experienced recurrent cholera outbreaks, with the largest outbreaks recorded in 2010 and 2011. Although recent outbreaks have been smaller in absolute numbers, the current 2026 outbreak is concerning because the case fatality rate of 6.76 per cent is higher than the rates recorded in 2024, 2022, 2019 and 2018, and is close to the high level observed during the major 2010 outbreak.

The current epidemic curve also shows a sharp rise in epidemiological week 26, underlining the need for rapid scaleup of surveillance, early case detection, timely referral and treatment, household disinfection, safe water interventions and community engagement.

Since 23 June 2026, several cases of acute watery diarrhoea (AWD) compatible with suspected cholera were reported in Fotokol, Mada, Makary and Kolofata health districts. Laboratory results confirmed the cholera outbreak in the Far North Region, with four culture-confirmed cases reported as of 29 June 2026. The outbreak is occurring in a cross-border context, with neighbouring Nigeria also affected by a cholera outbreak since May 2026.

The affected health areas are Amchide, Fotokol, Sagme, Bargaram, Hile-Alifa, Biamo and Makary. The cumulative attack rate is 11.84 cases per 100,000 population across the four affected districts. Mada has reported the highest number of cases, while Fotokol has the highest attack rate and case fatality rate.

title: Kyrgyzstan | Heat Wave - Early Action Protocol Activation Report (EAP2023KG02)
content:
IMPLEMENTATION OF PROJECT ACTIVITIES
Meteorological situation
The synoptic process that causes abnormal heat in Central Asia is called a summer thermal depression. This process is the formation of persistent high-pressure ridges (anticyclones) that block the movement of air masses, impede cloud formation, and cause warm air to descend, leading to severe overheating of the ground layer. According to long-term observations, the duration of a summer thermal depression in Central Asia ranges from 2-3 to 5-7 days, and in some years can last up to 1.5-2 weeks. In recent decades, global warming has been influencing the situation—the overall increase in average global temperature leads to more frequent and intense heat waves, which are becoming longer and more extreme. As in other areas of Central Asia, this process in Kyrgyzstan is characterized by the development of a high-altitude ridge, which intensifies the flow of hot tropical air from Iran and Afghanistan into Kyrgyzstan through Uzbekistan.

title: IOM Bangladesh Rohingya Humanitarian Crisis Response: Situation Report on Monsoon Landslides and Shelter Damage, Reporting Period: 5 - 7 July 2026 (48 hours)
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

Following prolonged and heavy monsoon rainfall across the Rohingya refugee camps in Cox's Bazar, two significant landslide incidents were reported during the early hours of 6 July 2026 in Camp 11 and Camp 15. According to information available at the time of reporting, the incidents resulted in reported fatalities, injuries, shelter damage, and the displacement of affected households. Reported casualty figures remain subject to verification and confirmation by the relevant Government of Bangladesh (GoB) authorities.

The incidents occurred following several days of sustained rainfall, which resulted in widespread soil saturation and increased landslide risk across the camps. Initial field observations suggest that prolonged rainfall and the resulting soil saturation were the primary contributing factors in both reported incidents. Site-specific conditions, including terrain, drainage, slope loading, and settlement patterns, are also being assessed as part of ongoing technical review.

Immediately following the incidents, IOM, together with the Camp-in-Charge (CIC), Disaster Management Unit (DMU) volunteers, Site Management Support (SMS) teams, Site Development engineers, the Bangladesh Fire Service and Civil Defense, community volunteers, and humanitarian partners, initiated search and rescue operations, emergency evacuations, shelter damage assessments, and immediate assistance to affected households. Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS), emergency shelter assistance, and relocation support were also activated for affected and at-risk families.

Beyond the two reported landslide incidents, continuous rainfall has caused widespread impacts across IOM's Areas of Responsibility (AoR). As of the reporting period, 1,066 shelter damage cases were reported, of which 802 were verified through rapid damage assessments. In addition, flooding affected the IOM-PHALS Soap Production Centre in Camp 20, damaging packaging materials and raw materials. No landslide has been reported at the facility; however, the site remains vulnerable due to its proximity to an adjacent hillside.

These incidents highlight the continued vulnerability of refugee settlements to monsoon-related hazards and reinforce the importance of sustained risk reduction measures. As a priority, IOM met with the RRRC and agreed on the compulsory relocation of extremely vulnerable families in areas of imminent landslide risk, in order to prevent further loss of life. Other priorities include technical assessment and stabilization of high-risk slopes, timely relocation of households in hazardous locations, strengthened community risk communication, improved drainage, and coordinated implementation of risk mitigation measures across sectors.

title: Situation Report No.5: Earthquakes in Venezuela 2026 (M7.2 and M7.5), 12 July 2026

  • The health response has transitioned from rapid damage assessments to restoring the continuity of essential health services. Functional constraints persist across the affected health network, particularly in La Guaira, where reduced hospital capacity continues to limit specialized care and increase pressure on referral pathways.
  • Recovery efforts are focused on restoring health system functionality through coordinated assessments, health facility recovery and Emergency Medical Team (EMT) support. Damage has been identified in 38 health facilities across the three most affected states, while Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) remains a priority need, particularly in La Guaira and temporary shelters**.**
  • PAHO/WHO is actively supporting the Ministry of Health (MPPS) in deployed seven Regional Response Team specialists covering health emergency coordination, logistics, information systems and media, epidemiology, risk communication and community engagement, EMT coordination, and rapid health facility assessment. In coordination with MoH, PAHO/WHO is supporting the virtual CICOM and EMT mobilization: Thirteen EMTs are operational in La Guaira, Caracas and Miranda and Aragua increasing clinical capacity in affected areas.
  • PAHO/WHO has locally distributed an initial 6 tons of supplies, delivering Trauma and Emergency Surgery Kits to 4 high-complexity hospitals and medication and equipment modules to 5 community health areas (ASIC) and a specialized clinic. A chartered plane (with ~27.5 metric tons of supplies) is now being coordinated, carrying Interagency Emergency Health Kits, additional surgery kits, and Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) treatment kits to further strengthen referral hospitals and primary care networks.

title: Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak: Democratic Republic of the Congo | Uganda Weekly External Situation Report 08, Data as of 05 July 2026
content:
Event description

The Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo continues to intensify, driven by sustained transmission in hotspot health zones of Ituri and North Kivu provinces. The outbreak is marked by growing numbers of community deaths, and the continued spread of infection into previously unaffected health zones. While Uganda has not reported any new confirmed cases during the past week, and the imported case reported in France has fully recovered without evidence of secondary transmission among identified contacts, the ongoing epidemic in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo continues to pose a significant regional and global public health threat.

Democratic Republic of the Congo

Compared with the previous update issued on 28 June 2026 (Situation Report #7), the epidemiological situation in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has deteriorated further. An additional 317 confirmed cases and 144 confirmed deaths have been reported, representing increases of 24.3% and 38.2%, in cumulative cases and deaths respectively. The crude case fatality ratio (CFR) rose from 28.8% to 32.1%. Geographic spread continues as the first confirmed case was detected in Lolwa health zone in Ituri Province, increasing the total number of affected health zones to 36.

Mabalako and Vuhovi health zones have now completed 21 consecutive days, without reporting a confirmed case and have been added to the list of areas with no recent transmission. However, Rimba Health Zone, which had previously gone 25 days without reporting a case, has now reported a new confirmed case. This brings the total number of previously affected health zones that have surpassed the 21-day threshold to eight. These include MitiMurhesa in South Kivu Province (46 days); Gety (45 days), Mambasa (33 days), and Aru (31 days) in Ituri Province; and Kalunguta (42 days), Goma (41 days), Vuhovi (24 days), and Mabalako (22 days) in North Kivu Province.

The outbreak remains active in 28 health zones across Ituri and North Kivu provinces that have reported confirmed cases within the past 21 days. During this period, 787 confirmed cases and 325 confirmed deaths were reported. Ituri Province continues to bear the overwhelming burden of the outbreak, accounting for 710 cases (90.2%) and 282 deaths (86.8%) across 21 active health zones. The remaining seven active health zones in North Kivu reported 77 cases (9.8%) and 43 deaths (13.2%).

The highest transmission was recorded in Bunia (237 cases), Rwampara (190 cases), Mongbwalu (103 cases), Nizi (62 cases), Nyankunde (51 cases), and Lita (24 cases) in Ituri Province. In North Kivu Province, Katwa (27 cases) and Butembo (21 cases) remained the main areas of transmission. Collectively, these health zones accounted for 90.9% of all confirmed cases reported during the past 21 days. A similar pattern was observed for mortality. Bunia reported the highest number of deaths (101), followed by Mongbwalu (66), Rwampara (45), Katwa (22), Nizi (18), Nyankunde (15), Lita (12), Mangala (11), and Butembo (11). Together, these health zones accounted for 92.6% of all confirmed deaths reported during the same period.

The crude CFR of the outbreak also increased over recent weeks. In Ituri Province, the CFR rose from 20.5% on 15 June to 29.7% on 05 July 2026, while North Kivu continued to record the highest provincial CFR, remaining above 56% throughout the reporting period. The largest increase in CFR was observed in Lita Health Zone (+36.4 percentage points), followed by Komanda (+22.1 percentage points), Nizi (+18.1 percentage points), and Bunia (+17.6 percentage points). These elevated CFRs likely reflect continued delays in case detection and healthcare-seeking behaviour, compounded by the persistently high proportion of deaths occurring in the community.

Since the beginning of the outbreak, the Democratic Republic of the Congo has reported 1624 confirmed cases, including 521 confirmed deaths (CFR 32.1%]. Ituri Province remains the epicentre of the outbreak, accounting for 90.9% (1477) of all confirmed cases and 84.3% (439) of all reported deaths nationwide. The most affected health zones are Bunia (452 cases, 121 deaths), Rwampara (349 cases, 72 deaths), Mongbwalu (288 cases, 149 deaths), Nyankunde (96 cases, 19 deaths), Nizi (78 cases, 19 deaths), Lita (33 cases, 12 deaths), and Mangala (33 cases, 14 deaths), all located in Ituri Province, as well as Katwa (52 cases, 38 deaths), Butembo (40 cases, 18 deaths), and Beni (29 cases, 17 deaths) in North Kivu Province. Together, these health zones account for nearly 89.3% of all confirmed cases and 91.9% of confirmed deaths reported nationally.

Investigation of 430 confirmed deaths as of 05 July 2026, showed that 397 (92.3%) occurred in the community or before admission to a treatment facility, highlighting persistent delays in case detection, referral, isolation, and access to clinical care. Only 33 deaths (7.7%) occurred after patients had been admitted to treatment centres or healthcare facilities.

As of 05 July 2026, a total of 12412 contacts were under follow-up of whom 9624 (77.5%) were successfully seen within the previous 24 hours. Ituri Province accounted for the majority of contacts under follow-up, with 9757 contacts, including 7574 (77.6%) seen during the reporting period. In North Kivu, 2050 out of 2655 contacts (77.2%) were followed up, while all contacts in South Kivu had completed the required 21-day monitoring period. Although contact tracing performance has improved overall, follow-up remains below optimal levels, leaving a significant proportion of contacts unreached and increasing the likelihood of undetected infections and continued transmission.

The proportion of new confirmed cases identified among registered contacts increased steadily as the outbreak progressed, exceeding 40% by late June 2026. Overall, 32.4% of confirmed cases were detected through contact follow-up. However, a substantial number of infections continued to occur outside known contact lists, indicating ongoing gaps in surveillance. These gaps are likely driven by insecurity in affected areas, population displacement and mobility, delayed case detection, community resistance, incomplete epidemiological investigations, and the movement of suspected cases and deceased individuals across affected areas.

content:
The tenth Situation Report provides an update on IOM’s response to the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela as of 9 July. It also includes the priorities of IOM’s Funding Appeal to scale up urgent assistance.

Highlights

In La Guaira, IOM and its partners strengthened assistance in transitory camps. At César Nieves Stadium, they continued improving spaces and distributed tarpaulins and kitchen sets, while at José María Vargas Sports Centre, services were expanded to include dental and psychiatric care, reaching 290 health and mental health consultations.

To date, IOM has reached 4,526 unique individuals through 7,273 assistance and distribution services, mainly in health, shelter and site coordination, and protection.

IOM maintains its USD 98 million Funding Appeal to assist 850,000 people and support 140 entities between July and December 2026.

IOM Activities

IOM continues supporting prioritized transitory camps in La Guaira, including César Nieves Stadium, José María Vargas Sports Centre and Playa Grande, through site coordination, shelter, registration, WASH, health and mental health, protection and information management.

At César Nieves Stadium, 341 tarpaulins and 334 kitchen sets were distributed. To date, 830 tarpaulins and 825 kitchen sets have been delivered.

At José María Vargas Sports Centre, a team of 12 professionals provided 290 health and mental health consultations, including dental care, internal medicine, paediatrics, gynaecology and obstetrics, psychiatry and psychology.

Registration continued at César Nieves Stadium, covering 489 families and 1,479 individuals, and at Playa Grande, covering 54 families and 160 individuals. Progress was also made on the Rapid Needs Assessment and on information management support to the Infrastructure and Temporary Accommodation Working Group.

IOM Planned Response

IOM will continue focusing on the improvement and management of transitory camps, WASH, health and MHPSS, protection, registration, needs assessments, mobility monitoring and inter-agency coordination.

Additional funding would enable IOM to scale up shelter assistance, essential items, early recovery, protection, health and mental health, data, DTM and coordination support.

title: Ebola Outbreak: Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda - External update #3 - 10 July 2026
content:
Highlights

• The seventeenth Ebola virus disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) continues to evolve, with 1,792 confirmed cases, including 625 deaths and 295 recoveries, reported across 37 health zones in Ituri, North Kivu and South Kivu as of 8 July. The Government has also reported two confirmed cases in Kisangani, Tshopo Province.

• The outbreak is unfolding in an area marked by persistent insecurity and displacement due to armed clashes, limiting humanitarian access and complicating Ebola prevention, surveillance and response. Ituri remains the epicentre, accounting for 91 per cent of confirmed cases and nearly 86 per cent of deaths.

• While no Ebola cases have been reported among refugees in the DRC to date, 19 internally displaced persons (IDPs) from the Kpangba, Kigonze and Bembeyi sites in Ituri are among confirmed cases. More than 2 million forcibly displaced people live in Ebola-affected or high-risk areas of eastern DRC, including 320,000 refugees and asylum-seekers, heightening the urgency of inclusive preparedness, risk communication, surveillance and access to national response systems.

• In Uganda, the outbreak remains relatively contained, with 20 confirmed cases as of 9 July, including two deaths, 17 recoveries and one patient currently admitted for care.

• UNHCR is supporting the Governments of the DRC and Uganda, alongside the World Health Organization (WHO), other United Nations agencies and local communities, to strengthen Ebola prevention and response and ensure that refugees, asylum-seekers, IDPs and host communities can access information, surveillance and essential services.

title: Central African Republic: Situation Report No. 75, as of 7 July, 2026
crisis: Central African Republic: Cholera Outbreak - Jun 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • Critical humanitarian situation in Am-Dafock following recent clashes
  • Heavy rains cause human and property damage in Ngaoundaye
  • Rafaï: More than 300 displaced and other vulnerable families receive livestock and poultry

GENERAL CONTEXT

Haut-Mbomou Prefecture – South-East

  • More than 1,000 people have fled from Zemio to Zapaï in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) out of fear for their safety, following the killing on 27 July of a religious leader who had been actively involved in community reconciliation efforts in the area. An unknown number of residents have also undertaken preventive displacement within Zemio town since the end of June, driven by fears of possible clashes between parties to the conflict. Communities are additionally living in fear of reprisals over alleged collaboration with one or another party to the conflict, limiting opportunities for community engagement activities. Furthermore, a local authority was killed by armed men on 5 July along the Dembia axis, while businesses in Zemio town were robbed, further exacerbating the climate of fear affecting the population.

HUMANITARIAN NEEDS AND RESPONSE

Vakaga Prefecture – North-East

  • On 2 July, humanitarian partners conducted a rapid humanitarian assessment in Am-Dafock, along the border with Sudan, with logistical support from MINUSCA, following the clashes that occurred in the town on 30 June. The assessment found that the humanitarian situation remains critical, with the most urgent needs relating to protection, health care and access to safe drinking water. The town’s only health facility had been looted and was occupied by armed elements at the time of the assessment. The only accessible water point is insufficient to meet the needs of the affected population. In addition, displaced people are unable to leave the site because of security concerns. A MINUSCA helicopter rotation on 4 July enabled the delivery of emergency assistance provided by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), International Medical Corps (IMC), the Central African Red Cross and an international orgnaization. The assistance included 425 tarpaulins, 680 buckets, medicines and hospital consumables, personal protective equipment and body bags. IMC is currently operating mobile clinics in Am-Dafock and has already provided essential health services to at least 140 people. However, logistical constraints continue to hamper the scale-up of the humanitarian response, as the main access road has become impassable during the ongoing rainy season. Approximately 24 metric tons of humanitarian cargo remain to be transported, including protection supplies, first-aid kits, soap, gloves and protective masks. With an estimated airlift capacity of two metric tons per helicopter rotation, at least 12 additional rotations will be required to deliver all pending relief items. Consequently, delays in the delivery of humanitarian assistance are expected, which could affect the timely provision of life-saving aid to affected populations.

Food Security

Nana-Gribizi Prefecture – Center

  • From 22 June to 3 July, Welthungerhilfe (WHH) conducted an agricultural entrepreneurship training program for 230 members from 11 agricultural groups, including 142 women and 88 men. Participants strengthened their skills in business management, planning, marketing, and the organization of agricultural activities. In addition, 37 members of two pastoral groups, including 26 women, received training on good livestock management practices, with a focus on animal nutrition, animal health, and reproduction. To further improve agricultural production practices, 166 lead farmers and technical focal points were trained in Kaga-Bandoro, Ouandago, and Mbrès. The training sessions covered good agricultural practices as well as crop-specific technical production packages tailored to several priority crops.

title: Venezuela Earthquakes: Situation Report #6 (July 9, 2026)
content:
Project HOPE is steadily expanding its earthquake response across northern Venezuela, shifting more attention to urgent health needs and the prevention of subsequent public health crises. The team has increased the reach of mobile medical teams; reinforced primary health facilities; broadened water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) efforts; and is expanding mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) to assist additional earthquake-affected communities. Preventing disease outbreaks and maintaining consistent access to care remain central priorities as thousands of people navigate uncertainty while living in temporary settlements or damaged neighborhoods.

Situation Overview

Humanitarian needs remain significant as response efforts continue. The death toll has been reported at over 3,800, with over 16,700 injuries, and approximately 17,800 displaced and/or homeless people. While debris removal and structural assessments are progressing, thousands of people remain affected and require humanitarian assistance. Health partners remain concerned about deteriorating sanitation conditions, limited access to clean water, and disruptions to routine healthcare, all of which increase the risk of secondary public health emergencies. Project HOPE’s teams continue to report increased cases of diarrheal disease, skin infections, urinary tract infections, dehydration, and respiratory illnesses, with mental health needs remaining high among families coping with displacement and uncertainty. Rainfall and overcrowded shelters are also creating favorable conditions for the spread of infectious diseases, reinforcing the importance of disease surveillance and WASH interventions.

title: Multi-Country Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease Outbreak Situation Report No. 8 (29 June - 5 July 2026)
content:
According to the World Health Organization, as of 4 July, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has confirmed more than 1,500 cases of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus (BVD). As of 5 July, Uganda has confirmed 20 cases, with no new cases during the reporting period.

Cross-border movements, displacement and population mobility are shaping disease transmission, requiring an urgent and rapid response to save lives and protect people on the move, while mitigating regional health risks. Given the unfolding public health risks, IOM’s preparedness and response efforts focus on supporting cross-border communities, points of entry (PoEs) and points of control (PoCs) to inform and guide broader public health interventions.

In line with the Inter-Agency Standing Committee (IASC) system-wide scale-up activation for infectious disease events, IOM is scaling up its response, enabling enhanced surge support, operational capacity and coordination across affected countries.
IOM’s response continues to focus on Priority 1a countries, DRC and Uganda, where active outbreak response operations are ongoing, and Priority 1b countries, Burundi, Rwanda and South Sudan, which face an elevated risk of cross-border transmission.
Preparedness interventions are also being implemented in other at-risk countries across the region, including Priority 2 countries,
Angola, the Central African Republic, Ethiopia, Kenya, the Republic of the Congo, the United Republic of Tanzania and Zambia, to strengthen readiness and enhance regional health security, while supporting continent-wide efforts, particularly as co-lead of the PoE technical working group at the continental level.

title: Vanuatu Dengue Outbreak Situation Report #6 (South-West Efate, Shefa Province)
content:
Key highlights include:

  • Nine new laboratory-confirmed dengue cases were reported during Epidemiological Week (EW) 27, bringing the cumulative total to 38 confirmed cases.
  • Weekly case numbers remain above the outbreak alert threshold of four cases per week, indicating ongoing dengue virus transmission.
  • Six cases (15.8%) have required hospitalization since the outbreak began. Of these, one patient remains hospitalized, while five have recovered and been discharged.
  • No dengue-related deaths have been reported to date.
  • The most affected locations are:
    • Pango Area Council – 34% of cases
    • Eratap Area Council – 21% of cases
  • Additional cases have been reported from Erakor, Eton, Port Vila, and Mele, indicating a widening geographic spread.
  • Males account for 55% of reported cases, and 64% of cases have occurred among individuals under 26 years of age.
  • Epidemiological investigations continue to identify evidence of local transmission.
  • Laboratory testing has confirmed the circulating strain as Dengue Virus Type 1 (DENV-1). All five samples tested were identified as DENV-1.
  • There has been no significant change in the outbreak situation since the previous report. Therefore, the outbreak status remains unchanged, and enhanced surveillance and response measures continue.

title: UNHCR Facilitated Return of Syrian Refugees - Lebanon, 30 June 2026
content: Since the escalation of hostilities on 2 March 2026, and until 30 June, the Syrian General Authority for Border and Customs (GABC) estimates that 581,409 Syrians crossed from Lebanon into Syria, while the Lebanese General Security (GSO) estimates that 491,265 Syrians departed through Ocial Crossing Points (OCPs) between 2 March and 26 June. While some movements to Syria were driven by the conflict in Lebanon, others reflect previously planned movements. Syrians crossing include people known, and not known to UNHCR, namely both refugees and Syrians who have stayed in Lebanon under various visa and sponsorship arrangements or returning from temporary visits. During June, a slight increase was observed in daily movement to Syria, with over 4,500 Syrians crossing per day through OCPs, mainly due to the end of the school academic year and the start of the summer season. As of the end of June 2026, only 6% (29,054 individuals) of Syrians who left Lebanon through the OCPs, based on GSO and UNHCR Syria data*, have so far been verified to be known to UNHCR**. Further verification, data collection and triangulation are ongoing.

title: Middle East Situation Lebanon - Flash Update #14 (22 June - 05 July 2026)
content:
• As of 6 July, almost 500,000 individuals remain internally displaced within Lebanon, as many families are unable to return to their home areas due to inaccessibility, destruction or continued insecurity.

• Protection monitoring shows a shift from large-scale displacement towards more complex return and local integration dynamics. While the overall number of displaced people is declining, those who remain displaced are facing growing challenges, including difficulty accessing adequate housing, worsening economic conditions, increased protection risks for women and children, and weakened social cohesion within communities.

• Returns to conflict-affected areas in Lebanon are taking place more quickly among Lebanese internally displaced persons (IDPs) than among displaced refugees. For Syrian refugees, returns to the South remain limited due to a mix of protection, legal, housing, and economic barriers. Rising rental costs, limited availability of affordable housing, unpaid rent debts, and, in some areas, additional municipal requirements continue to make access to housing and durable solutions more difficult.

title: Earthquakes in Venezuela: Situation Report #16 (09 July 2026, Time: 09:00 pm)
content:
Situation Report No. 16
Earthquakes in Venezuela
09 July 2026
Time: 9:00 pm

Highlights

  • Following the 24 June earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 (18:00 local time), authorities report more than 1,100 aftershocks.
  • Official toll: 3,889 people dead and 16,740 injured.
  • A total of 6,462 people have been rescued.
  • Tom Fletcher, the United Nations' humanitarian chief, met with national
    and international humanitarian organizations supporting the earthquake response.
  • An additional appeal for US$298 million was launched to scale up the earthquake response and address the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people over the next six months.
  • The United Nations system and its partner organizations, in coordination with the Government, are responding with multisectoral actions and will continue to scale up assistance to affected people.

Situation overview

Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre located along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). Authorities report 1,142 aftershocks.

More than a week after the earthquakes, authorities report a toll of 3,889 people dead, 16,740 injured, and 6,462 rescued since the onset of the emergency. Authorities also reported that approximately 17,907 people lost their homes.

The Government response remains focused on search and rescue operations, the preparation and expansion of transitional camps and assistance to affected populations. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination with the authorities, are implementing multisectoral response activities and will continue to scale up assistance to affected people. United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher continued his visit to Venezuela. He met with national and international organizations, as well as other counterparts, to strengthen joint efforts with the sole objective of supporting those most in need.

title: Afghanistan: Weekly Market Report: Issue 302: Week 1 – July 2026
content:
Key Highlights

Exchange Rate and Trade Dynamics:

• Exchange Rate: During the first week of July, the Afghani depreciated to AFN 65.7/USD, weakening by 1.7% compared to the previous week. Despite this decline, the currency remained 5% stronger than last year and 13% stronger than the three-year average, continuing to provide some support in containing imported inflation.

• Trade: Market supply remained generally adequate, supported by domestic harvests and ongoing regional trade. However, Afghanistan's dependence on imported goods continues to expose domestic markets to fluctuations in the exchange rate, fuel costs, and regional trade conditions, which contribute to price volatility across the country and expose the economy to external vulnerabilities.

Food Items:

• National average food prices showed divergent trends during the first week of July, with modest weekly changes across most staples.

• Wheat and Flour: Wheat grain prices rose marginally this week, while high-price and low-price flour also recorded moderate increases. On an annual basis, wheat grain (+13%), high-price flour (+7%), and low-price flour (+11%) remained elevated, mainly due to higher transportation costs associated with renewed import routes.

• Rice: Both rice categories declined slightly this week. Despite these weekly decreases, rice prices remained significantly higher than last year (high-quality +27%; low-quality +34%) and above the three-year average level.

• Other Staples: Cooking oil, pulses, sugar and salt prices edged down this week. Sugar posted a notable weekly drop, though it remained above last year's levels (+9%). Cooking oil prices held steady, staying negligibly above last year (+2%). Salt declined weekly but remained higher year-on-year (+8%).

• Vegetables: Seasonal harvests continued to support domestic vegetable markets with slight weekly fluctuations. Compared to the previous week, tomato (+2.3%) and onion (+2.5%) prices rose slightly, while potato prices remained broadly stable (-0.6%). Compared to last year and the three-year average, potato and tomato prices remains significantly higher, while onion prices have declined.

Non-Food Items:

• Fuel: Diesel prices rose by 7.2% during the week, mainly reflecting reduced fuel imports, particularly from Russia. Compared to last year and the three-year average, diesel prices remained 9% and 12% higher, respectively.

• Fertilizers: Fertilizer prices changed only marginally, with DAP declining by 0.2% and Urea by 1.4% over the week. Compared to last year, DAP and Urea prices remained considerably higher (+17% and +49%, respectively), while improved seed and animal feed prices continued to remain below both last year and the three-year average.

• Livestock: The price of a one-year-old live female sheep declined marginally (-0.4%) during the week and was 5% below last year's level and 2% below the three-year average, contributing to slightly weaker pastoralist ToT.

Labour Market:

• Labour market conditions remained subdued. The unskilled labour wage declined marginally (-0.5%), while labour availability remains low at 1.9 days per week. Labour availability remained 18% below both last year's level and the three-year average, underscoring continued pressure on household income opportunities for casual labourers

title: UNFPA Situation Report: Lebanon Crisis (23 June - 7 July 2026)
content:
The humanitarian situation in Lebanon remains fragile despite a reduction in hostilities, with significant and persistent humanitarian, protection, and early recovery needs. Daily airstrikes and military operations, particularly in southern Lebanon, continue to pose risks to civilians and limit safe returns, highlighting the potential for renewed escalation despite ongoing diplomatic efforts. Since 2 March 2026, a reported 4,304 people have been killed and 12,203 have been injured.

Women and girls are bearing the brunt of the crisis, facing heightened protection and gender-based violence (GBV) risks, disrupted health services, including for maternal health, and reduced access to safe and dignified support.

Since the onset of the crisis, UNFPA has reached over 150,000 displaced people with sexual and reproductive health and GBV services. These services have been delivered through support to 55 health facilities, nine mobile medical units, 24 mobile GBV teams, and 19 women and girls’ safe spaces, serving collective shelters and host communities.

UNFPA launched a revised Flash Appeal in June, aligned with the revised Inter-Agency Lebanon Flash Appeal appealing for US $25 million to meet the urgent needs of 450,000 people from March to August 2026. To date, only 16 per cent of the required funding has been secured.

title: Bangladesh Red Crescent Society Situation Report 2: Monsoon-triggered landslides and flooding in Cox's Bazar, Bandarban and Chattogram, Bangladesh (9 July 2026, 16:00 HRS)
content: The situation has continued to deteriorate following persistent heavy rainfall, resulting in widespread flooding, landslides, casualties, displacement and damage to households, infrastructure and livelihoods. According to the latest Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD) forecast, heavy to very heavy rainfall is expected to continue through 11 July 2026, maintaining a high risk of additional flooding and landslides across the southeastern region. BDRCS continuously monitoring the situation through its central Emergency Operations Centre (EOC) and continues to coordinate closely with its district units, the Population Movement Operation (PMO) in Cox’s Bazar, district administrations, the Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD) and other humanitarian partners. title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #9 (8 July 2026)
content:
The ninth Situation Report provides an update on IOM’s response to the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela as of 8 July. It also includes IOM’s Flash Appeal funding priorities to scale up urgent assistance.

Highlights

IOM launched a USD 98 million Appeal to assist 850,000 people and 140 entities between July and December 2026, prioritizing shelter, early recovery, health, WASH, protection, data, DTM and coordination.

At César Nieves Stadium, registration resumed, with 20 new families registered, bringing the total to 482 families, or 1,479 people. At José María Vargas Sports Complex, IOM’s Emergency Medical Team provided 132 health and mental health consultations.

To date, IOM has reached 4,011 unique individuals with 6,713 assistance and distribution services, mainly in health, shelter and protection.

IOM activities

IOM continues supporting prioritized transitory camps in La Guaira, including César Nieves Stadium, José María Vargas Sports Complex and Playa Grande, with site coordination, registration, WASH, protection, health and inter-agency coordination.

At César Nieves Stadium, registration and food distribution coordination continued, while WASH improvements advanced through toilet signage by sex and shower installation. At José María Vargas Sports Complex, 132 medical and MHPSS consultations were provided.

Protection activities included six cases assisted through protection triage, PSEA sensitization, psychosocial support, SEA risk analysis and placement of PSEA information materials in key camp areas.

Six humanitarian cargo flights have been mobilized to date, including five sent by DHR of the Government of the United States in coordination with IOM, and one flight with IOM supplies from Panama, supported by DHL.

IOM planned response

IOM will continue focusing on site coordination and management, registration, WASH, health and Mental Health, protection, data collection, DTM and inter-agency coordination in prioritized transitory camps and affected communities.

Additional funding through IOM’s USD 98 million Appeal would enable the scale-up of emergency shelter assistance, core relief items, early recovery support, protection services, health and mental health care, mobility monitoring and information management.

title: VNM: Flood - 07-2026 - Flash Floods and Landslides in Northern Viet Nam #3 (2026-07-09)
content:
Description

Despite the weakening of Typhoon Maysak, its circulation, combined with prevailing weather conditions, has continued to bring heavy rainfall to the northern mountainous provinces of Viet Nam, increasing the risk of flash floods, landslides and localised flooding.

According to the Vietnam Disaster and Dyke Management Authority (VDDMA), heavy rainfall is expected to continue across parts of the northern mountainous region over the coming days. Local authorities have been instructed to maintain 24-hour duty rosters, closely monitor weather developments, and continue preparedness and response activities, while central and Central Highlands provinces strengthen preparedness measures ahead of the peak disaster season.

According to rapid reports from the Departments of Agriculture and Environment of Lai Chau and Dien Bien provinces, heavy rainfall and landslides that occurred between 7 and 8 July 2026 caused significant damage to housing, agriculture, and transportation infrastructure. In Lai Chau Province, three houses were destroyed, 18 houses were damaged by landslides and five additional houses were affected. In Dien Bien Province, six houses were damaged by landslides and three additional houses were affected. Agricultural losses in Lai Chau included damage to 40.5 hectares of rice fields and crops, the loss of 17 livestock and 0.76 hectares of fishponds washed away.

Transportation infrastructure was also significantly affected. Landslides and road damage disrupted traffic along National Highway 279 in Dien Bien Province, National Highway 4D in Lai Chau Province, as well as several provincial, inter-commune and village roads in both provinces. Local authorities immediately mobilised personnel and heavy equipment to clear landslides, restore road access and assist affected households with early recovery activities.

Separately, a whirlwind lasting approximately 15 minutes struck Binh Thanh Commune, Hung Yen Province, on the afternoon of 8 July, damaging tiled and metal roofs of several houses. Affected households have started repairing the damage using their own resources.

Weather forecasts indicate that heavy rainfall may continue across the northern mountainous region, increasing the risk of additional flash floods, landslides and localized flooding. Authorities continue to monitor the situation closely while conducting damage assessments and preparedness activities in areas at risk.

title: BGD: Flood - 07-2026 - Situation Report-4, Monsoon depression in Cox’s Bazar (2026-07-09)
content:
Sources for data marked as Other

The well-marked low persists over Northwest Madhya Pradesh & adjoining area. It is very likely to move north-northwestwards and recurve northeastwards thereafter. Under its influence steep pressure gradient persists over North Bay and adjoining area. The axis of monsoon trough runs through Rajasthan, the center of the wellmarked low, Bihar, West Bengal to Assam across southern part of Bangladesh. Monsoon is active over Bangladesh and strong over North Bay. According to the Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD), active monsoon conditions are expected to continue until at least 11 July, with heavy to very heavy rainfall forecast across Cox's Bazar and the Chattogram Division. The five-day rainfall forecast indicates that very heavy rainfall (≥88 mm/day) is expected across several sub-districts of Cox’s Bazar between 9–12 July, with Ukhiya forecast to receive the highest and most persistent rainfall. Teknaf, Maheshkhali, Kutubdia, Ramu, Cox’s Bazar Sadar, and Chakaria are also expected to experience very heavy rainfall on multiple days. Rainfall is expected to decrease significantly across all sub-districts on 13 July, reducing light to moderate levels. The prolonged period of intense rainfall during 9–12 July may increase the risk of flash flooding, waterlogging, landslides, and localized disruptions, particularly in the highly affected areas. A BMD landslide warning forecasts 200–500 mm of rainfall between 9 and 11 July, maintaining a high landslide risk in Teknaf, Ukhiya, and Cox's Bazar Sadar. The Needs Assessment Working Group (NAWG) Anticipatory Impact Analysis continues to identify Cox's Bazar as highly vulnerable to flash flooding. Continued rainfall is expected to increase the risk of flooding, landslides, infrastructure damage, access constraints, and displacement. Humanitarian partners should maintain heightened preparedness, monitor weather advisories and high-risk locations, disseminate early warning messages, support relocations where necessary, and exercise caution during field movements.

Risk Analysis

Across the 33 Camps: Between 5 and 9 July 2026, a total of 304 weather-related incidents were reported, affecting 5,863 households (28,091 people) across the 33 camps. The incident caused damage to 3,127 shelters and displaced 4,732 individuals. To date, *15 fatalities and 18 injuries have been recorded. These figures underscore the significant humanitarian impact of the ongoing monsoon conditions and highlight the need for continued monitoring, preparedness, and response efforts, particularly in areas at heightened risk of flooding, water logging, and landslides. Impact on BDRCS Priority Camps: In BDRCS Priority Camps (11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 17, 18, 19), approximately 109 incidents (36%) with 1,896 Households or 9,241 Individuals (30%) are affected. These incidents have caused significant impacts to infrastructures inside the camp including 1,466 damaged shelters (47%), and 59 damaged WASH facilities (water points, latrines) which is 29% total. Additionally, 7 deaths (47%) have been reported within these camps due to landslide. Impact on BDRCS Priority Camps Remarks: The % reflected above are computed in reference to the total data reported per category (e.g. incident, population, shelter, etc.) across the 33 camps. Host Communities Persistent heavy rainfall has significantly exacerbated flooding across Cox's Bazar District, with Chakaria, Pekua, Matamuhuri, Maheshkhali, Ramu, and Teknaf among the worst-affected areas. Floodwaters have inundated 54 unions and 3 municipalities, affecting an estimated 80,000 people. During the past 24 hours, temporary flooding has also been reported across most parts of the district, disrupting mobility, communication, access to essential services, and daily livelihoods. To date, 6 fatalities have been reported in the host communities, including 4 deaths caused by landslides in Cox's Bazar Sadar and Chakaria, 1 death resulting from the collapse of a mud wall in Pekua Upazila, and 1 death caused by drowning in Maheshkhali. The evolving situation continues to place both refugee and host communities at heightened risk as heavy rainfall persists.

title: Georgia Pluvial/Flash Flood in Eastern Georgia 2025 - DREF Final Report (MDRGE020)
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event

01-10-2025

What happened, where and when?

At the end of September 2025, heavy and prolonged rainfall struck eastern Georgia, with Lagodekhi Municipality in Kakheti, experiencing the most severe impact. Rising river levels and overflows triggered flash floods across at least 13 villages, including Kabali, Ninighori, Giorgeti, Tsodniskari, and nearby communities. Floodwater damaged ground floors of the residential houses, courtyards, and farmland, destroying household belongings, food stocks, and agricultural inputs. Several road sections were submerged, restricting mobility and access to essential services for several days. As the municipal authorities started with infrastructure rebuilding and accounting for overall scope of the disaster, GRCS engaged in the response by mobilizing staff and volunteers from Lagodekhi and neighboring branches to conduct rapid needs assessment and plan for targeted assistance as per official request of the municipal authorities.
